chapters.title: Chapter 701: Beyond the Elders’ Reach
paragraphs: The gateway opened on a wet morning, and Elder Shan could not enter it.

Leon watched from beside the repaired terraces as Shan approached the inner threshold. Pale light filled the opening that had remained sealed throughout their earlier ordeal. Rain ran down the stone above it and dripped onto Shan’s shoulder.
He stepped forward, stopped, and looked back at Ruan.
"The same response," she said, checking her instruments.

Shan concealed his cultivation and tried again. The threshold remained closed to him, though the light beyond it continued moving. Ruan added her concealment array for the final test, with no better result.
Then Ji approached.
She rested her hand against the boundary, waited, and withdrew it.
"Enough," she said. "Nobody applies force."

The true Grotto-Heaven had become accessible at the three-month mark from Ruan’s initial assessment. Its entrance complex still admitted everyone standing there. Beyond the inner threshold, however, the newly opened realm refused the strongest people in the gathering.
Leon looked from his master to the waiting disciples.
He had known this might happen. Seeing Ji step aside made it feel rather different.
The eligible personnel waited while Ruan completed the nonliving tests.

Probes crossed and returned without damage. A weighted marker came back on its retrieval line, followed by a recording plaque showing pale stone under steady light. Ruan compared each result against the measurements she had taken before the opening.
Only when she was satisfied did two Golden Core scouts approach.
They crossed with instructions to remain close to the gate. One returned almost immediately; the other stayed within sight of the boundary to test the communication link.
His voice emerged clearly from Ruan’s plaque.
"Solid ground. No immediate movement. Returning to the marker now."
They repeated the exchange at different distances. Ruan sent an instruction the scout could not have anticipated, received his reply, and had him bring the recording back for comparison.
An eligible Foundation Establishment disciple completed the same short crossing afterward.
"Golden Core and below," Ruan confirmed. "The threshold responds to the cultivation structure. Concealing the aura doesn’t change what it admits."

Leon studied the quiet opening. His native foundation was well below the limit, and the older foundation that produced his public reading was still within it. Nothing in the tests suggested the gate cared how much damage a person could cause after crossing.
Seraphine waited beside the others with her sword wrapped. He caught her looking toward the light, then toward the scouts’ recording equipment.
She wanted to see it too.
Ji called the expedition together beneath the shelter at the foot of the terraces.
"The elders remain outside," she said. "We hold the complex and the basin perimeter. Inside, Leon commands the gathering team."
The disciples turned toward him. Among them were the two who had asked about carrying supplies through distorted terrain. One inclined his head without surprise.
"He knows this entrance and has already brought our people safely out of it," Ji continued. "He also has my authority to stop the expedition. If he orders a return, you return."
Leon stepped forward as she indicated the preliminary sketch.
The scouts had verified only a small area around the inner gate. Their marks showed where the level ground extended and where the first uncertain edge began. Most of the page remained blank.
"We establish our return point here," he said. "The recorders stay with the supplies until the immediate surroundings are checked. Nobody begins collecting because something looks close."
A disciple carrying extraction cases raised a hand.
"Do you want samples from the foothold itself, Senior Brother?"
"After Ruan confirms removing them won’t affect the entrance. Mark anything interesting first."
The disciple nodded and wrote it down.
Ji let Leon finish assigning the initial work before drawing him aside.
"The link works across the open gateway," she said. "That does not tell us how far it will carry inside. Check it as you move. If it fails, return to the last position where it worked."
Leon nodded. He remembered the useless plaques in the overlapping layers well enough.
"And if the route changes?" he asked.
"You stop advancing. We will monitor the entrance from here, but I cannot promise help somewhere I cannot reach." She lowered her voice. "You understand why I’m making this clear?"
"Because being able to fight doesn’t mean I can’t get lost."
"Among other things." Her gaze moved briefly toward his household. "Keep them close until you know what you’re standing in."
"I intend to."
She straightened the edge of his outer robe where the rain had folded it against his shoulder, then seemed to notice the gesture and dropped her hand.
"Bring back your measurements, disciple. The treasures can follow."
Leon smiled. "I’d prefer both."
"Then make sensible choices."
He checked the communication plaque at the threshold himself before entering. Seraphine stood ready behind him, with Ira, Vyra, and Loriel waiting beside the first group of Palace personnel.
"The initial markers only," Leon reminded them.
Vyra checked the supply list once more and tucked it away. "Ready, Young Master."
He stepped through.
The rain stopped touching his face.
Dry air brushed his wet sleeves, carrying a faint mineral smell. His boots settled on pale stone, and for a moment he simply enjoyed ground that remained where it appeared to be.
Then he looked up.

The sky extended far beyond anything he had expected from the entrance complex. Thin cloud hung above a distant ridge, lit from within by slow violet flickers. His lightning affinity stirred at the charge in the air, though he kept his circulation at its ordinary pace.

He stood on a broad shelf with the gateway behind him. The scouts’ markers outlined the checked ground near its center. Farther out, the stone ended in a drop that exposed other stretches of terrain at different heights.
Leon followed one ridge with his eyes and lost track of where it joined the next. A dark interval separated them, yet trees on either side seemed almost close enough to touch.
He sent his perception cautiously toward the nearer edge. The distance refused to settle into a measurement he trusted.
Seraphine emerged beside him and went still.
Across the first gap stood pale mineral spires streaked with violet. Light gathered along their edges whenever the distant clouds brightened.
"Young Master," she said quietly. "Look at the growth along those fractures."
He remembered the dawnspar she had cut from the sea stack.
"The same material?"
"It looks like it. I’d need to examine it." She followed the line of spires across the terrace. "There could be a whole bed."
Ira came through next and looked from the marked ground to the distant crystals.
"Four hundred paces?" she asked.
"By eye," Vyra said, joining them. "We’ll measure before we rely on it."
Loriel paused beside a small growth near the foothold’s edge, keeping within the scouts’ markers.
"These are healthy," she said. "With all that lightning in the air, I’d expected more signs of stress." She looked toward the distant trees. "I’d like to see what grows farther in."
So would Leon. He wanted the minerals, the plants, and a chance to understand how this place sustained them together.
Behind him, the recorders began setting down their cases. He confirmed their arrival to Ruan, then looked back across the gap.
The crystal terrace had seemed directly ahead when he entered. Now the same violet spires appeared slightly to his right, though the foothold beneath his boots had not moved.
Leon raised a hand before anyone approached the edge.
"Mark that position," he told Vyra. "Let’s find out whether the route moved with it."

chapters.title: Chapter 702: What the Terrace Reveals
paragraphs: The crystal terrace was still sliding right. Beneath Leon’s boots, the entrance foothold remained perfectly still.

He kept his hand raised while the last of the expedition assembled behind him. Across the gap, violet-streaked spires passed slowly in front of the distant ridge. He could still see the scouts’ marks on the ground near his feet; whatever was moving, it had not yet disturbed their return point.
"Vyra, how far has it moved?"

"Still marking it, Young Master." She had driven a stake at the foothold’s edge and was sighting past it. "Its leading edge has passed the split in that ridge. The marked ground beneath us hasn’t moved."
"Can we reach it?" Leon asked.
"That’s what I don’t know yet." She did not lower her arm. "Give me a minute."

A disciple carrying an extraction case set it down well inside the markers. Leon appreciated that. He wanted a closer look at the crystals himself, but he had no wish to begin his first command by fishing somebody out of a gap.

As the terrace continued right, a lower shelf emerged from beneath it. Broader and flatter, it lay perhaps fifty paces below the foothold. A slope of broken pale stone connected the two. By the time the moving terrace paused, Leon could follow the entire descent with his eyes.
"There’s a slope under it," Seraphine said quietly. "Young Master, can you feel where it joins?"
"I’m checking."

Leon extended his perception down the exposed slope. Its loose surface covered solid stone, and he found no spatial break along the descent. He checked from another position, then had Vyra compare the view from the foothold’s opposite corner.
"Slope’s fixed," she said. "Didn’t move with the terrace. Whatever’s sliding up there, the ground we’d walk on is staying put."
"Then we may have a way down," Leon said.
Along the shelf’s upper edge the stone was scored in long parallel grooves, worn smooth, and there were mineral crusts built up in layers along the grooves like tide lines on a harbor wall.
It’s done this before. Many times.
He still had no idea how long the shelf would remain exposed.
"Keep watching it," Leon told Vyra. "We finish the base before anyone goes down."
Over the next forty minutes, Leon checked the approach with the scouts while Tian Mingxu organized the base.

His deputy was a broad-shouldered Late Golden Core disciple with twelve years of field experience. She had spent the arrivals at the gateway counting, moving a knot along a cord for each person who passed.
"Forty-eight through," she said when he approached. "All matched to the roster. The return watch will count them again."
"You count them out and in," Leon said.
"People first, supplies second," Tian said. "I once sent scouts looking for a missing handler who was asleep behind the medicine cases. Nobody had seen him leave the line."

She had organized the eighteen who would remain, including herself, while Leon confirmed the forward party. Supply cases were stacked in order of what would be needed first. Two watches were posted at the gateway and one at the foothold’s edge. A cleared patch of stone near the entrance had four stakes and a rope around it.

"Reception point," said Tian. "Anybody coming back with material drops it there. Nobody carries anything past that rope until it’s been logged and my recorder has seen it." She finally looked at him. "I’ll need your samples recorded too, Senior Brother, so they aren’t counted twice."
"Understood."
"We’re ready here," Tian said. "You can take your thirty whenever the scouts are satisfied."

Thirty went down the slope: Leon, the four women, and twenty-five Palace personnel — extraction specialists, two recorders, four scouts, and the rest carriers and handlers. Tian remained with the other seventeen at the base.
The communication check went through at the top of the slope and again at the bottom. Both answered cleanly.

The shelf glowed faintly in patches. Violet veins forked through dark stone near the back, while an amber band crossed the middle. Toward the far edge, dull red crust radiated enough heat for Leon to feel it on his face from twenty paces away.
At the center of it all, where the three colors met, the stone had split open into a shallow basin, and something in the basin was moving.

It looked almost liquid. When Leon crouched beside it, however, his perception found concentrated energy rising from below. He could distinguish none of the three deposits’ dominant affinities in the pool itself.
A source.
Behind him, the extraction specialists had gone very quiet.

"Senior Brother." The eldest of them, a thin man with ink-stained fingers and an assay lens hanging from a cord around his neck, had knelt at the edge of the violet vein. His name was Bai Heng and he had been doing this for thirty years. "The violet is lightning-bearing ore. I’d stake my name on that. The amber I’m less sure of — it reads earth-dense, but there’s something in it I can’t identify without cutting a sample." He moved to the red crust and held his hand above it. "Fire. Absolutely fire. But the grain is wrong for anything I’ve handled."
"Wrong how?" Leon asked.
"Too even." Bai Heng frowned at it. "Fire ore is usually streaky. This looks like somebody laid it down on purpose."
"Can we take it safely?" Leon asked.
"The violet and the red, yes. Safely, with proper cuts." He looked toward the basin. "I wouldn’t cut anywhere near that. Not until I know what feeds it."
Leon stood at the basin’s edge and let himself enjoy it for a moment.

More than a year of subjective research and cultivation had consumed his ten purchased reservoirs. He had reached Mid Foundation Establishment, but the next stage would need fresh supplies, and he had been thinking rather often about their cost.
And here was a shelf full of raw affinity ore sitting around a source that kept feeding it.
Raw ore would need assessment and refining before he could cultivate with it. Even so, finding a supply he could help gather was considerably more satisfying than looking at another purchase price.
That’s a very good morning.
"Senior Brother."
It was one of the scouts, a young woman named Wen Shu who had been posted at the shelf’s upper edge. She was pointing back the way they had come.
The crystal terrace had started moving again. Slowly — a knuckle-width every few minutes by Vyra’s count — but it was no longer sliding right.
It was sliding back.
"How long do we have?" Leon asked Vyra.
"About three hours before it covers the shelf, if it holds this rate," Vyra said, checking her marks. "I’ll watch the slope separately. We leave before it reaches our way out."
Bai Heng had stood up with his lens in his hand.
"Three hours," he said. "Senior Brother, that’s enough for a proper harvest. Not everything. But if we start cutting now instead of arguing about the amber, it’s a great deal more than samples."
Leon looked from the exposed beds to the returning terrace. For once, he had brought people who knew exactly how to turn a discovery into something he could use.
"Then start cutting," he said.

chapters.title: Chapter 703: More Than One Kind of Wealth
paragraphs: The violet came out of the stone in long flat slabs that crackled when they were lifted.

Bai Heng’s team scored around each vein with insulated chisels, levered the stone free, and passed it to carriers wearing thick gloves. Twice a slab discharged as it came loose, snapping violet light across the cut and leaving a sharp metallic smell.

"Good, that’s a live one," Bai Heng said after the second discharge. He caught a carrier reaching for it too soon and tapped the man’s glove with his chisel. "Good doesn’t mean touch it yet. Wait for the charge to settle."

The red crust came away hot. Carriers wrapped it in damp insulating cloth, then packed it into lined cases. One man swore under his breath whenever steam obscured the clasp he was trying to fasten. His partner waited until he finished before turning the case around for him.
The amber they left alone for the first hour. Bai Heng spent that hour cutting a single sample the size of his thumb and staring at it through the cracked lens.

"Earth-aligned," Bai Heng said eventually. "But unusually reluctant to release its energy. I can draw from the cut face; deeper in, I get almost nothing." He turned the sample. "That could be useful. It could also make refining it a nuisance."
"Is it safe to take?" Leon asked.
"The sample hasn’t reacted to cutting or storage. We can lift more with the same precautions." Bai Heng looked up. "I don’t know its best use yet. I would very much like enough to find out."
Leon had split the thirty into four teams and kept them within a hundred paces of each other, which was about as spread as he was willing to allow on ground nobody understood.
He did not stand over any of them.

Seraphine had put herself at the shelf’s forward edge where the ground dropped into dark air and stayed there, watching the approaches. Ira moved between the working positions, keeping the routes clear. Vyra worked with the recorders, matching each case to the bed it came from before it joined the growing stacks. Loriel moved between the teams checking hands, breathing, and the color of people’s faces — and on her third pass stopped at the edge of the red crust and crouched.
"There’s moss growing directly on the fire ore," Loriel said. "I’d expect a scorched underside, but the new growth looks healthy."
"Something you could use?" Leon asked.
"Possibly. I want to see what happens when the heat changes." She examined the rock beneath it. "May I take a little with its original stone, Young Master?"
"Take what you need," he said.
Leon went back to the source.
It happened while Bai Heng’s team was cutting the largest violet vein, the one that ran closest to the basin.
The vein came loose, and underneath it, running back toward the basin, was a channel.

It was small — a groove in the stone no wider than a finger, filled with the same shimmering unformed energy as the source. And as Leon watched, the energy in it moved. It flowed outward from the basin toward the newly exposed cut. A faint violet sheen gathered where it reached the remaining mineral.
He crouched and followed the channel back with his perception, and found that it was not the only one.
There were dozens. The whole shelf was threaded with them, running out from the basin to every deposit — violet, amber, red — like roots from a single trunk.

Leon stayed beside the cut for twenty minutes, comparing the nearest channels. The flow feeding the cut violet had quickened after extraction. The channels feeding the untouched amber ran slowly, barely moving. The red ran at a middling pace and pulsed, fast then slow, fast then slow.

All three drew from the same source at different rates. Near the violet cut, he could now make out a thin crystalline film, too slight to harvest. The nearby amber retained its earth-aligned energy, and he detected no fire spreading into either deposit.
Leon sat back on his heels.
Balance need not mean equal flow.

The Lord’s advice had helped him stop forcing all nine branches through equal circulation rates. Building his foundation had taken months of adjustments to their returns and their demands on his reserve.

Here he could watch a similar problem being answered outside his own body. Harvesting changed one deposit’s demand, and the feeding flow changed with it while the neighboring deposits remained distinct.
If I can work out what changes first, I might save myself a month of guessing.

He wanted to test the thought immediately, which was a good reason to write it down first. Twenty minutes beside one harvested bed could not tell him whether the channel, the mineral, or something beneath both governed the change. Copying the visible arrangement into his circulation would be guesswork.
He could, however, take home a better question and the materials to investigate it.
"Vyra. I need a record of these channels. Positions, widths, flow direction. And Bai Heng—"
Bai Heng looked up. "Senior Brother?"
"When you cut the amber, I want a sample from right beside a channel and one from as far from any channel as you can get. Same for the violet. They go in my allocation."
Bai Heng set aside the larger slab he had been choosing and crouched beside the fine channel instead.
"I’ll cut them myself," Bai Heng said.
He started to mark the nearer sample, then paused. "Do you want the same weight from both positions, Senior Brother?"
"Yes," Leon said. "And keep their orientation marked. I want to compare the energy before either piece is refined."
"Then I should leave a strip of the surrounding stone attached," Bai Heng said.
Leon leaned closer as Bai Heng indicated the proposed cut. He had been about to ask for the ore alone.
"Please do."

The old man scored two arrows into the stone and handed the recorder his measurements. Leon watched him work, pleased he had asked. He could sense the flow more clearly than Bai Heng, but that would not help much if he destroyed what carried it while collecting his evidence.
Well into the second hour, carriers were stacking slabs by the dozen. One of the recorders flexed his cramped fingers while Vyra checked the next case.

It was a good harvest. Leon did not need anybody to tell him that; he could see it in the carriers’ faces and hear it in the way Bai Heng had stopped narrating and started simply working. There would be worthwhile credit for the gathering teams and a useful supply for his own research once his share had been refined.
He was checking the terrace’s progress with Vyra when the ground moved under the amber team.

It was small. A shift in the loose stone near the edge of the band, the kind of thing a carrier might put down to his own weight. One of Bai Heng’s assistants glanced down, frowned, and went back to cutting.
A second disturbance lifted loose chips forty paces away beside the red crust. Before they settled, Wen Shu raised her lantern over another moving patch near the violet.
Leon sent his perception below the cuts. Several bodies were moving through buried passages, converging on the working teams.
"Everybody off the cuts!" Leon’s voice carried across the shelf. "Back to the solid ground. Now!"

chapters.title: Chapter 704: Before the Dust Settles
paragraphs: They came up through the stone in four places at once.

The creatures had low, heavy bodies the size of large dogs, overlapping gray back plates, and shovel-shaped heads above powerful digging limbs. The first came up beneath the amber team’s abandoned cut, surfacing through loose stone with a grinding scrape, and swung its head toward the nearest carrier.

The Palace personnel moved at Leon’s warning, lifting tools and retreating toward solid ground. A handler beside the red crust was rising from one knee when the rock beneath his planted foot gave way. He fell sideways as a burrower surfaced beside him.
Seraphine reached it before it could turn on him.

Lightning carried her across thirty paces. Light followed cleanly through her blade as she changed direction, without the hesitation she had worked to eliminate during her Core preparations. Her sword passed between the creature’s first two plates before it had fully cleared the ground.
She was already turning toward the next one.
"Shalegnaws!" Bai Heng shouted from behind the amber team. "Ore eaters. We’re standing in their feeding ground!"
"How many?" Leon called.
"Packs of ten to twenty, usually! Foundation-stage, all of them, except—"
The ground in the middle of the shelf heaved, and the thing that came up out of it was twice the size of the others and plated in something that caught the light violet.
Bai Heng backed another step. "That one’s the leader."
The rest of the pack surfaced around the scattered teams, and for about ten seconds the shelf was dangerous.

Wen Shu was near the violet with a lantern and a short blade and three of them surfacing in a ring around her. She backed against the largest slab and raised her blade, denying them a clear approach from behind. Ira arrived at the nearest burrower’s flank, drove her lance through its back plate, and swept the haft into the second creature as she pulled free.
The third looked at Ira and went back into the ground.
"Coward," said Ira, with approval.

Vyra had not moved from the recorders’ position and did not need to. Four burrowers were coming up the shelf’s eastern side toward the carriers stacking slabs, and she laid a single line of Crownfire across the stone in front of them — narrow, low, steady, and precisely placed. The first burrower tried to cross it and changed its mind with considerable speed. The other three did not try.
"East side’s closed," Vyra said. "They’ll dig round. I’m watching where."

One recorder caught his partner by the shoulder before he could run after a dropped case. Together they backed toward the carriers, who had set their loads down and drawn short blades. A scout took the exposed corner of the group. They needed only to hold it while the women cleared the approaches.
Leon saw Wen Shu reach for a fallen handler’s pack and waved her back.
"Leave the equipment. Get him behind you."
She changed direction at once. The pack slid into a widening cut a moment later, but its owner was already on his feet. Leon would rather replace a set of straps than carry someone up the slope.

Loriel knelt beside the injured handler at the red crust. His lower leg lay at an angle that made Leon wince even from across the shelf. As she reached for him, another burrower surfaced to her left. She turned, touched two fingers beneath its jaw, and released a precise pulse. The creature collapsed beside the cut, leaving her free to examine the knee.
"Knee," she said to the handler. "It’s out, not broken. This will hurt."
The handler gripped her sleeve. His shout as she reset the joint carried across the shelf.

The leader turned toward Leon beside the source. Its pressure was Golden Core, and its violet plating dragged a shower of loose chips from the edge of the opening as it hauled itself clear. It charged low, shovel-head aimed at his knees.
Leon checked the space behind it. Nobody was in the line of his response, so he let it come halfway across the open ground.

He folded the space immediately above its next foothold. The beast’s forelimbs dropped farther than it expected while its hindquarters carried forward. Its armored belly struck the stone, leaving its head exposed as it scrabbled for purchase.
Leon walked up to it and put a compressed lance of ice through the seam behind its head.
It stopped moving.

Leon let the fold close and checked the other teams. Seraphine had cut down two more beasts, and Ira finished a third near Wen Shu’s slab. Vyra burned down a burrower that lunged toward the carriers, then extended her flame along the eastern burrows as the last attackers retreated underground. Tools lay scattered around the abandoned cuts, but the gathering teams were together behind cover.
The whole thing had taken perhaps forty seconds.
On the far side of the amber band, Bai Heng had his assay lens halfway to his eye and had apparently forgotten to finish lifting it.
"Nobody’s dead," Loriel reported, a few minutes later. "The handler’s knee is back in and he’ll walk on it by tonight. Two scrapes and a cut hand from a chisel. That’s all."
"And the pack?" Leon asked Seraphine.
"Eleven dead, including the leader," Seraphine said. "Four went underground. They’re moving away; I’ll keep watch."
Bai Heng had come across the shelf and was crouched beside the big one’s carcass with a look of unashamed greed.

"Look at the plating, Senior Brother." Bai Heng tapped an exposed edge with his chisel. "Shalegnaws incorporate minerals from their food. This one has layers of lightning-bearing material all through its shell. The smaller plates should be useful too, though we’ll have to assay them separately."
"Take them," Leon said.
Bai Heng inspected the carcass once more. "Twenty minutes for the plates, with two people helping."
Leon checked the terrace. Vyra was already at his shoulder.
"An hour and forty minutes," she said, "if the rate holds. It hasn’t changed."
"Do it," Leon told Bai Heng. "Then return to the amber. Leave the deeper cuts alone."
They worked the last stretch hard, and they worked it well.

Bai Heng’s team took the amber in the end — slabs of it, dense and heavy and strange, stacked beside the violet and the wrapped red. The carriers stripped the burrowers’ plating with a practiced efficiency that suggested they had done this with other beasts. Wen Shu held the upper edge and called the terrace’s position every ten minutes in a voice that got steadily calmer as the day went on.

With forty minutes left before the shelf would be covered, the terrace’s shadow reached the retreat marker Vyra had placed beside the slope. The route itself was still clear. Leon called the end of collection.
"Everything that’s cut comes with us. Everything that isn’t, stays."
Nobody argued. Half the violet band was still in the stone, and the deepest amber, and a patch of red crust that Bai Heng looked at the way a man looks at a meal he has to leave.

Leon could have cracked the remaining beds out in a few minutes. He did not, because he did not know what breaking the stone around an active source would do to the source — and the source was what he actually wanted.
If it replenishes, we’ll want more than one visit.
They went up the slope in order, carrying their loaded cases. Tian counted thirty returning, and the communication check answered cleanly at the top.
While the first cases were being logged, Leon looked back. The terrace was sliding across the ground where he had stood beside the source. Later, the last exposed strip disappeared beneath it.
Bai Heng was the one who did the first count, at the reception rope, with Tian’s recorder beside him.
He went through it twice. Then he sat back on his heels, took off the cracked lens, and looked at Leon.
"This is more than we’d hoped for from the first excursion," Bai Heng said. "More useful material than I brought enough assay slips to label. I’ll have to borrow some."
Then he held up one of the amber samples from beside a channel, and turned it in the light.
There was a faint line in it — fine, pale green, running through the amber like a hair.

"There’s something else mixed into this sample," Bai Heng said. "Only beside the channel. I didn’t find it in the other cut." He lifted it toward the light again. "If it washed in from elsewhere, that source may be worth finding too."

chapters.title: Chapter 705: A Share Worth Taking
paragraphs: Bai Heng laughed out loud when he saw the contribution estimate.
He sat on an upturned crate beside Tian’s recorder, a slate balanced on his knee. After ten minutes of sums, he put down the stylus and checked the total with one dusty finger.
"Something wrong?" said Leon.

"No. No, Senior Brother, nothing’s wrong." Bai Heng held up the cracked assay lens on its cord. "I’ve been using this for nine years. The crack’s been there for seven. A proper lens from the formation hall costs a year and a half of my contribution." He put it down on the crate beside him. "I can buy a new one. After one day."
"Buy one with a case this time," Leon said.
"I dropped this one down a quarry face," Bai Heng admitted, smiling. "A case would have helped."

Before releasing any material for personal use, Tian finished reconciling the field log with the base record. Every slab went across the reception rope and into her recorder’s ledger — Palace holdings on one side, distributable gains on the other, and a separate column for personal allocations. Leon’s channel samples went into that column under his name, counted against his share. So did Loriel’s moss, which she had taken from the red crust and which Tian’s recorder logged asunidentified living material, one sealed jar.
"And the plating?" said Leon.

"Distributable," Tian said. "The record includes your kill and the other household contributions. Any plates you select come out of your allocation. The work credit will be assessed separately under Palace rules."
"I wasn’t going to argue."
"I prefer to have it written down while everyone remembers," Tian said. She passed him the record to check.

By evening, everyone had been counted, the harvest was stored, and cooking fires were burning inside a ring of loose stones. Tian staggered the watches so all forty-eight could eat without leaving the gateway unattended.
Leon took his bowl over to the gathering party. Bai Heng made room on a crate, still wearing the old lens, and offered him the better end of a piece of dried fish.

An extraction specialist everyone called Old Pan had improved the field rations with spices from his own pack. He passed the pot around but firmly refused to let Ira empty the last of his pepper into it. Wen Shu ate three bowls and fell asleep sitting up. The handler with the knee told the story of the burrower six times, and by the sixth the creature had become roughly the size of a house.
"It was the size of a dog," said Loriel, passing him more rice.
"A very large dog," the handler insisted.
"You were on the ground," Loriel said. "I believe it looked large. Now straighten that leg before it stiffens."
The handler obeyed, accepting the rice with a muttered thanks.

Seraphine sat to Leon’s left. When she reached for his empty bowl, he caught the ladle instead and filled hers before his own. She gave him a brief smile. Wen Shu woke when Old Pan lifted the pot from the fire and asked whether there was any left. Nearby, Ira accepted a second helping from Old Pan, apparently willing to forgive the pepper dispute.
Vyra arrived after checking the last receipt. Ira had saved her a bowl beside the fire, covered with a plate to keep it warm.
Leon listened as Bai Heng described the lens he intended to buy. The old man knew its specifications remarkably well for someone who claimed he had stopped looking at the price.
He’s going straight to the formation hall when we get back.

Leon understood the feeling. His own samples were packed nearby, and for once the prospect of another experiment did not begin with an empty reservoir. He accepted more fish and let himself enjoy the evening.

The report went out through the gateway relay that night: one excursion, one engagement, no fatalities, harvest logged, full personnel accounted for. Ji’s acknowledgment came back inside the hour. It said, in its entirety:Good. Continue.
The next morning, Wen Shu returned to the question of the green inclusion.
She studied the exposed rock above the covered shelf through a sighting glass, then brought Leon a sketch.
"There’s green staining along the northern rock face," Wen Shu said. "It follows old runoff grooves toward the shelf. Bai Heng thinks it resembles the inclusion in his sample."
"Can you follow it?" Leon asked.

"Only part of the way. Beyond that spur, the ground drops out of sight." She pointed to her sketch. "But from the high point, you can see a basin farther north. Perhaps a thousand paces away. There’s greenish mist over it."
Leon went up to the high point and looked.

Beyond the terrace and a stretch of broken pale ground, mist hung above a shallow basin. Something glinted along its floor. The runoff might lead there, or the similar color might mean nothing; either way, Leon wanted a closer look.
Bai Heng came up beside him with his cracked lens, looked for a long while, and then said, very quietly: "Senior Brother. I think that’s a spring."
"What kind?" Leon asked.

"The kind that leaves crystals where it dries." He lowered the lens. "If it’s what I think it is, it deposits cultivation crystals every time it rises. You don’t harvest a spring like that once. You come back to it."
Leon looked at the basin and thought about ten empty reservoirs.
"Then we go look at it," he said.
They left later that morning. The same thirty took the northern slope, leaving Tian and seventeen others at the entrance base.

The communication check went through at the foothold, then at five hundred paces, then at eight hundred. Wen Shu marked every hundred paces with a stake. The ground was broken and uncertain and twice the scouts called a halt while Vyra sighted a stretch that did not agree with itself, and twice they found it was only a trick of the light rather than anything moving.
They rounded the last rise and gained a clear view of the basin.

It was larger than it had looked from the foothold — perhaps two hundred paces across, a shallow bowl of pale stone with green mist hanging a few feet above its floor. Near its center the ground was wet and glistening, and all around the wet patch, crusted onto the stone in rings like the rings of a tree, were crystals.
Pale green, translucent, and in some of the older rings grown thick enough to cast shadows.
"Look at those layers," Bai Heng said. "Repeated deposits. If we can measure what one cycle leaves—"
He stopped.
Seraphine had stopped too. She had gone completely still at the head of the column, with one hand raised.
Leon came up beside her.
At the basin’s near edge, where the oldest and thickest crystal rings met the stone, somebody had been cutting.

Clean cuts. Recent ones — the faces of the stone still bright where the crystal had been levered out. A rack of crates stood beside them, neatly stacked. Beyond the crates, at the basin’s far side, was a line of tents in a color none of the Palace’s expedition had brought.
Smoke was rising from one of them.
"That," said Vyra, very quietly, "isn’t ours."

sentences.text: Bai Heng laughed out loud when he saw the contribution estimate.
He sat on an upturned crate beside Tian’s recorder, a slate balanced on his knee.
After ten minutes of sums, he put down the stylus and checked the total with one dusty finger.
"Something wrong?" said Leon.
"No.
No, Senior Brother, nothing’s wrong." Bai Heng held up the cracked assay lens on its cord.
"I’ve been using this for nine years.
The crack’s been there for seven.
A proper lens from the formation hall costs a year and a half of my contribution." He put it down on the crate beside him.
"I can buy a new one.
After one day."
"Buy one with a case this time," Leon said.
"I dropped this one down a quarry face," Bai Heng admitted, smiling.
"A case would have helped."
Before releasing any material for personal use, Tian finished reconciling the field log with the base record.
Every slab went across the reception rope and into her recorder’s ledger — Palace holdings on one side, distributable gains on the other, and a separate column for personal allocations.
Leon’s channel samples went into that column under his name, counted against his share.
So did Loriel’s moss, which she had taken from the red crust and which Tian’s recorder logged asunidentified living material, one sealed jar.
"And the plating?" said Leon.
"Distributable," Tian said.
"The record includes your kill and the other household contributions.
Any plates you select come out of your allocation.
The work credit will be assessed separately under Palace rules."
"I wasn’t going to argue."
"I prefer to have it written down while everyone remembers," Tian said.
She passed him the record to check.

Tian staggered the watches so all forty-eight could eat without leaving the gateway unattended.
Leon took his bowl over to the gathering party.
Bai Heng made room on a crate, still wearing the old lens, and offered him the better end of a piece of dried fish.
An extraction specialist everyone called Old Pan had improved the field rations with spices from his own pack.
He passed the pot around but firmly refused to let Ira empty the last of his pepper into it.
Wen Shu ate three bowls and fell asleep sitting up.
The handler with the knee told the story of the burrower six times, and by the sixth the creature had become roughly the size of a house.
"It was the size of a dog," said Loriel, passing him more rice.
"A very large dog," the handler insisted.
"You were on the ground," Loriel said.
"I believe it looked large.
Now straighten that leg before it stiffens."
The handler obeyed, accepting the rice with a muttered thanks.
Seraphine sat to Leon’s left.
When she reached for his empty bowl, he caught the ladle instead and filled hers before his own.
She gave him a brief smile.
Wen Shu woke when Old Pan lifted the pot from the fire and asked whether there was any left.
Nearby, Ira accepted a second helping from Old Pan, apparently willing to forgive the pepper dispute.
Vyra arrived after checking the last receipt.
Ira had saved her a bowl beside the fire, covered with a plate to keep it warm.
Leon listened as Bai Heng described the lens he intended to buy.
The old man knew its specifications remarkably well for someone who claimed he had stopped looking at the price.
He’s going straight to the formation hall when we get back.
Leon understood the feeling.
His own samples were packed nearby, and for once the prospect of another experiment did not begin with an empty reservoir.
He accepted more fish and let himself enjoy the evening.
The report went out through the gateway relay that night: one excursion, one engagement, no fatalities, harvest logged, full personnel accounted for.
Ji’s acknowledgment came back inside the hour.
It said, in its entirety:Good.
Continue.
The next morning, Wen Shu returned to the question of the green inclusion.
She studied the exposed rock above the covered shelf through a sighting glass, then brought Leon a sketch.
"There’s green staining along the northern rock face," Wen Shu said.
"It follows old runoff grooves toward the shelf.
Bai Heng thinks it resembles the inclusion in his sample."
"Can you follow it?" Leon asked.
"Only part of the way.
Beyond that spur, the ground drops out of sight." She pointed to her sketch.
"But from the high point, you can see a basin farther north.
Perhaps a thousand paces away.
There’s greenish mist over it."
Leon went up to the high point and looked.
Beyond the terrace and a stretch of broken pale ground, mist hung above a shallow basin.
Something glinted along its floor.
The runoff might lead there, or the similar color might mean nothing; either way, Leon wanted a closer look.
Bai Heng came up beside him with his cracked lens, looked for a long while, and then said, very quietly: "Senior Brother.
I think that’s a spring."
"What kind?" Leon asked.
"The kind that leaves crystals where it dries." He lowered the lens.
"If it’s what I think it is, it deposits cultivation crystals every time it rises.
You don’t harvest a spring like that once.
You come back to it."

chapters.title: Chapter 706: Words He Should Not Know
paragraphs: Leon put the bulk of the party behind the ridge line with Vyra and did not take them any further.
"Vyra, keep the other twenty-four behind this rise," Leon said. "You have command. If we need to withdraw, take them to the last marker and contact the base."
"And you?" said Vyra.
"Me, Seraphine, Ira, Loriel, and Bai Heng." He glanced at the extraction master. "I want someone who can tell me what they’ve actually been taking."
Bai Heng glanced at the distant tents, then secured his lens cord beneath his collar and nodded.

The five walked into the basin in plain sight. Leon kept his presence at its familiar public level, the Peak Golden Core reading the Palace’s artifacts registered. Seraphine walked near his shoulder, with Ira and Loriel flanking Bai Heng.
Somebody in the tents had seen them before they reached the first crate.

A hanging strip of cloth stirred above the nearest shelter, embroidered with symbols Leon did not recognize. There was no Palace insignia on the stacked cases or the equipment beside them. He resisted the urge to look back toward the ridge; Vyra knew her work, and advertising the rest of the party would gain him nothing yet.
Bai Heng slowed beside a freshly cut crystal face.
"Keep beside Loriel," Leon told him quietly. "You’ll have time to examine it after we speak."
The old man lowered his lens and continued with them.

Fifteen people emerged from the tents. They wore gray leather coats with high collars and split backs, fastened with pale bronze fittings. Curved blades and short spears hung openly at their sides. One man carried a heavy crossbow whose unusual winding mechanism drew a low murmur from Bai Heng.
About half had thin blue lines extending down their foreheads from hairline to brow. Leon could see no painted edges. The markings appeared to lie within the skin.
Their leader was a tall woman with iron-gray hair and one of the blue markings. She stopped twenty paces away, looked over the five approaching strangers, and raised a hand to halt them.
When she spoke, the sounds were entirely unfamiliar. Her words rose sharply at the ends of phrases, separated by clipped syllables he could not even begin to parse.
Yet he understood her.
"This spring is ours. You’ve wandered onto a claimed site. Turn around and leave the way you came."
The meaning arrived as clearly as if she had spoken beside him in Moonfall. He could hear the impatience too, although he could not identify a single word carrying it.
Leon did not let anything show on his face.
Beside him, Seraphine spoke quietly. "Young Master, I understand her. But I don’t recognize the language."
"Neither do I," Leon said.
He deliberately used the language he spoke with the Palace disciples and watched her response.
"How long has it been yours?"
The woman’s brows drew together. She glanced at the man beside her, and he gave a slight nod. Whatever they had expected from Leon’s speech, the question had reached them.
It goes both ways.
Leon detected no obvious activation from either group. The effect might belong to an artifact he could not sense, or to the place itself. He had too little evidence to choose.
Useful. I’d still like to know what’s doing it.
For now, the woman was waiting for him to leave, and the men behind her had their hands on their weapons.
"Since we arrived," the woman said. "Which was before you."
"How long before?" Leon asked.
"Long enough." She jerked her chin toward the cut stone and the stacked crates. "We found it, we cleared it, we are harvesting it. That is how claims are made."
"You claim the whole spring because you found it first?" Leon asked.

"We cleared it. We hold it," she said. Her eyes went over the five of them and settled, briefly, on Leon’s apparent cultivation. Something in her face eased very slightly. "You are a small party and you are late. Go back and tell whoever sent you that the spring at the green basin belongs to the Harrowmark Expedition, and that anyone who comes to dispute it will be met."
Leon looked past her at the crates.
"Bai Heng."
Bai Heng raised his lens. "The thicker outer rings, Senior Brother. A substantial portion has been removed. See those grooves running toward the water? Their cuts cross several of them."
"Does that matter?" Leon asked.
"It might. If the grooves feed the outer beds, I’d preserve them until we’d measured a cycle." Bai Heng lowered the lens. "I’d need a closer examination to be certain."
Leon turned back to the woman.
"Does your expedition own the source, or have an agreement with anyone who does?" Leon asked.
"We don’t need anyone’s agreement."
He glanced at the uncut beds on their side of the basin. "Then you arrived first. That doesn’t mean I’ve agreed to leave the entire spring to you."
Leon wanted the spring, and he wanted to know how another expedition had reached it. Neither wish required pretending he would accept an order simply because it came from someone with more people.
The woman looked over his party again. Her gaze paused on Seraphine’s sword, then moved to Ira and Loriel. Whatever she made of their apparent cultivation, it did not persuade her to negotiate.
She glanced to her left, at a broad man with the blue line on his forehead and a curved blade already half-drawn.
He did not wait for anything further.

He came across the twenty paces fast — a real Golden Core, and a practiced one, the blade coming off his hip in a flat horizontal cut aimed to take Leon across the chest before he could raise his hands. There was force behind it. Something ran along the edge of the blade that made the air around it shimmer.
It never reached him.
Leon did not move his feet. He took the last pace of the man’s charge and folded it.

The blade entered the fold a hand’s width from Leon’s chest. Its path turned aside, carrying the strike through empty air beside him. The attacker’s shoulders followed his committed swing, opening his stance before he could correct it.
Leon shifted the space beneath the man’s forward foot. His footing dropped just enough to bring him onto one knee, arm still extended at the end of the failed stroke.
Leon closed the fold around his wrist and held it there.

The man pulled against the restraint. When his wrist did not move, he drove more energy into the effort, enough to crack the stone beneath his planted knee. Leon held him without adjusting his stance.
The basin went very quiet.
The other fourteen stood twenty paces away, watching their comrade struggle. The crossbowman had started to lift his weapon; now he held it awkwardly across his waist.
Leon still had both hands loose at his sides. The restrained man’s strength was nowhere near enough to trouble him.

Seraphine kept her attention on the remaining armed strangers, her sword still sheathed. Ira watched their leader with frank interest. Loriel glanced at the kneeling man’s wrist, then returned her attention to the line ahead.
The gray-haired woman looked from the trapped blade to Leon’s face. For the first time, she seemed unsure what to say.
"Now," Leon said, certain that she would understand him. "Let’s try that conversation again."

chapters.title: Chapter 707: The Price of the First Strike
paragraphs: The swordsman tried to pull his arm free again. It stayed where Leon had put it.
For four seconds, everyone across the basin watched. Then two men rushed forward, and a third raised his crossbow.

The gray-haired leader stayed still, her gaze fixed on the trapped wrist. The men coming at Leon were a spearman with a blue line on his forehead and a thickset man carrying a hooked blade. They approached from either side of the kneeling swordsman while the crossbowman sighted on Leon’s chest.
Leon did not bother turning.

Seraphine reached the spearman before he finished his second step. A cut through the bronze fitting sent his spearhead clattering away. Before he could recover, she struck his temple with the flat of her blade and caught his collar, lowering him heavily onto the stone.

The thickset man reached Leon, only for Ira to drive the butt of her lance into his stomach. He folded over it, dropped his blade, and sank onto the stone. When Ira drew the weapon back, he stayed down.
The crossbow went off.

The bolt crossed the twenty paces between the crossbowman and Leon’s chest in a blur of bronze and stopped a hand’s width short, hanging in a fold of space that went nowhere. Leon let it hang there long enough for everybody to see it.
Then he let it drop.
It clattered on the stone at his feet, and the crossbowman lowered his weapon very slowly.
"Anyone else?" Leon asked.
The crossbowman shook his head. Even the man gasping around Ira’s lance managed to keep still.
The gray-haired woman opened her hands at her sides. Her gaze passed over the two men Seraphine and Ira had put down, then returned to the swordsman still kneeling before Leon.
"We yield," she said.
The words came to Leon as clipped foreign sounds and arrived as perfectly clear meaning, and he was already starting to get used to that, which was its own kind of strange.
"All of you?" Leon asked.
"All of us." Her jaw tightened. "You have made your point."

"Not quite yet." Leon released the swordsman’s wrist, and the man pitched forward onto his hands and stayed there, breathing hard. "You attacked first. On ground you’d claimed by walking onto it before we did. So here are my terms."
He did not raise his voice. He did not need to.

"Everything you’ve harvested from this spring comes to me. So does every treasure you’re carrying, every piece of equipment worth more than its weight in rations, and every route record you have. You keep your food, your water, your bedding, and enough tools to get yourselves somewhere else."
"That is robbery."
"Yes," said Leon. "It is."
She stared at him.

"You drew on me," he went on. "Your swordsman came across the stone with a blade already moving. If I hadn’t stopped him, would you be offering to return my belongings?" He shrugged slightly. "You lost. This is what losing costs."
The woman looked toward the ridge behind him, then at her crossbowman. The man set his weapon on the stone.
Leon waited. He had no interest in bargaining down the price of an attack on his people.
"Agreed," she said.
He called Vyra in after that, and the twenty-five came over the rise in good order and took the basin in about four minutes.

The fifteen from Harrowmark sat in a line along the eastern edge under Ira’s supervision, which was supervision in the sense that Ira sat on a crate facing them and ate an apple very slowly. Nobody in that line made any sudden movements.

Loriel checked the three injured men. Ira’s opponent had a cracked rib, the spearman a concussion, and the first swordsman had bitten his tongue when Leon forced him to his knees. She treated them without asking. Leon left her to it; he had agreed to let them walk away, and he meant it.
Vyra had the recorders work in pairs, one checking each surrendered item while the other noted it down.

"Spring crystal already cut," she said, reading from a slate. "Eleven crates. Logged as seized stock, not as harvest — they didn’t come out of our cuts and they don’t go in the same column." She moved down. "Personal treasure. Three storage pouches, contents unknown until opened, logged unopened. One pouch of what looks like refined crystal — better grade than anything in the crates. Equipment: the crossbow, which Bai Heng wants to look at very badly. Two survey instruments I don’t recognize. Four blades with bronze fittings."
"And the route records?" Leon asked.
"A bound book and a rolled chart." Vyra laid both beside the slate. "The leader was reluctant to hand these over. We should have her explain them before she leaves."
"Keep her here," Leon said. "And put aside a sample of that refined crystal for my allocation."
"Already noted, Young Master."
Leon opened the pouch of refined crystal himself and looked at it for a while.
The crystals were pale green, cleanly cut, and hummed faintly in his palm with energy that did not belong to any single affinity. He held it toward the leader.
"From this spring?"
She nodded reluctantly. "The outer growth. Refined twice."
And now I get to find out what it does.
He closed the pouch, pleased despite the trouble. The spring had looked promising before. This was something he could test.
His internal plaque warmed against his chest while the recorders were checking the third crate.
He had expected Wen Shu, who was holding the ridgeline to the south. It was Tian Mingxu, from the entrance base.
"Senior Brother." Her voice came through level, which in Tian meant considerably more than it would in anyone else. "The gateway’s gone."
Leon stopped moving.
"Say that again."

"The gateway we came through. The watch saw its edges draw together. It vanished before they could finish calling me." A pause. "We’ve examined the site from the marked boundary. There’s no visible opening left."
"Your people?"
"All eighteen here. I’ve counted twice. Nobody was near the edge when it went and nobody’s hurt."
"When?"
"Three minutes ago. I counted everyone before contacting you. We have a record of the closure and the site as it stands. Nobody has tried to cross."

"Keep it that way," said Leon. "Don’t send anyone toward where it was. Hold the camp, record anything that changes, and check the ground every hour. If something opens, you tell me before anyone walks into it."
"Understood."

There was no point asking about Ji. Their plaques had never reached across the realm boundary, even while the gateway stood open. His master could be a few steps away on the other side and still know nothing of this.
"Tian. You did well."
"I couldn’t stop it," Tian said.
"That wasn’t your job. Keeping those eighteen alive is. Stay clear of it."

Leon kept the plaque in his hand after Tian ended the connection. He had expected his master to be waiting when he returned. Until this moment, he hadn’t realized how much comfort he’d taken from that.
Seraphine watched him from beside the crates. He gave her a small nod, then called the forward party together and told them what had happened.
Two carriers exchanged uneasy looks. A recorder sat down on a crate, his writing brush still in his hand. Wen Shu asked another scout to take her watch before coming down to hear Leon’s instructions.
"We have supplies and a secure base," Leon told them. "We’ll keep gathering information. If you notice anything about these people’s equipment that might help, tell Vyra."
The recorder looked toward the confiscated survey instruments, then stood and went to fetch his slate.
Seraphine came and stood at his shoulder.
"Young Master," she said, very low.
"I know."
"Do we know when it opens?"
"We don’t knowifit opens," he said quietly. "Not on any schedule anyone’s told us about. Not from any direction I’ve seen."

He looked across the basin at the line of fifteen people in gray leather coats, sitting on the stone with their bruises and their confiscated gear. They had come in from somewhere. They had been here longer than the Palace had. Their leader kept watching the bound book beside Vyra’s slate.
Leon picked it up. He couldn’t read a word of it.
A few minutes ago, he had wanted to know where Harrowmark had found more treasure. Now he carried the book toward their leader with a different question.

Even the man gasping around Ira’s lance managed to keep still.
The gray-haired woman opened her hands at her sides.
Her gaze passed over the two men Seraphine and Ira had put down, then returned to the swordsman still kneeling before Leon.
"We yield," she said.
The words came to Leon as clipped foreign sounds and arrived as perfectly clear meaning, and he was already starting to get used to that, which was its own kind of strange.
"All of you?" Leon asked.
"All of us." Her jaw tightened.
"You have made your point."
"Not quite yet." Leon released the swordsman’s wrist, and the man pitched forward onto his hands and stayed there, breathing hard.
"You attacked first.
On ground you’d claimed by walking onto it before we did.
So here are my terms."
He did not raise his voice.
He did not need to.
"Everything you’ve harvested from this spring comes to me.
So does every treasure you’re carrying, every piece of equipment worth more than its weight in rations, and every route record you have.
You keep your food, your water, your bedding, and enough tools to get yourselves somewhere else."
"That is robbery."
"Yes," said Leon.
"It is."
She stared at him.
"You drew on me," he went on.
"Your swordsman came across the stone with a blade already moving.
If I hadn’t stopped him, would you be offering to return my belongings?" He shrugged slightly.
"You lost.
This is what losing costs."
The woman looked toward the ridge behind him, then at her crossbowman.
The man set his weapon on the stone.
Leon waited.
He had no interest in bargaining down the price of an attack on his people.
"Agreed," she said.
He called Vyra in after that, and the twenty-five came over the rise in good order and took the basin in about four minutes.
The fifteen from Harrowmark sat in a line along the eastern edge under Ira’s supervision, which was supervision in the sense that Ira sat on a crate facing them and ate an apple very slowly.
Nobody in that line made any sudden movements.
Loriel checked the three injured men.
Ira’s opponent had a cracked rib, the spearman a concussion, and the first swordsman had bitten his tongue when Leon forced him to his knees.
She treated them without asking.
Leon left her to it; he had agreed to let them walk away, and he meant it.
Vyra had the recorders work in pairs, one checking each surrendered item while the other noted it down.
"Spring crystal already cut," she said, reading from a slate.
"Eleven crates.
Logged as seized stock, not as harvest — they didn’t come out of our cuts and they don’t go in the same column." She moved down.
"Personal treasure.
Three storage pouches, contents unknown until opened, logged unopened.
One pouch of what looks like refined crystal — better grade than anything in the crates.
Equipment: the crossbow, which Bai Heng wants to look at very badly.
Two survey instruments I don’t recognize.
Four blades with bronze fittings."
"And the route records?" Leon asked.
"A bound book and a rolled chart." Vyra laid both beside the slate.
"The leader was reluctant to hand these over.
We should have her explain them before she leaves."
"Keep her here," Leon said.
"And put aside a sample of that refined crystal for my allocation."
"Already noted, Young Master."
Leon opened the pouch of refined crystal himself and looked at it for a while.
The crystals were pale green, cleanly cut, and hummed faintly in his palm with energy that did not belong to any single affinity.
He held it toward the leader.
"From this spring?"
She nodded reluctantly.
"The outer growth.
Refined twice."
And now I get to find out what it does.
He closed the pouch, pleased despite the trouble.
The spring had looked promising before.
This was something he could test.
His internal plaque warmed against his chest while the recorders were checking the third crate.
He had expected Wen Shu, who was holding the ridgeline to the south.
It was Tian Mingxu, from the entrance base.
"Senior Brother." Her voice came through level, which in Tian meant considerably more than it would in anyone else.
"The gateway’s gone."
Leon stopped moving.
"Say that again."
"The gateway we came through.
The watch saw its edges draw together.
It vanished before they could finish calling me." A pause.
"We’ve examined the site from the marked boundary.
There’s no visible opening left."
"Your people?"
"All eighteen here.
I’ve counted twice.
Nobody was near the edge when it went and nobody’s hurt."
"When?"
"Three minutes ago.
I counted everyone before contacting you.
We have a record of the closure and the site as it stands.
Nobody has tried to cross."
"Keep it that way," said Leon.
"Don’t send anyone toward where it was.
Hold the camp, record anything that changes, and check the ground every hour.
If something opens, you tell me before anyone walks into it."
"Understood."
There was no point asking about Ji.
Their plaques had never reached across the realm boundary, even while the gateway stood open.
His master could be a few steps away on the other side and still know nothing of this.
"Tian.
You did well."
"I couldn’t stop it," Tian said.
"That wasn’t your job.
Keeping those eighteen alive is.
Stay clear of it."
Leon kept the plaque in his hand after Tian ended the connection.
He had expected his master to be waiting when he returned.
Until this moment, he hadn’t realized how much comfort he’d taken from that.
Seraphine watched him from beside the crates.
He gave her a small nod, then called the forward party together and told them what had happened.
Two carriers exchanged uneasy looks.
A recorder sat down on a crate, his writing brush still in his hand.
Wen Shu asked another scout to take her watch before coming down to hear Leon’s instructions.
"We have supplies and a secure base," Leon told them.
"We’ll keep gathering information.
If you notice anything about these people’s equipment that might help, tell Vyra."
The recorder looked toward the confiscated survey instruments, then stood and went to fetch his slate.
Seraphine came and stood at his shoulder.
"Young Master," she said, very low.
"I know."
"Do we know when it opens?"
"We don’t knowifit opens," he said quietly.
"Not on any schedule anyone’s told us about.
Not from any direction I’ve seen."
He looked across the basin at the line of fifteen people in gray leather coats, sitting on the stone with their bruises and their confiscated gear.
They had come in from somewhere.
They had been here longer than the Palace had.
Their leader kept watching the bound book beside Vyra’s slate.
Leon picked it up.
He couldn’t read a word of it.
A few minutes ago, he had wanted to know where Harrowmark had found more treasure.
Now he carried the book toward their leader with a different question.

chapters.title: Chapter 708: A World Beyond the Map
paragraphs: "Where did you come in?" Leon asked.

The gray-haired woman looked up at him from the stone. She had been sitting apart from her people since the seizure, her hands resting empty on her knees. Leon set the confiscated book on a crate between them.
"Through our gate," she said.
"Which is where?" Leon asked.

"Two days’ travel from here, to the west and down. A cleft between two standing stones." She regarded him with open curiosity now, which was an improvement on contempt. "It is how everyone from Tessaryn enters."
"Tessaryn?" Leon repeated.
"My home." She said it as if the word should mean something. When it did not, she tilted her head. "You do not know it."
"No."
"The Vaeloran coast? The Hundred Ports?" She studied his face. "The Salt Crown?"
Leon shook his head to each.

He had read enough Palace maps to recognize the major territories around Moonfall. None of her names meant anything to him, but that proved very little. There were whole regions he knew only as patches of ink, and others he had never seen on a chart at all.
Her expression suggested she found his ignorance equally surprising.
"Tell me your name," he said.
"Idrett Haske. Expedition commander." A faint dry edge came into her voice. "Formerly."

The book held a working log, dense with symbols Leon could not read. When he asked whether she had anything showing her homeland, Idrett pointed to a flat disc of dark glass among the confiscated possessions. Vyra brought it over.
"It keeps what the bearer sees," said Idrett. "Ours was made for the crossing. Every expedition carries one, so that if we do not return, somebody may one day learn what happened to us."
"Show me," Leon said, sliding it across the crate.
She pressed her thumb into its center, and the glass woke.

The image came up above it, faint but clear. A harbor at dawn — a long curving quay of pale stone, ships with sails dyed deep red, and beyond them a city climbing a hillside in terraces of white and ocher. The light was wrong. Leon noticed it before he noticed anything else. It was warmer than any light he had seen in this world, with a faint copper cast.
Then the sky.
Two suns stood above the harbor. One large and pale gold, low on the horizon. One smaller, higher, the color of a coin.
Leon looked at it for a long time.
"That’s where you left from," he said.
"That is the Salt Crown. The capital of the Hundred Ports." Idrett watched his face. "You have not seen two suns before."
"Not here."

The image moved on — a road through dry hills, the red-sailed harbor receding behind, and then a standing arch of dark stone in the middle of open plain, with a wavering surface inside it. Leon leaned closer. The way the road disappeared into that surface resembled a spatial entrance, although a recording could tell him nothing about its workings.
The arch stood in open sunlight. No buried nexus, no stormglass platform. This approach to the realm had been built somewhere entirely different.
The last image was the passage itself: a gray tunnel of distorted light, and then the pale stone of this realm, and a group of people in gray leather coats blinking in the flat daylight.
"Tessaryn is your world?" Leon asked. "Not a territory within it?"
"Our world," Idrett said. "The Salt Crown rules the Hundred Ports. It certainly does not rule all of Tessaryn."
Leon glanced at the two suns as the recording returned to its first image.
"And your entrance is still open?"
"It was when our scouts last checked. We’ve been here nineteen days. We expected to return through it."
"When did they check?" Leon asked.
"Six days ago."
That was too old to trust. His own entrance had existed this morning.
"You’ll get a copy of your route," he said. "But I’m not promising you’ll find a gate at the end of it."
Idrett’s hand tightened around the disc. For the first time since surrendering, she looked past her missing equipment toward the western ridges.
The Palace personnel took it harder than he did, which he had expected.

Bai Heng had watched the whole record with his cracked lens forgotten in his hand. When it ended he said, very quietly, "Two suns," and nothing else for several minutes. Wen Shu kept looking from the record to Idrett’s face and back again, as though one of them might start making sense of the other.
"A different world," said one of the recorders. "Adifferent world. And they walked in through a door."
"Their door, into our realm," said another. "Or the realm’s not ours. The realm’s just — here. And we both walked into it."
That, Leon thought, was precisely right.
He had crossed between worlds himself. His own dimensional world held people with lives they had brought from elsewhere. The existence of other worlds had never been a question for him.
He had still been thinking of this expedition as a Palace venture, with competitors somewhere beyond its guarded entrance.
How many doors does this place have?
It was a place other worlds could reach. Other gates, other people, other expeditions with their own reasons for being here and no particular interest in the Jade Moon Palace’s claim.

He kept his own history to himself. Instead, he asked the recorder to make a careful copy of the transit images. Whatever they found next, Ji would need more than a story about strangers with marks on their foreheads.
He asked his questions after that, plainly, and Idrett answered most of them.
"Do you know any other possible exits?" Leon asked.
"No."
"Did anyone test whether your gate admits people from other worlds?" Leon asked.
"I do not know. We have never tried to bring anyone through." She considered it. "I would not assume it."
Leon opened the book. "How much of this place have you mapped?"

"Our route. Our gate to here, and three days in two other directions." She nodded at the book lying open between them. "It is all in there. Our observations, not the realm’s shape. We saw what we walked past."
"What else have you seen?" he asked.
"Other expeditions. Four, from a distance. Two I would not approach." She hesitated. "And the storm."
"What storm?" Leon asked.
Idrett pulled the book closer and turned to a sketch near the back — a long curved band drawn across the page, with shading along one edge and small marks along the other.

"It moves," she said. "Slowly, from the east. Four days ago we watched it pass across a plain north of here. Before it came, the ground was gray crust. Hard, and charged — if you touched it, it bit." She tapped the marks. "After it passed, the crust was gone. Stripped off. And underneath were mineral beds. Rich ones. We took some before the next group arrived."
"How many groups?" Leon asked.

"Three reached it within a day." She traced the band forward. "It is still moving. By our reckoning it will cross the northeastern flats in two to three days. And from what we saw on the way here, others are already going to meet it."
Leon released Harrowmark that afternoon.

Fifteen people in gray leather coats, with their food, water, bedding, and basic tools. Idrett had translated the route markers while a recorder copied them, and Vyra handed her the finished chart. The original stayed with Leon, its entrance site clearly marked for investigation.
"You’ll have been expecting worse," Leon said.

"I have been expecting worse since your swordswoman took Rennick’s spear." Idrett shouldered her pack. "You took everything of value we had. You did not kill anyone. That is more than I would have done in your place."
"I know," said Leon. "Which is why I’ll tell you this once. If any of you comes at mine again, you won’t get this conversation."
She looked at him for a moment.
"Understood," she said, and led her people west.
Leon went back to the bound book, and to the sketch near the back, and to the long curved line of a storm crossing a map of a world nobody in the Palace had ever seen.
Along its path, marked in Idrett’s small hand, were four circles.
Beside two of them she had written a symbol he could not read. She had explained it before she left:others heading here.

chapters.title: Chapter 709: Fuel He Can Use
paragraphs: By the following morning, Bai Heng had found something wrong with Harrowmark’s refined crystal. He was humming over it when Leon arrived.

His refining kit occupied a flat stone beside the spring: a nest of ceramic crucibles, a small regulated heat plate, a set of sieving screens that folded down to nothing, and a hand-array for separating impurities that he had clearly used so many times its grip had worn to the shape of his fingers.
"Start small," he said, when Leon came over. "That’s the whole trick with anything I haven’t handled. Small, and watch it, and don’t be clever until it’s told you what it does."
He had three of the seized Harrowmark crystals set out in a row — the green ones from the refined pouch. Beside them, a raw chunk of spring crystal cut from the ring structure that morning.

"See these dark flecks?" Bai Heng held a green crystal under his lens. "Their process leaves those behind. There are fractures too, possibly from heat. It may be perfectly usable for them, but I want a cleaner sample before you try it." He tapped the raw chunk. "We’ll start with this."
It took him most of the day.

He ground the raw chunk, sieved it through three screens, and heated it on the plate at a rate so slow that Leon found it painful to watch. He ran the hand-array over the result and pulled out a thin gray sediment that he set aside in a separate dish. A second heating and another pass through the finest screen left barely enough material to cover the bottom of the crucible.
By evening, a fist-sized raw crystal had become a pale green residue about the volume of a thimble, and separate dishes of sediment, spent lattice, and cloudy liquid.

"Roughly one part in six by weight," Bai Heng said, checking his balance. "The rest is in those dishes, apart from what evaporated. I’d like to study the sediment before calling all of it waste." He sealed the thimble of residue in a clean jar. "It’s clean. As clean as I can make it with what I’ve got. No affinity to speak of — it’s mostly neutral, with a faint lean toward life. I’d guess that’s the spring."
"Can I have it?"
"It’s your allocation." Bai Heng handed the jar across. "Tell me what it does."

Leon took it into the small tent the household had pitched for him at the spring’s edge, and Seraphine stood at the flap and made it clear to everybody within fifty paces that the Young Master was resting.
He sat on the ground with the jar in his hands and ran a single, careful circulation first, to be certain the Scripture was exactly where he had left it.
The nine branches maintained their differing rates, returning smoothly through the foundation he had established. Satisfied, he turned to the sample.
He opened the jar and loosened a small portion of the residue’s stored energy.

He admitted a trace to the neutral center first. The purchased condensate had required almost no adjustment; this sample carried a lingering quality he could feel but could not yet identify. He separated what did not settle cleanly and kept it outside the circulation.

The usable portion fed the nine branches at their established rates. Leon increased the supply a little, waited, then repeated the test while watching the returning flows. After four full cycles, he found no accumulating strain.
He remained at Mid Foundation Establishment. The quantity was far too small for advancement, but it had sustained the Scripture without disrupting it.
It works.

It was a thimble. It proved that Bai Heng’s method worked on spring crystal, with expedition equipment, for Leon’s circulation specifically. It did not prove anything about the storm-field minerals, or the violet ore from the terrace, or any of the other things he had started wanting.

But he had burned through ten reservoirs of purchased condensate — a hundred and ten million Causality of fuel — and had come into this realm with none left, and wondering where the next supply would come from.
He had just watched an old man produce some from a rock.
I can get more of this.

He sat with the empty jar for a while, enjoying that thought. Before he forgot, he wrote down the quantity he had rejected and how the usable portion had behaved. Bai Heng had asked for the results, and Leon wanted the next batch cleaner.
Then he did the other thing, which he had been thinking about since Tian’s voice came through the plaque.
With Seraphine guarding the tent, Leon opened a narrow connection to his dimensional world. He checked the space behind him, then widened the aperture enough for his second body to step through.

The clone had been training and exploring there, occasionally returning to the people under his care to give guidance or settle something that required him. Most days, he preferred to let them manage their own affairs.

None of that needed recalling or reporting. He had been present for it, just as he had been present at the spring. Sharing attention between two bodies had felt strange at first. By now, he usually noticed it only when both needed something delicate at once.

Having both in the tent was briefly distracting. From the floor, he watched himself step around the bedding. From beside the wall, he saw his seated body’s untidy hair and the empty jar balanced on one knee.
I should probably comb that.
He moved his standing body out of sight of the flap and let his attention settle.

There was no reason to take the household down every unknown route he wanted to inspect. His original body would remain with them. Alone, the clone could explore faster and take risks he would never impose on the collectors.

Harrowmark’s recorded entrance was one lead. Other expeditions might know more, and any rich deposits he found could supply the Scripture. He wanted all three: a way out, information, and resources worth the trouble of gathering.
The map gave him a starting point, not a promise. He would check routes as he explored, without leading the whole expedition after a six-day-old report.
Getting it out of the camp was the part that required care.

A second Leon walking past the crates would have ended any number of secrets at once. So the second body went out through the tent’s back wall, through a fold of space that ended forty paces behind the southern ridge, and it went out with its aura suppressed and its face in shadow under a cloak that had come through the connection with it.
Seraphine, standing at the flap, did not turn around.
"Out?" Seraphine asked quietly.
"Behind the ridge," Leon answered from his seated body.
She glanced through the flap. "Tell me if you find anything dangerous. Before you get occupied with it."
"I will." He smiled at her. "You can stop watching the doorway now."
"Once you close the aperture."
He checked behind him. Fair enough.
Behind the southern ridge, his second body settled the cloak over its shoulders, looked across the unmapped ridges, and started walking. Leon closed the connection to his dimensional world.
In the tent, the original stood up, put the empty jar in his pocket, and went out to find out whether Bai Heng had eaten anything since morning.
