No affinity to speak of — it’s mostly neutral, with a faint lean toward life.
I’d guess that’s the spring."
"Can I have it?"
"It’s your allocation." Bai Heng handed the jar across.
"Tell me what it does."

Leon took it into the small tent the household had pitched for him at the spring’s edge, and Seraphine stood at the flap and made it clear to everybody within fifty paces that the Young Master was resting.
He sat on the ground with the jar in his hands and ran a single, careful circulation first, to be certain the Scripture was exactly where he had left it.
The nine branches maintained their differing rates, returning smoothly through the foundation he had established.
Satisfied, he turned to the sample.
He opened the jar and loosened a small portion of the residue’s stored energy.
He admitted a trace to the neutral center first.
The purchased condensate had required almost no adjustment; this sample carried a lingering quality he could feel but could not yet identify.
He separated what did not settle cleanly and kept it outside the circulation.
The usable portion fed the nine branches at their established rates.
Leon increased the supply a little, waited, then repeated the test while watching the returning flows.
After four full cycles, he found no accumulating strain.
He remained at Mid Foundation Establishment.
The quantity was far too small for advancement, but it had sustained the Scripture without disrupting it.
It works.
It was a thimble.
It proved that Bai Heng’s method worked on spring crystal, with expedition equipment, for Leon’s circulation specifically.
It did not prove anything about the storm-field minerals, or the violet ore from the terrace, or any of the other things he had started wanting.

But he had burned through ten reservoirs of purchased condensate — a hundred and ten million Causality of fuel — and had come into this realm with none left, and wondering where the next supply would come from.
He had just watched an old man produce some from a rock.
I can get more of this.
He sat with the empty jar for a while, enjoying that thought.
Before he forgot, he wrote down the quantity he had rejected and how the usable portion had behaved.
Bai Heng had asked for the results, and Leon wanted the next batch cleaner.
Then he did the other thing, which he had been thinking about since Tian’s voice came through the plaque.
With Seraphine guarding the tent, Leon opened a narrow connection to his dimensional world.
He checked the space behind him, then widened the aperture enough for his second body to step through.
The clone had been training and exploring there, occasionally returning to the people under his care to give guidance or settle something that required him.
Most days, he preferred to let them manage their own affairs.
None of that needed recalling or reporting.
He had been present for it, just as he had been present at the spring.
Sharing attention between two bodies had felt strange at first.
By now, he usually noticed it only when both needed something delicate at once.
Having both in the tent was briefly distracting.
From the floor, he watched himself step around the bedding.
From beside the wall, he saw his seated body’s untidy hair and the empty jar balanced on one knee.
I should probably comb that.
He moved his standing body out of sight of the flap and let his attention settle.
There was no reason to take the household down every unknown route he wanted to inspect.
His original body would remain with them.
Alone, the clone could explore faster and take risks he would never impose on the collectors.
Harrowmark’s recorded entrance was one lead.
Other expeditions might know more, and any rich deposits he found could supply the Scripture.
He wanted all three: a way out, information, and resources worth the trouble of gathering.
The map gave him a starting point, not a promise.
He would check routes as he explored, without leading the whole expedition after a six-day-old report.
Getting it out of the camp was the part that required care.
A second Leon walking past the crates would have ended any number of secrets at once.

So the second body went out through the tent’s back wall, through a fold of space that ended forty paces behind the southern ridge, and it went out with its aura suppressed and its face in shadow under a cloak that had come through the connection with it.
Seraphine, standing at the flap, did not turn around.
"Out?" Seraphine asked quietly.
"Behind the ridge," Leon answered from his seated body.
She glanced through the flap.
"Tell me if you find anything dangerous.
Before you get occupied with it."
"I will." He smiled at her.
"You can stop watching the doorway now."
"Once you close the aperture."
He checked behind him.
Fair enough.
Behind the southern ridge, his second body settled the cloak over its shoulders, looked across the unmapped ridges, and started walking.
Leon closed the connection to his dimensional world.
In the tent, the original stood up, put the empty jar in his pocket, and went out to find out whether Bai Heng had eaten anything since morning.

chapters.title: Chapter 710: Beyond the Gathering Route
paragraphs: Bai Heng looked up from the map. "And if your plaque stops answering?"
Leon had been considering the same problem. Leaving the spring meant putting distance between himself and people he was responsible for.
Eighteen stayed at the entrance base under Tian, where they had been since entry — keeping the supply camp, watching the place where the door had been, and checking the ground every hour.

Twelve stayed at the spring under Bai Heng. That was the decision that took longest, because it meant leaving an old extraction master with eleven crates of confiscated crystal in a realm where at least one expedition had already shown what it did to people it found near valuables.
"Then you don’t wait for me," Leon said. "You fall back toward Tian along our marked route. We’ve tested your link to the base this morning. Keep checking it."
Four of the twelve would guard the spring. The other eight, including Bai Heng, would gather and process its crystals. They would take only the outer growth the extraction master judged safe to cut.
Leon tapped the second marker south of the basin.
"Use this as your assembly point. If you have to withdraw, take the people first. Anything you can’t carry stays."
"Eleven crates," Bai Heng said, without quite making it an objection.
"I know how many. We can recover crates."
The old man studied him, then nodded. "Understood, Senior Brother."

Tian received the same instructions over the plaque. Bai Heng would report to her at dawn and dusk, while Leon’s group would test its connection along the northern route. If contact failed, his party would return to the last tested point before dusk on their third day away. Until then, neither camp was to count on an immediate response from him.
Vyra had both camp leaders repeat the arrangements before she closed the map.
Eighteen went north toward the storm: Leon, the four women, and thirteen Palace personnel — Wen Shu and two other scouts, four field collectors, two recorders, and four carriers.
Leon counted the departing eighteen himself before they left. Between the base, the spring, and this column, all forty-eight Palace entrants were accounted for.
His other body was already beyond the camp, walking east beneath a borrowed cloak.
The first stretch north of the spring looked much like the country around the terrace.

They crossed broken pale ground where distance remained unreliable. The scouts placed stakes every few hundred paces, and Vyra checked their sightings before allowing the carriers forward. The plaque check with the spring went through cleanly at the first marker, weaker at the second, and not at all at the third.
"Range," said Vyra. "Or terrain. Either way, it’s gone."
"Go back to the second and check again," Leon said.

The reply came through once the scout retraced her steps. Vyra marked that position, then sent their planned return time to Bai Heng. Leon watched her put the plaque away with considerably less satisfaction than he had felt carrying it that morning.
He could cross rough ground quickly. Eighteen people with gathering equipment could not. If trouble came at the spring, Bai Heng would have to follow the withdrawal plan.

By afternoon they reached long, low ridges running east to west. Each rose a little higher than the last, with shallow valleys between them where green grass grew knee-high. Leon slowed at the first patch. He had grown used to seeing plants cling to crystal and crust.
Loriel stopped at the edge of the first valley and put her hand in it.
"Roots in soil," Loriel said, parting the blades. "No crystal growth around them."
"Worth collecting?" a carrier asked.
"A little soil, if we can spare a jar." She smiled up at him. "I’d like to know what else grows here."
The carrier found one. Leon waited while she took her sample; a patch of ordinary green was pleasant to look at after so much pale stone.
Ira had fallen into step beside Leon on the second ridge, and was looking north with narrowed eyes.
"You’re somewhere else," she said quietly.
He glanced at her.
"Not all of you. But you keep looking east when there’s nothing there." She did not turn her head. "Is it — are you all right?"
"I’m fine," Leon murmured, waiting until the carrier ahead was out of earshot. "Rocks so far. A better view than this one."
"Good." A pause. "Tell me if there’s something on it besides rocks."
"You’ll be the first."
She nodded once and went back to watching north.
Four kilometers to the east, on a spine of bare rock the gathering column could never have climbed, Leon lay flat on a ledge in his second body and looked down.

He had been moving since dawn — faster alone than any column could go, across ground a party of eighteen would have needed ropes for. Out here he had nobody to keep alive but himself, and he could take whatever line the rock allowed.
He had found a pass.

Not a large one: a gap between two ridges, perhaps thirty paces wide, running north toward the storm field on a line that appeared to cut several hours off Idrett’s recorded route. The ground through it was firm. The distances agreed with themselves.
And there was something in the pass that was not rock.
A camp — or what was left of one. Stakes, a cold firepit, a torn length of blue canvas. Tracks going north, many of them, heavy and recent.
Leon lay on the ledge and looked at the tracks for a long while.
A fair-sized party. Recent, too.
Several prints still held sharp edges in the loose dust. He followed them with his gaze until they disappeared around the bend, but saw nobody moving.

He did not know who they were. He did not know where they had come from or what they wanted. The shorter route was promising. The abandoned camp meant somebody else might already be waiting at the far end.
He fixed the pass’s position in his mind, then slid back off the ledge and kept moving north.
Back on the second ridge, Leon stopped the column.
"Wen Shu."
The scout came up.
"The route in Idrett’s book. How far to the storm field from here?"
"Another day and a half at this pace," Wen Shu said. "The book takes us around the long western ridge."
"I have another route I want checked," Leon said. "About four kilometers east. There should be a pass running north between those ridges."
He indicated the direction without explaining how he knew. Wen Shu glanced at him, then unfolded her chart.
"How far should I scout it?"
"To the northern opening. Check the ground yourself. We don’t take the carriers through until you’re satisfied."
She left with another scout. Leon kept the column on the broad ridge while, farther east, his second body continued alone. When Wen Shu returned, she confirmed the pass and the tracks.

They reached its southern opening before stopping for the night. The next morning’s crossing saved them several hours of the longer western route, enough to reach the plain before making the return journey for their scheduled contact check.
Shortly after noon on the second day, the eighteen came over the last ridge and stopped.

Below them the land fell away into a vast flat plain, twenty kilometers across at the least, and most of it was gray. Hard gray crust, cracked and glinting in the pale light, stretching away to the north and east until it met the horizon.
And along the eastern edge of the plain, moving slowly west, was the storm.

A curving wall of dark air rose perhaps a kilometer above the plain, violet flashes running through it. Behind its passage, the gray crust had vanished. Patches of exposed mineral caught the light all the way to the distant workings.
Seraphine made a small sound beside him.
"There," she said, pointing. "And there. And—"
Along the edge of the stripped ground, spread out at intervals of a kilometer or so, were camps.

Leon counted six of them before he stopped. Bright tents stood behind clusters of workers. Along the nearest, a line of people was laying out extraction tools in a neat row along the edge of the exposed beds, waiting for the storm to move another step west.
At least six other groups had reached the mineral field ahead of them. Leon lowered the chart. They would have to find somewhere worth taking before the storm passed.

chapters.title: Chapter 711: What the Storm Uncovers
paragraphs: The camps along the storm’s edge were not all the same, and Leon spent the first hour learning to tell them apart.

The nearest belonged to a group in long dark blue coats who moved with military precision — scouts at the edges, a clear command tent, extraction tools laid out in exact rows. They had watched the Palace scouts appear along the ridge and had adjusted their perimeter by thirty paces without anyone appearing to give an order.
"Disciplined," Seraphine said. "Watch how they cover their collectors. They’ll be quick to respond if we approach."

The next was louder. A dozen people around a fire with no obvious command structure, several of them arguing, one of them waving what looked like a long flat blade at another. Their tents were patched. Their tools were scattered.
"That one keeps pointing at the blue coats," Ira said. "I don’t think they’re getting along."

Beyond them, a small group had set up a trestle table at the edge of their claim and was doing business. Leon watched two people from the blue-coat camp walk over to it, stand talking for a quarter of an hour, and walk back with a crate.
"Traders," said Vyra. "Or a group that decided it’s easier to sell what they’ve dug than defend it."

There were three more beyond those, too far off to read clearly. One flew a banner. One had a perimeter of what looked like stakes driven into the crust with something bound to them. One seemed to be doing nothing at all.
Leon could not see enough of the distant camps to judge their numbers. Even the nearest had people moving in and out of tents, making a reliable count difficult.
And not one of them is Harrowmark.
The storm moved while they watched. Leon turned his attention from the camps to the crust breaking beneath it.

It was not steady. It crept west for perhaps half an hour, barely moving, and then it lurched — a sudden forward surge of a hundred paces, the violet flickering in its heart going bright and continuous — and where it had surged, the crust came apart.

He saw it happen from the ridge. The gray crust did not crack. Itlifted, peeled up off the ground in plates and sheets as the charged air at the storm’s edge passed over it, and the plates tumbled back into the storm and vanished. What was left behind was bare mineral bed, glittering and wet-looking and entirely exposed.
"The storm eats the crust," said Wen Shu, very quietly. "It strips it off and takes it."
"And leaves what was underneath," Leon said.
One of the field collectors — a young man called Lu Pei, whom Bai Heng had trained for two years — had his glass up and was scanning the nearest stripped bed. He barely lowered it when he spoke.

"There’s red," he said. "Fire — that dull red, like the terrace. And there’s blue-white along the far side, that’ll be ice-bearing. And something gray-green in between that I don’t — " He lowered the glass, frustrated. "Senior Brother, Bai Heng would know that in a second. I don’t. I can tell you it’s worth taking. I can’t tell you what it is."
"That’s enough for now," Leon told him.
"I’d need to cut a sample to be sure of anything."
"You’ll get the chance," Leon said. "Keep looking. Tell me if you see a clear approach."

Leon looked at the stripped ground with the specific attention of a man who had watched a thimble of spring residue feed his circulation two days ago. Red and blue-white: Fire and Ice, both of them his. He wanted samples of the gray-green material too, although he would wait for an examination before deciding what it was worth.

The camps occupied the exposed beds east of the storm, extending their gathering lines west as it moved away. Stakes and guards marked the richer patches. Farther north, a raised shelf of unbroken crust interrupted the line of workings. Nobody was cutting there yet.
Let’s see what’s under that.

Leon moved the Palace party along the ridge to a low rise east of the workings. The raised shelf lay roughly two kilometers to their northwest, beyond the northernmost marked claims. From here, they could reach it without crossing an occupied mineral bed.

"Nobody goes near the active front," he said. "Not the collectors, not the carriers, and not the scouts. When it strips ground, we let it settle before we walk on it. I’m not putting anybody into charged air to get to a rock first."
"The others are," said one of the carriers.
"They know more about this storm than we do," Leon said. "Or they’re gambling. Either way, we wait."

He spent the next two hours watching, increasingly aware of the time they would need to get back within plaque range. There would be no long excavation tonight. If they found something worthwhile, they could mark it, take samples, and decide how to work it after reporting to the spring.
The northern shelf resisted the first sweep of charged air. Plates peeled away on either side while its thick surface merely trembled.
On the next surge, a crack opened across it.
Lu Pei lowered his glass. "That section’s deeper than the rest."

Leon had seen it too. The moving wall curved around the stubborn shelf, leaving it protruding into the cleared ground. Then another violet flare ran through the storm. A slab the size of a house lifted, broke in two, and vanished into the churning air.
Color shone beneath it.

A broad mineral belt ran north along the shelf, its exposed portion dense with red and blue-white growth. Gray-green deposits filled the hollows between them. Farther in, violet veins appeared as the remaining fragments tore free.
Lu Pei brought his glass up so quickly he knocked it against his cheek.
"Careful," Loriel said, steadying his elbow.
"Look at how close the seams are," he said. "If they’re sound beneath the surface—"
"We take samples first," Leon reminded him, already studying the approach.

The storm continued west, leaving the belt’s eastern margin clear. No stakes stood there. The nearest rival collectors were still working the smaller beds to its south, although that would change as soon as someone looked up.
Leon felt a familiar eagerness. He had spent too much on cultivation to watch a field like this disappear into other people’s storage pouches.
Beside him, Lu Pei checked the padding inside his sample case, tugging each divider into place. His careful hands were steadier now that he had work to do.
"How many samples can you carry?" Leon asked.
"Enough to tell Master Bai what we found. More if the carriers help."
"They will. Start with the exposed seams. Don’t waste time digging for the deepest growth."
Lu Pei nodded and fastened the case across his chest.

"Wen Shu, check the approach. Lu Pei, bring the sample tools. We’re taking the eastern margin, behind the storm’s passage. Keep at least three hundred paces from the charged air. If it turns or spreads toward us, pull back."
"Two kilometers of open ground," Wen Shu said. "The camps will see us."
"Then we go now." Leon turned toward his household. "Seraphine, front. Ira, left flank. Vyra, keep the column together and the collectors covered. Loriel, with the collectors."
"Yes, Young Master," said Seraphine, and was already moving.
They came off the rise in good order and started northwest across the cleared plain toward the belt, and for about two minutes nobody else on the field seemed to notice.
Then the blue-coat camp noticed.
Leon saw their perimeter shift — a clean, disciplined contraction, and then a group of perhaps twenty breaking off from it and moving toward the exposed shelf, fast, in formation.
A moment later the loud group noticed too, and did not move in formation at all. They simply came, in a scattered straggling rush across the crust, the man with the long flat blade out in front.
Beyond the blue coats, figures were gathering beneath the distant banner. A third party broke away from that camp.
Leon kept pace with his collectors. He could reach the belt far ahead of them, but leaving the column exposed between three approaching groups would be a foolish way to claim it.
Seraphine glanced back, waiting for his instruction.
"Keep going," he said.
The blue coats accelerated. Leon watched their leading swordsman change course toward the same clear strip he had chosen.
They had both seen where to plant the first marker.

He wanted samples of the gray-green material too, although he would wait for an examination before deciding what it was worth.
The camps occupied the exposed beds east of the storm, extending their gathering lines west as it moved away.
Stakes and guards marked the richer patches.
Farther north, a raised shelf of unbroken crust interrupted the line of workings.
Nobody was cutting there yet.
Let’s see what’s under that.
Leon moved the Palace party along the ridge to a low rise east of the workings.
The raised shelf lay roughly two kilometers to their northwest, beyond the northernmost marked claims.
From here, they could reach it without crossing an occupied mineral bed.
"Nobody goes near the active front," he said.
"Not the collectors, not the carriers, and not the scouts.
When it strips ground, we let it settle before we walk on it.
I’m not putting anybody into charged air to get to a rock first."
"The others are," said one of the carriers.
"They know more about this storm than we do," Leon said.
"Or they’re gambling.
Either way, we wait."
He spent the next two hours watching, increasingly aware of the time they would need to get back within plaque range.
There would be no long excavation tonight.
If they found something worthwhile, they could mark it, take samples, and decide how to work it after reporting to the spring.
The northern shelf resisted the first sweep of charged air.
Plates peeled away on either side while its thick surface merely trembled.
On the next surge, a crack opened across it.
Lu Pei lowered his glass.
"That section’s deeper than the rest."
Leon had seen it too.
The moving wall curved around the stubborn shelf, leaving it protruding into the cleared ground.
Then another violet flare ran through the storm.
A slab the size of a house lifted, broke in two, and vanished into the churning air.
Color shone beneath it.
A broad mineral belt ran north along the shelf, its exposed portion dense with red and blue-white growth.
Gray-green deposits filled the hollows between them.
Farther in, violet veins appeared as the remaining fragments tore free.
Lu Pei brought his glass up so quickly he knocked it against his cheek.
"Careful," Loriel said, steadying his elbow.
"Look at how close the seams are," he said.
"If they’re sound beneath the surface—"
"We take samples first," Leon reminded him, already studying the approach.
The storm continued west, leaving the belt’s eastern margin clear.
No stakes stood there.
The nearest rival collectors were still working the smaller beds to its south, although that would change as soon as someone looked up.
Leon felt a familiar eagerness.
He had spent too much on cultivation to watch a field like this disappear into other people’s storage pouches.
Beside him, Lu Pei checked the padding inside his sample case, tugging each divider into place.
His careful hands were steadier now that he had work to do.
"How many samples can you carry?" Leon asked.
"Enough to tell Master Bai what we found.
More if the carriers help."
"They will.
Start with the exposed seams.
Don’t waste time digging for the deepest growth."
Lu Pei nodded and fastened the case across his chest.
"Wen Shu, check the approach.
Lu Pei, bring the sample tools.
We’re taking the eastern margin, behind the storm’s passage.
Keep at least three hundred paces from the charged air.
If it turns or spreads toward us, pull back."
"Two kilometers of open ground," Wen Shu said.
"The camps will see us."
"Then we go now." Leon turned toward his household.
"Seraphine, front.
Ira, left flank.
Vyra, keep the column together and the collectors covered.
Loriel, with the collectors."
"Yes, Young Master," said Seraphine, and was already moving.
They came off the rise in good order and started northwest across the cleared plain toward the belt, and for about two minutes nobody else on the field seemed to notice.
Then the blue-coat camp noticed.
Leon saw their perimeter shift — a clean, disciplined contraction, and then a group of perhaps twenty breaking off from it and moving toward the exposed shelf, fast, in formation.
A moment later the loud group noticed too, and did not move in formation at all.
They simply came, in a scattered straggling rush across the crust, the man with the long flat blade out in front.
Beyond the blue coats, figures were gathering beneath the distant banner.
A third party broke away from that camp.
Leon kept pace with his collectors.
He could reach the belt far ahead of them, but leaving the column exposed between three approaching groups would be a foolish way to claim it.
Seraphine glanced back, waiting for his instruction.
"Keep going," he said.
The blue coats accelerated.
Leon watched their leading swordsman change course toward the same clear strip he had chosen.
They had both seen where to plant the first marker.

chapters.title: Chapter 712: The Limit They Trusted
paragraphs: The blue-coat swordsman reached the broken shelf just as the ground opened beneath his next step.
He checked his footing. Leon kept walking.

A small fold shortened the gap ahead of the Palace column, bringing two firm surfaces together long enough for the carriers to cross. Seraphine glanced down as she passed over it. Behind her, Vyra guided the last collector through before Leon let the distance settle back into place.
They reached the mineral belt first.
"Wen Shu. Mark from here to that outcrop." Leon pointed north. "Two hundred paces."

The scout drew pegs from her belt. Red and blue-white seams crowded the exposed stone beneath her boots, with gray-green growth filling the spaces between them. Beyond the outcrop, the same deposits continued farther than Leon could see.
He wanted considerably more than two hundred paces. He also wanted something his four collectors could actually work before they had to leave.
"Shallow cuts first," he told Lu Pei. "Find out what we can carry."
The collector knelt, then looked up again as the blue coats approached.

Their leading swordsman stopped outside Wen Shu’s unfinished line. A broad-shouldered woman in a long blue coat raised her hand behind him, and the others spread into positions facing the remaining approaches.
Leon watched her. She studied the ground he had claimed, then the unmarked beds to its north.
Before either spoke, a voice carried across the crust.
"Leave those stakes where they are. Saves us the trouble."
The loud group had caught up.

Fifteen people approached from the east, led by the scarred man with the long, flat blade. Most carried Golden Core cultivation openly. Several wore bronze plates at their waists, and matching plates had been fitted into their weapons.
Leon noticed those before he paid much attention to the leader’s grin.
Behind him, the carriers stopped beside their empty cases.
"Keep them together," he told Vyra.
"Yes, Young Master."
The scarred man planted his blade against his shoulder.
"Durrow. Ashvard Crew." He glanced at Leon’s pegs. "You’ve picked our ground."
"You can pick some farther north," Leon said.
"The thick seams are here."
"I noticed."
Durrow looked past him at the collectors, then at the four women. His gaze lingered on Seraphine’s sword before returning to Leon.
From the blue coats, the woman called, "There’s enough exposed ground for all three parties."
"Then take your share, Orrin," Durrow said. "This is ours."
He lowered his blade. Behind him, the people carrying bronze plates moved apart, settling into a broad crescent.
Their noise stopped. Boots scraped against stone as they adjusted their spacing, and energy passed between the plates in thin copper lines.
So they do know how to work together.
Leon moved clear of his collectors. Seraphine stayed near their front while Ira took the open flank, her lance held low.
Durrow smiled again when Leon stopped alone before the crescent.
"Nobody above Golden Core gets through those gates," he said. "You’re standing in front of nine."
He tapped his blade against the nearest copper line. The other eight cultivators answered, and their combined pressure gathered along its edge.

The formation drew on each of them in turn. Leon felt the pressure change as one man corrected his contribution, then another. They had practiced this. Whatever arguments filled their camp, none of them needed instructions now.
A young Palace carrier tightened both hands around his empty case. Loriel touched his shoulder and guided him behind a low shelf, where the other specialists had gathered.
Leon was briefly annoyed at the wasted time. Lu Pei should already have been taking samples. Instead, half the people he had brought were watching a stranger decide whether to kill them for rocks.
Then Durrow glanced at his companions, smiling with the ease of a man whose strongest move had always been enough.
Leon knew that look. He was looking forward to removing it.
To Leon’s right, the blue-coat swordsman took a step back. Orrin caught his sleeve and drew him nearer her people.
Durrow saw it too.
"Last chance," he told Leon.
Leon looked at the copper lines crossing the ground between his boots.
They were trying to bind him before the strike. He could feel the restraint tightening around his legs, confidently seeking purchase.
"Move your people back," Leon said to Orrin.
Durrow swung.
The formation flared, driving its gathered force through the long blade. The cut spread as it crossed the last few paces, wide enough to catch Leon even if he dodged toward either side.
He stepped into it.

Space bent around his raised hand. The blade’s path shortened abruptly, bringing Durrow within reach before the man had finished extending his arms. Leon caught his wrist and drove a pulse of his own power through the restraint closing around him.
The copper lines snapped.
Bronze plates burst from their fittings. Eight cultivators staggered as their shared circulation broke, and Leon pulled Durrow forward, taking the blade out of his failing grip.
He struck the man once in the chest.
Durrow hit the stone beyond the pegs and rolled, leaving his companions staring at the empty place where their formation had been.

A cultivator on the outer flank tried to cut toward the Palace collectors. Seraphine knocked his weapon aside and put him down with a blow beneath the ribs. Ira intercepted another with her lance shaft and sent him sprawling beside him.
The rest stopped moving.
Leon turned the captured blade in his hand. One bronze fitting still clung to its spine, smoking faintly.
He had expected the formation to hold together a little longer.
Across the boundary, Orrin was looking from the broken plates to him. Her swordsman had lowered his weapon without appearing to notice.
Durrow dragged himself onto one knee.
"What are you?" he demanded.
Leon walked toward him. "The person who told you to pick somewhere else."
Durrow’s left hand disappeared beneath his coat.
Leon saw the movement, the sudden tightening of the man’s shoulder, and the narrow black blade coming up toward his throat.
He drove the captured sword through Durrow’s chest.
The dagger fell short of his boot.
Leon waited until the body went slack, then withdrew the sword and looked at the others. One woman still held half a formation plate. She dropped it immediately.
"We yield," she said.
"Put down the weapons."
She obeyed. The remaining members of the crew followed, including the two still struggling to stand near Seraphine and Ira.
Leon had no interest in chasing fourteen people across a mineral field. Their packs, however, looked heavy.
"Your gathered treasure and valuable equipment stay," he said. "You can leave with food, water, bedding, and basic tools. Carry him with you."
Nobody argued.

Vyra brought a recorder forward. The surrendered packs contained four crates of mixed ore, a pouch of refined crystals, several good cutting implements, and route records that would need explaining later.
Lu Pei glanced at the tools. Leon caught the look and nodded toward them.
"Have those checked before you use them."
"Yes, Senior Brother."
Two Ashvard survivors wrapped Durrow’s body in his spare cloak. Leon watched them lift it, then returned his attention to the other expeditions.
The banner party had halted well short of the belt.
Orrin said something to her swordsman. He stepped back, and she approached alone, both hands empty.
This time, she stopped before the first peg.
"I think," she said, "we should discuss what you’re about to cut."

chapters.title: Chapter 713: The Price of Keeping It
paragraphs: "You’ll lose part of that deposit before it reaches your boxes," the woman said.
Leon glanced at Lu Pei, who had just set a chisel against a blue-white seam.
"Wait a moment."
The collector lifted his hand.

Their visitor stood outside the pegs, her short sword still sheathed. Up close, Leon could see pale marks along her fingers and an old burn disappearing beneath one cuff. Her coat had been repaired at both elbows.
"Captain Hale Orrin," she said. "Vessian Company."
"Leon. Jade Moon Palace." He indicated the seam. "What are we going to lose?"
"The part you probably came here for." Orrin looked toward her own collectors. "May I bring someone over?"
"One person," Leon said.

She beckoned to an older man carrying a shallow ceramic case. While they waited, the banner expedition turned away from the contested belt. Its bearers followed a leader toward the southern workings, keeping their weapons lowered.
Leon let them go. He already had enough unfamiliar equipment to sort through.
Orrin’s specialist stopped beside Lu Pei and opened his case. Inside were small jars, flat wedges, and sheets of thick, dull cloth.
"Two neighboring chips," Orrin said. "As similar as your collector can make them. We’ll handle one."
Lu Pei looked at Leon before touching his chisel.
"Go ahead," Leon said.
The first chip came free with a soft click. A faint blue haze lifted from its freshly broken edge, barely visible against the stone.

For the second, the Vessian specialist spread a paste across the intended cut. He worked a wedge beneath it, lifted the fragment into the cloth, and folded the material around it without exposing the underside.
Lu Pei brought his lens close to the uncovered chip.
"The surface is dulling."
"Watch the fracture," the specialist said.
A hairline crack ran through the blue-white growth. As Leon watched, its light faded from the outside inward.
He crouched beside Lu Pei. The energy escaping from it was slight, but steady.
"How long until it stops?" he asked.
"Depends on the deposit," Orrin said. "Sometimes you get a useful piece home. Sometimes you carry a pretty stone."
"And yours?"
"Much better odds." She nodded toward the wrapped fragment. "You can test it when we finish talking."
Leon straightened. "What do you want?"
"A share of what you cut here. We provide the treatment, packing material, and people to teach your collectors."
Orrin indicated the unclaimed ground beyond his northern outcrop.
"My company will work there. We don’t need your entire section."
"But you want some of it."
"Yes," she said. "Ours may be richer. Yours may be easier to extract. I would rather benefit from both."
Leon liked that answer more than he would have liked a sudden declaration of friendship.
Behind Orrin, her swordsman was helping a collector move a case clear of a loose slab. He kept glancing their way. Whatever he had thought of Leon during the race, it had changed considerably.
"State the share," Leon said.
"Two loads in five."
Ira made a small sound behind him.
Vyra stepped closer. "For packing lessons?"
"For keeping what you harvest," Orrin replied. "The treatment materials come from our stock. We brought them through the gate ourselves."
"You’ll also be gathering on the neighboring beds without a dispute," Vyra said. "That has value."
"It does. So does having neighbors who understand a boundary." Orrin looked at Leon. "One load in four."
"One in five," Leon said. "With the method demonstrated until our people can repeat it. And a copy of your observations about this region."
The captain considered him. Her fingers rested against the seam of her coat, motionless.
"Observations," she said at last. "Not our private techniques, and not the locations of stores we’ve left elsewhere."
"That’s fine."

"Only material cut from this section while we’re assisting you. Nothing taken from Ashvard." Vyra pointed toward the seized crates. "Equal loads, sorted by the material inside. No selecting the best case for yourselves."
"Agreed," Orrin said. "I’ll need the same treatment when we divide them."
"You’ll get it," Leon told her.
The captain offered her hand. Her grip was dry and firm.
"You handled Ashvard before?" Leon asked.
"We worked the same field yesterday. They preferred easier neighbors." Orrin looked toward the departing survivors. "Their formation encouraged some expensive habits."
"Did you expect it to work on me?"
"I expected to see whether it did."
Leon considered that, then laughed once. She had watched from a safe distance while other people supplied the answer. He might have done the same.
Orrin’s expression eased a little.
"My collectors are coming here because I told them we have an agreement," she said. "I want them to return to their own camp this evening."
"They will," Leon said. "As long as they keep their part."
"That is what I told them."
He watched her specialist patiently explain a wrapping fold to Lu Pei. Orrin had something useful to sell and people she wanted to keep alive. For now, that was enough to work with.
Leon released it, pleased with the bargain. A smaller haul that remained useful suited him better than dragging wasted energy back to Bai Heng.
"How much time do you have?" Orrin asked.
"Until this evening. We leave with enough time to make a scheduled contact tomorrow."
"Then stop trying to take the deepest growth." She turned toward Lu Pei. "The thin branches separate quickly. Your tools will spend half the afternoon fighting those solid roots."
Lu Pei looked down at the chisel he had chosen and replaced it with a narrower one.
"And after transport?" he asked. "Does this treatment interfere with refining?"
"It must be washed away first," the specialist said. "Your refiner will see why if he heats a trace separately. Give him some unused paste."
He set aside a small jar.

Leon was glad Bai Heng would be examining it. The unfamiliar material in front of him was promising, but he had no intention of trusting every consequence of a foreign recipe simply because the first demonstration worked.
Orrin fetched a chart while her specialist showed Lu Pei how to spread the paste thinly enough to avoid wasting it.
Her map covered the storm plain and several approaches. The written symbols meant nothing to Leon. She named the marked features aloud while one of his recorders copied them in familiar characters.
"The ground sinks here after a discharge," she said, tapping a shallow depression. "We lost a cart wheel in it. This ridge is firm. The water below it tastes bitter; we haven’t used it."
"Any exits?" Leon asked.
"None that I can promise you." Orrin met his gaze. "We’re looking too."
He nodded and let her continue. He would rather have that answer than certainty she couldn’t support.
When they returned to the samples, Lu Pei had finished checking the untreated fragment. The wrapped one still held a brighter glow beneath its thin coating.
"The loss is much smaller," he said. He sounded almost offended on behalf of the first chip. "We’d have been opening every seam to the air."
"Now you won’t," Leon said.
He looked across the two hundred paces of mineral growth. A few hours suddenly seemed far too short.
"Show the others," he told Lu Pei. "Then take everything we can preserve."

"The thin branches separate quickly.
Your tools will spend half the afternoon fighting those solid roots."
Lu Pei looked down at the chisel he had chosen and replaced it with a narrower one.
"And after transport?" he asked.
"Does this treatment interfere with refining?"
"It must be washed away first," the specialist said.
"Your refiner will see why if he heats a trace separately.
Give him some unused paste."
He set aside a small jar.
Leon was glad Bai Heng would be examining it.
The unfamiliar material in front of him was promising, but he had no intention of trusting every consequence of a foreign recipe simply because the first demonstration worked.
Orrin fetched a chart while her specialist showed Lu Pei how to spread the paste thinly enough to avoid wasting it.
Her map covered the storm plain and several approaches.
The written symbols meant nothing to Leon.
She named the marked features aloud while one of his recorders copied them in familiar characters.
"The ground sinks here after a discharge," she said, tapping a shallow depression.
"We lost a cart wheel in it.
This ridge is firm.
The water below it tastes bitter; we haven’t used it."
"Any exits?" Leon asked.
"None that I can promise you." Orrin met his gaze.
"We’re looking too."
He nodded and let her continue.
He would rather have that answer than certainty she couldn’t support.
When they returned to the samples, Lu Pei had finished checking the untreated fragment.
The wrapped one still held a brighter glow beneath its thin coating.
"The loss is much smaller," he said.
He sounded almost offended on behalf of the first chip.
"We’d have been opening every seam to the air."
"Now you won’t," Leon said.
He looked across the two hundred paces of mineral growth.
A few hours suddenly seemed far too short.
"Show the others," he told Lu Pei.
"Then take everything we can preserve."

chapters.title: Chapter 714: A Haul Worth Leaving With
paragraphs: Lu Pei ruined his first cut by trying to save the coating.
The paste stretched too thin across the underside. When he lifted the blue-white branch, a line of pale vapor escaped beneath his thumb.
He swore, set it down, and reached for the jar again.
"Better to lose a spoonful than the sample," the Vessian specialist told him.
"I know that now."
Leon watched the second attempt hold. The branch went into its wrapping without another leak, and Lu Pei finally allowed a carrier to take it from him.

Soon the collectors had settled into a rhythm. One exposed the seam, another treated the cut, and the carrier beside them opened a prepared case before the material came free. Nobody had to stand holding a volatile specimen while someone searched for a lid.

Vyra moved between the cases with the recorders. She had marked separate places for red, blue-white, violet, and unidentified material, with the foreign treatment supplies kept within reach of all four collectors.
Leon stayed where he could see the approaches.

The storm continued west. Its distant crackling carried over the field, occasionally loud enough to interrupt conversation. He checked the charged edge whenever it brightened, then returned his attention to the people moving among the beds.
No one approached the Palace boundary.
A pair of cultivators from the southern camps paused within sight of the broken bronze plates. After a brief conversation, they chose another route.
Ira noticed them leaving.
"They didn’t even ask," she said.
"Do you want them to?" Leon asked.
She leaned on her lance. "Depends what they’re asking."
He smiled and went to check the cases.

The gray-green material proved troublesome. It came away in heavy, irregular pieces, several with red growth trapped inside. Lu Pei could not identify it confidently, and the Vessian specialist knew only that some buyers valued it.
"We keep it separate," Leon said. "Bai Heng can decide what it is."
"Separate from the fire-bearing cuts too?" Lu Pei asked.
"Until we know whether they affect each other."
The collector wrapped two small comparison samples and marked where each had come from. Leon approved. A large pile without useful records would leave them repeating half the work later.
One carrier struggled to settle a filled case into its sling. Leon caught the far handle before it tipped and helped him lower it.
"Too heavy?"
"The shape’s awkward, Senior Brother." The man rubbed his shoulder. "I can manage the weight."
"Move some into the next case. You still have to carry it through the pass."
They repacked it together. By the time Leon let go, the sling sat evenly and the carrier could turn without striking the lid against his knee.
Across the line, Orrin’s people were taking the longer red seams. Their tools bit deeper than the Palace collectors’ smaller kit, but each cut required several people to lift it.
She caught Leon watching.
"More trouble to separate," she said. "Less exposed surface afterward."
"Better for a long journey?"
"Usually." Orrin checked her workers before looking back. "Your people learn quickly."
"They have a reason to."
"So do mine."
She nodded toward one of her younger collectors, who had begun wrapping a piece before the senior worker finished checking it. The older man tapped his wrist, and he stopped at once.
Leon left her to her section. Competence did not make the Vessian Company harmless, but he preferred a neighbor whose interests he could understand.

By late afternoon, fifteen matched cases stood ready for division. Smaller samples and the seized Ashvard stock had been packed separately, with the latter secured in the storage space available to the expedition.

Vyra and Orrin checked the new harvest together. They divided the cases by their recorded contents, settling the few differences with smaller wrapped cuts. The Vessian Company received three loads of comparable value. Twelve remained with the Palace party.
Leon lifted the lid of one containing violet growth and red fragments, each protected in its own compartment.
He already knew which samples he wanted for his allocation.
"Close it," Vyra said beside him. "You’ve looked three times."
"I was checking the seal."
"Then let it stay sealed."
He shut it, still smiling.
Lu Pei approached with the last sample jar held against his chest.
"Master Bai said I needed more field experience before he’d let me work on difficult materials alone," he said. "I think this counts."
"Show him what you brought back," Leon told him. "Then ask."
The young man looked toward the cases again. His excitement was easier to understand now that Leon had seen how carefully he handled them.
"What would you work on?" Leon asked.
Lu Pei seemed surprised by the question. "Materials that change during refining. Most of the ones I’m allowed to handle are predictable."
"And you’re tired of those?"
"A little." He glanced toward the old cuts, then admitted, "A great deal, actually. I know that sounds ungrateful."
"It sounds familiar."

Leon remembered looking at a circulation he had made work, then immediately wanting to know what else it could manage. There was always another adjustment, another possibility that refused to leave him alone.
"Keep good notes," he told Lu Pei. "You’ll have more to show him than a box of strange rocks."

The collector smiled and went to check his labels. Leon watched him tuck the last jar into its padded slot, then helped a carrier tighten the case around it. That sample had taken too much effort to lose on the way home.
Leaving was less pleasant.

Beyond their final cuts, an untouched violet seam ran beneath a shelf of red mineral. Leon could have broken the stone above it easily. Taking the growth out intact, treating it, and packing it would consume time they had already promised elsewhere.
He looked at it once more before turning away.
Still going to think about that on the walk back.
Orrin accompanied them to the edge of the workings.
"If you return, ask for Vessian," she said. "We may have moved with the storm, but the southern traders will probably know where."
Leon nodded. "If we need more of that paste, we’ll bring something worth trading."
"I’d prefer that to another demonstration."
Her gaze briefly touched the broken formation plates. He let the remark pass.

All eighteen left together before evening, following Wen Shu toward the surveyed pass. They covered the first stretch before resting, then resumed early the next morning. Familiar ground and the checked shortcut let the carriers keep a steadier pace than on the outward journey.
They reached the last working plaque marker while daylight still lay across the ridge.
Bai Heng answered on the second attempt.
"Senior Brother?"
"All eighteen accounted for," Leon said. "We’re coming in with material for you."
"Everyone here is well. Tian’s base too. What kind of material?"
"Several kinds. Some we can’t identify."
A pause followed.
"How far away are you?" Bai Heng asked.
Leon laughed. "We’re walking now."
The old man met them at the spring with clean trays already laid out. After checking the first wrapped sample, he scraped a trace of coating into a dish and examined the growth beneath it.
"Well," he said softly. "Someone knew how to bring this home."

chapters.title: Chapter 715: Fuel He Could Afford
paragraphs: Bai Heng put the foreign packing paste on an empty heating plate before he touched the ore.
It smoked, curled, and left a brown smear across the ceramic.
"Glad you brought the instructions," he said.
Leon stood beside his workbench. "They said to wash it off first."
"They were right." Bai Heng scraped the residue into a waste dish. "Good for transport. Bad in a refining vessel."
He had spent the evening examining the returned samples. By morning, his trays held small portions arranged according to the qualities he could confirm, with the uncertain pieces set aside.

The red growth carried Fire readily. The blue-white sample responded to cold. Both held enough energy to interest Leon, but neither was as uniform as the purchased condensate he had already exhausted.
"What about the gray-green?" Leon asked.
"Later. I want to know whether it belongs in a furnace before I put it in one."
That was fair. Leon pulled a stool closer and watched the first wash separate from the red mineral.

Bai Heng worked slowly through the opening stages, keeping each portion small. His first heating released energy faster than he wanted. He lowered the plate’s output, changed the vessel, and repeated the process with a fresh piece.
The second result settled more cleanly.

Lu Pei stood beside him, recording the difference. Once, he began explaining how they had lifted the material from its seam, and Bai Heng stopped working to ask him precisely where the darker growth had been attached.
Leon let them talk. The young collector had earned the chance to answer.
By afternoon, Bai Heng had prepared three measured samples from Leon’s allocation. Two came from different parts of the red seam. The third came from the blue-white growth.
"Don’t treat the red ones as identical," he warned. "They aren’t."
"How much of the remaining stock can you process this way?"
"Enough for more than these little tests. How useful that is depends on what you need from it." Bai Heng handed him the containers. "Tell me where it gives you trouble."
Leon took them back to his tent.

Seraphine checked the privacy precautions while Vyra arranged the household’s watch. To the rest of the camp, their Young Master was examining his portion of the harvest and resting after the journey.
Inside, Leon set the three containers beside his notes and entered the dimensional world.

Xyra adjusted the local time for him without difficulty. With a thousand moments available for every one outside, he could examine the samples carefully while his household continued its ordinary afternoon.
His second body remained in the Grotto-Heaven. He left it observing a quiet stretch of ridge while most of his attention settled on the cultivation work.
The first red sample behaved well at a slow intake.
Its energy entered the neutral center, passed into the Fire branch, and returned through the arrangement he had spent so long developing. Leon let several cycles finish before increasing the supply.
The next increment arrived faster than expected.
He stopped drawing from the sample and waited for the excess to clear. Nothing tore. There was only a growing imbalance he had caught before it could become harmful.
He looked at the amount left in the container.
That little change did all that?
The mineral released energy unevenly as its remaining structure loosened. His old condensate had spoiled him; once he chose a rate, it had mostly given him what he expected.
This supply required closer attention.
Leon recorded the change, then tried the second red sample at the same initial rate. It responded more slowly, yet held its output longer when he reduced the draw.
Bai Heng’s warning had been useful.

He spent the next sessions comparing how the samples released energy with how his circulation accepted it. Forcing the same intake on both produced different returns. Compensating by pushing all nine branches equally only made him spend energy where he did not need it.
He remembered the Lord of Illusion and Mystery’s casual observation.
Balance did not require equal flow.
He had already used that insight to improve the Scripture. Now he needed to apply it before the energy reached the branches as well.

Leon began adjusting the draw according to the returning current. When the red sample released more readily, he narrowed its intake instead of forcing the whole circulation to accommodate the surge. When it slowed, he allowed the return to settle before drawing again.
The Fire branch stopped pulling the others out of their established rhythm.
He tried the adjustment again while standing, then while taking a slow turn around the chamber. The first few steps distracted him enough that he drew too much from the sample.
Leon stopped, made a note, and started over.
Useful would be doing this without staring at it the whole time.
He reduced the size of each correction. It took longer to respond, but the returning current stayed easier to read. After several attempts, he could walk without losing track of the intake.

He sat down before trying anything more demanding. The temptation to combine every test was familiar, and usually expensive. Today he had three measured samples, records he wanted to compare, and no reason to waste either by being impatient.
For the next session, he wrote down the point where his attention had slipped. That was the part he would need to improve.
That was progress. He repeated it until he could distinguish a useful correction from simply having chosen a fortunate moment.
The blue-white sample demanded its own adjustments. Leon tested it separately first, then admitted small amounts alongside the red, keeping their differing responses in view.
He finished with stable circulation and a page full of alterations to investigate further.
Mid Foundation Establishment remained Mid Foundation Establishment. There had been no sudden leap, and he had spent part of the samples learning what not to do.
He was still delighted.

The remaining harvest could support longer work. He would need Bai Heng’s help, careful refining, and more experiments, but the next session no longer began with the thought of purchasing another immensely expensive reservoir.
I can afford to get some things wrong.
That was almost as satisfying as the successful test.
When Leon returned to the tent, the afternoon outside had advanced only a little. He closed the aperture and found Seraphine sitting beside the entrance with a cup waiting for him.
"Well?" she asked.
"It works. Unevenly." He accepted the cup. "But I can use it."
She smiled at his expression. "You look happier than after the fight."
"The fight didn’t take very long."
"And this did?"
"Enough that I want to tell Bai Heng exactly what happened before I forget anything."
Seraphine glanced at the notes in his hand. "I don’t think you’ll forget."
He sat beside her, enjoying the warmth of the cup against his fingers. From outside came Lu Pei’s voice, still explaining the unfamiliar wrapping to someone who had probably heard it twice already.
Then Leon’s attention shifted.
Far beyond the camp, his other body had reached a narrow stream crossing a rocky slope. The water should have spilled downhill through a gap in the stone.
Instead, it turned neatly around the gap and continued along the hillside.
Someone had built a wall to keep it there.

chapters.title: Chapter 716: Someone Tends This Place
paragraphs: The wall was only as high as Leon’s hand, but he had not seen anything like it since leaving the foreign camps.

His second body crouched beside the water. Flat stones had been fitted together along the lower edge of the slope, holding a shallow stream against the hillside. Mud filled the smaller gaps. Where one stone had split, another had been pressed against it from the outside.
Water ran past the repair without escaping.
Leon followed the channel with his eyes. It curved behind a shoulder of rock and disappeared beneath hanging grass.
At the spring, his original body set down its cup.
"What is it?" Seraphine asked.
"Water going somewhere it shouldn’t."
She waited.
"There’s a channel," Leon said quietly. "Built along a slope. I’m going to follow it."
Seraphine glanced toward the closed flap. "Carefully."
He nodded. There was no need to leave the household or call the expedition together. He was already at the channel, looking at a repair nobody in the Palace had made.
The second body rose and moved along the uphill side, keeping off the narrow strip beside the water.

He had first thought it might be a natural seam. Plenty of things here looked arranged until he examined them closely. The moving terrace had been stranger than a crooked stream, and the mineral field had laid out its colors with remarkable regularity.
But someone had packed mud behind those stones.

A little farther on, sediment had been lifted out of the channel and piled against a dry rock. Grass shoots grew through the older heaps. The newest held dark clumps with pale roots exposed where they had been pulled loose.
Leon stopped beside it.
So somebody keeps it clear, too.
He looked back along the slope. No figures moved between the rocks. He heard running water, the brush of grass against his cloak, and a faint clicking from something hidden beneath a leaf.
The stillness gave him no reason to assume the place was empty.
He continued without disturbing the sediment.
Beyond the shoulder of rock, the channel divided. One branch followed the hillside. The other descended through a notch fitted with a flat piece of wood.
The wood had been cut to fit.
Leon leaned close enough to see the worn edge where it slid against stone. Raising it would let more water into the lower branch. Pressing it down would send the greater portion onward.
He left it where it was.
Beside the wooden piece, three shallow grooves had been worn into the stone. He studied them before realizing they marked different positions for the water gate.
Someone could change the flow without judging it afresh every time.

Leon had spent much of his recent work making circulation respond to changing conditions. Here, somebody had solved a smaller, ordinary problem with a fitted plank and three marks. He liked the practicality of it.
He also liked that the plank could be replaced. When the edge wore too thin to hold the water back, its owner would only need another piece of wood cut to the same shape.

That suggested repeated use, though it gave him no reliable age for the channel. He resisted the urge to turn a few scratches into a whole history. The people who knew might be somewhere ahead, and he would learn more by looking.
The lower channel led toward a patch of green sheltered between two ridges. From above, it had looked like another stretch of vegetation growing where moisture gathered.
Now he could see narrow beds separated by paths.
He stopped walking.

Short plants with dark, rounded leaves occupied the upper rows. Below them grew a paler species, each stem supported by a forked stick. Water entered through small openings at the ends of the beds and drained through shallow cuts on the opposite side.
The plants carried spiritual energy. Leon could feel that much from the path’s edge, although he knew neither their names nor what they might be used for.
He wanted Loriel here immediately.
The thought was followed by the inconvenient fact that she was far away with the gathering party, and he had no intention of exposing his clone to bring her over for a look.
At the spring, his original body reached for his notes.
Seraphine watched him turn to a clean page.
"Plants?" she asked.
"Rows of them." He began sketching the leaf shapes. "Can you ask Loriel to come in when she’s free?"
Seraphine left quietly. Leon kept drawing while his other body moved to a better position above the beds.

There were differences between the rows that he might have missed without the irrigation channel. Some had been thinned. Small weeds lay drying beside one path, roots turned upward. A dead stem had been cut near its base instead of being left to rot among the others.
This was more than a convenient watering spot for passing cultivators.
Someone had prepared ground, planted it, and returned to tend what grew.
That did not tell him who.

Another expedition might have established a camp here long before the Palace arrived. Harrowmark had already spent nineteen days inside when he questioned them. There could be people who had entered much earlier, or people who had never come through a gateway at all.
The last possibility held his attention.
He had been searching the realm as though everyone in it must be another visitor. These narrow beds made that assumption feel careless.
Loriel entered the tent and sat beside his sketch.
"What am I looking at?" she asked.
"A cultivated patch. My other body found it beyond the northern ridges."
She drew the page closer. "Are these supports?"
"Forked sticks. One for each of the pale plants."

"Then someone expects those stems to carry more weight." Loriel studied the rough drawing. "I can’t identify them from this. If you get closer, look at the undersides of the leaves. Don’t touch the pale ones until you know whether that coating comes off."
"I’m not collecting anything yet."
"Good." She looked up. "Someone’s garden?"
"That’s what I’m trying to find out."
His second body stayed above the beds. The plants were tempting, but taking a handful before he knew their use or their owner would gain him very little.
Whoever tended them might know which nearby growth was valuable, what the weather did, and where the paths led. They might even know something about leaving.
Leon would rather learn that first.
He followed the main channel farther along the slope. Beyond the planted patch, it passed beneath a low stone cover, protecting the water from loose soil sliding down the bank.
A broken piece of that cover lay beside the path.
Its replacement was a thin slab braced with two freshly cut sticks. Pale wood showed where the bark had been trimmed away, and damp mud had been pressed around its edges.
Leon crouched again.
The mud bore finger marks. Water had not yet softened them, and a bead of moisture clung beneath the freshly cut end of one stick.
He looked toward the bend where the channel disappeared between the rocks.
He had been following an old construction through the hillside.
Someone had repaired it recently enough that the wood was still wet.

"Built along a slope.

Seraphine glanced toward the closed flap.
"Carefully."
He nodded.

He had first thought it might be a natural seam.
Plenty of things here looked arranged until he examined them closely.

A little farther on, sediment had been lifted out of the channel and piled against a dry rock.
Grass shoots grew through the older heaps.
The newest held dark clumps with pale roots exposed where they had been pulled loose.
Leon stopped beside it.

He looked back along the slope.
No figures moved between the rocks.

The wood had been cut to fit.

chapters.title: Chapter 717: The People Beyond the Bend
paragraphs: "Leave it there. You’ll have half the bank in the water."
Leon stopped beside the fresh repair.

The voice came from beyond the bend, followed by a scrape and an irritated sigh. He moved far enough to see between two hanging branches. An older woman stood ankle-deep in the channel, holding a flat stone against her hip. On the bank above her, a young man had both hands around a clump of grass.
"I only meant to clear the edge," the young man said.
"And what’s holding the edge together?"
He looked down at the roots. After a moment, he let go.

The woman passed him the stone. Her gray hair was pinned beneath a faded blue scarf, and wet mud covered the knees of her trousers. There was a knife at her belt, a basket on the bank, and nothing about either person to suggest an expedition preparing to move on.
Leon watched her place a smaller stone beneath the one they had been arguing over. The young man steadied it without being told this time.
He waited until she climbed out of the water before stepping onto the open path.
"Excuse me."
The young man straightened so quickly that he nearly dropped the stone. The woman reached for her knife, then stopped with her fingers on its handle.
Leon kept his hands visible and stayed well clear of the beds.
"My name is Leon. I’m traveling with a gathering party. Is this your garden?"
"Mine to work," she said. "Where did you come from?"
"The southern ridges. I found the channel and followed it."
Her gaze passed over his dry boots, his clothes, and the path behind him.
"You didn’t open any of the gates?"
"No."
"Good. People see a little water and decide everything below it needs more." She took her hand from the knife. "What do you want?"
"To ask whether you trade. And, if you’re willing, learn where I am."
The young man glanced at her, visibly interested in the second part. She ignored him while she wrung water from the bottom of her trousers.
"Edda Fen," she said. "That’s Nerin. You can talk while we finish. Stand on the stones, though. The pale stems bruise easily."
Leon shifted onto the paved strip she indicated. Nerin carried their tools toward the lower beds, looking back twice before reaching them.

Their words reached him as easily as Harrowmark’s had. He could hear the unfamiliar sounds, yet he understood even the woman’s irritation over the damaged bank. Whatever made that possible was doing the same for her; she had answered without asking him to repeat himself.

Leon was grateful for it now. He could have frightened them off with a gesture he meant as reassurance, or bought something dangerous without understanding its use. He still wanted to know what was making the translation happen.
At the spring, Leon’s original body remained seated beside Loriel and Seraphine. He had gone still while following the conversation through his other body, one hand resting on the unfinished sketch.
"There are two people," he told them quietly. "A woman and someone working with her. I’ve introduced myself."
Loriel leaned closer to the drawing. "Ask about the pale ones when you can."
He nodded, then returned most of his attention to the garden.
Edda was checking the wooden gate he had examined earlier. She raised it to the middle groove and watched the water spread through the lower channel before moving on.

Nerin had begun replacing a forked support beneath one pale stem. He looked perhaps seventeen, with a narrow face, sunburn across his nose, and a badly mended sleeve. The thread holding it together was much brighter than the cloth.
"Is your party staying at the old quarry?" Nerin asked.
"No. We have a camp beside a crystal spring farther south."
"I haven’t been that far." Nerin pushed the support into the soil. "People have been coming down the eastern paths, though. More than usual."
"People you know?" Leon asked.
"Some. Others dress strangely." Nerin examined Leon’s coat, then seemed to realize what he had said. "Different from us, I mean."
Leon looked down at himself. He had grown used to Palace clothing. Apparently, that only made him an ordinary sort of stranger in one world.
"Yours is probably easier to work in," he said.
"It was, before he tore it," Edda said. "Nerin, check the next row."
The apprentice moved away, although he remained close enough to listen.

Edda knelt beside the dark-leaved plants and separated two stems. Leon could feel the spiritual energy within them, quiet and steady compared with the mineral growths he had collected. These had been given space, water, and time by someone who expected to return.
"What are those used for?" he asked.

"Most buyers want the roots. I keep some for seed." Edda pointed with the back of her knife. "The pale ones are reedlace. Different buyers, different preparation. If you’re looking for dried stock, I have a little."
"May I look underneath a leaf?"
That earned him a more attentive glance.
"Use the stick beside you. Don’t rub the coating off."
Leon lifted a leaf carefully. A fine pattern of branching veins showed beneath its pale surface. He studied it long enough to remember, then lowered it without touching the stem.
Edda watched his face. "You don’t know it."
"No. Someone with me knows plants much better than I do. She’d be annoyed if I brought her a damaged handful and asked what it was."
"She’s sensible, then."
He smiled. Loriel would probably like this woman, provided neither tried to reorganize the other’s garden too quickly.
Edda took a small cloth packet from her basket. Inside were several dried pieces of reedlace stem, cleanly split along their length. She let him examine one but kept the packet in her hand.
Its preparation was beyond his knowledge. He could judge the energy left within it, yet that told him little about how well it had been preserved or what a healer might actually want from it.
"I’ll bring her before discussing a purchase," Leon said.
"That would save us both trouble." Edda wrapped the packet again. "How many are with you?"
"There are eighteen in my field party. Four collectors."
"Four who know what they’re doing?"
"With minerals. They’ll listen if you explain the plants."

She considered that while checking another stem. Leon liked that she had asked about hands rather than swords. The number of people capable of protecting a harvest and the number capable of collecting one had proved rather different lately.
Nerin returned with a wooden pail and poured a little water over Edda’s hands. She rinsed off the mud, then passed it to Leon when he asked to clean the stick he had used.
He accepted. The cool water washed a smear of mud from his fingers.

Nothing here felt temporary. Even the pail had a replacement handle worn smooth where someone carried it. He had seen traveling camps with more expensive equipment and less evidence that anyone intended to stay.
They might have arrived years before us.
Harrowmark’s nineteen days no longer seemed a useful measure of anything.
"Is your settlement nearby?" Leon asked.
"Asterbank. Beyond that shoulder." Edda indicated the western hill. "You won’t see the roofs from here. The wind’s worse on this side."
"And you come out every day?"
"When the garden needs me." She looked toward the repaired channel. "More often when the bank gives way."
Nerin picked up the basket. "It was worse before she moved the upper beds."
"You weren’t here before I moved them," Edda said.
"My father was. He told me."
Leon looked from the young man to the neat beds beneath the ridge. "Your father works here too?"
"He makes drying screens," Nerin said. "I help when she doesn’t need me."
The answer came easily. No guarded glance, no attempt to work out what Leon wanted to hear. Nerin was explaining his family, and already looking as though he wanted to ask about Leon’s.
"How long has your family been in Asterbank?" Leon asked Edda.
She gave him a puzzled look. "As long as anyone bothers remembering."
"I meant, when did you enter this place?"
"The garden?"
"This realm," Leon said. "Through a gateway."
For a moment, even Nerin forgot his questions.
Edda lowered the cloth she had been using to dry her hands.
"I was born in Asterbank," she said. "So was my mother. Her mother taught her to grow reedlace in those lower beds."
Leon glanced at the rows again.
He had helped open a passage that the Palace believed led into a newly formed realm.
Edda was pointing out her grandmother’s garden.
