chapters.title: Chapter 718: A Tenth of the Bloom
paragraphs: Edda took him for a fool for perhaps three breaths.
Then her expression changed, and she looked at his clothes again.
"You really did come through one of those openings."
"Yes," Leon said. "Recently."
Nerin set down the basket he had just picked up.
Edda gave him a resigned glance before turning back to Leon. "Well. That explains the questions."
"Do many people ask them?"

"Not me. My grandmother spoke about visitors. Different clothes, different names for everything. Some stayed near the settlement for a while." Edda folded her damp cloth. "I thought you were from beyond the eastern hills."
Leon wanted to ask a dozen things. He settled for the one that mattered most to everyone waiting at the spring.
"Do you know how those visitors left?"
"No," she said. "I never met them."
"Were there records?"
"Perhaps somewhere. The stories I heard were mostly about what they bought and what they paid with."
Nerin shifted closer. "My father says one gave his grandfather a lamp that didn’t need oil. It broke before I was born."
Edda nodded. "I’ve heard that one too."
Leon let the subject rest. Pressing them would not turn an old family story into directions to an exit.
Still, his thoughts had begun moving quickly.

The Palace’s measurements had been taken through an unstable entrance complex. They had watched its boundary strengthen and waited for the passage to become safe. None of them had stood here while those changes occurred. They had interpreted what they could measure from outside.
If Edda’s account was true, the developing connection explained those readings much better than the birth of this entire place.
Master is going to want to hear this.

He almost reached for the communication plaque before remembering how little use it would be. Ji was outside, beyond a gateway that no longer existed. He would have to bring the information back himself.
Nerin had been patient for as long as he could manage.
"Is there really another sky?" he asked.
Leon looked up. Pale clouds moved above the ridge, ordinary enough that he had stopped studying them days ago.
"Yes."
"Different from this one?"
"Sometimes. The place I came through has storms and clear days too. I don’t know how much of what you’re used to would be different."
Nerin considered that answer with obvious disappointment.
"What were you expecting?" Leon asked.
"I don’t know. Something." The young man glanced at his teacher. "You said the visitors wouldn’t be like us."
"I said you shouldn’t assume they were," Edda replied. "He’s still got two hands."
Nerin looked at Leon’s hands, then laughed at himself. Leon found himself smiling too. He understood the disappointment. Having discovered another world, a person wanted it to look the part.

Edda began gathering the tools they had left along the bank. Leon carried the pail to the covered channel while Nerin collected the spare supports. Their conversation continued as they worked, no longer quite so wary.

He learned that Asterbank sold dried plants to several neighboring settlements, that the ridge path forked above a stand of red-barked trees, and that the lower route became unpleasant after heavy rain. Edda supplied directions by landmarks. The marks she scratched into the dirt meant nothing until she explained them.
Leon memorized the spoken instructions. He would have a recorder draw a proper route later.
When they returned to the pale plants, Edda stopped beside a stem whose closed bud had begun leaning away from its support.
She touched the wood, tested the soil, and called Nerin over.
"Earlier than I expected. We’ll need the shallow baskets ready tomorrow."
"For the garden?" Leon asked.

"For the bloom." Edda tilted the support so the bud had room. "These feel it before the field plants open. If the weather holds, the first beds in the hollow should be ready the morning after tomorrow."
"What happens then?"
"Enough energy moves through the ground to bring half the hollow into season at once. Not all at the same moment, though. That catches people out."

She named three plants he did not know. Sun cups opened first on the warm slopes. Frost-thread followed in shaded ground after the surge reached it. Emberseed released its useful pods later, once the stalks darkened.
The names were simple enough. Knowing when to pick them was another matter.

Edda described buyers rejecting whole baskets of sun cups because the centers had already turned dull. Nerin added that squeezing frost-thread into a sack ruined the pale growth along its stems. She let him finish, then reminded him that he had learned that lesson with her sack.
"How much do the sun cups hold?" Leon asked.
"Enough that refiners come for them. Whether they’re worth your time depends on what you need."

He thought of Bai Heng’s small sample containers and the pleasure of finally having fuel he could replace without spending a fortune. Then he thought of Loriel, studying unfamiliar leaves from a sketch while their owner spoke casually of a whole hollow coming ready.
She’ll want to see that.
So did he.
"Would you take a party there?" Leon asked.
Edda studied him. "A party that listens?"
"The four collectors will. I’ll make sure the others stay out of their way."
"And if someone decides our baskets look easier to take than their own?"
"They won’t take yours while you’re working with me."
He answered plainly. Edda looked at the sword at his side, then at his face. Whatever she made of him, it was enough to continue.
"One part in ten," she said. "Of what your party gathers during this bloom. I show you the grounds and the proper cuts. Nerin helps with sorting."
"Comparable portions," Leon said. "You don’t get the best tenth and leave us the damaged pieces."
"Neither do you."
"Agreed. We divide by kind and quality before anyone takes a personal share. This outing only."
Edda nodded. "And I want to see your containers before we leave."

Leon agreed to that too. The terms were simple enough to remember, and he intended to have them recorded when his people arrived. Her knowledge would be part of the cost of obtaining the harvest. What remained would be divided under the Palace’s existing arrangement.
There was no reason to make the bargain more complicated than that.
Edda did ask one more thing: whether his people would be paid from their remaining portion. When he said they would, she seemed satisfied.
"I’ve worked beside hired hands who gained nothing by taking care," she said. "You can usually tell by the second basket."

Leon remembered Lu Pei explaining the mineral wrapping long after they had returned to camp. The collector had been tired, dirty, and delighted with what they had brought back. He wanted his people to feel that way about this harvest too.

He asked about dangers on the way, and Edda described loose ground along one descent and animals that sometimes fed on the opened flowers. She knew where people usually waited and which slopes could be reached without trampling someone else’s crop. The hollow itself was wild gathering ground, she said. Her garden was not.
Leon assured her that he understood the distinction.
"I’ll return with my people tomorrow afternoon," he said. "If the route takes longer than expected, we won’t leave you waiting past sunset."
"Come here," Edda said. "There’s dry ground above the channel. You can sleep there and we’ll leave early."
Nerin brightened at the prospect of eighteen visitors. Edda handed him the basket before he could start asking about them.

As they prepared to leave, Leon took one final look at the leaning bud. A thin line of yellow showed between its closed petals. He could feel a faint concentration of warmth there that had not been obvious when he arrived.
"How will we know the sun cups are ready?" he asked.

"How long does that take?"
"Sometimes less time than people spend arguing over whose patch it is."
Leon looked at her.
Edda tied her tool roll shut. "Bring people who can work quickly."

He watched the pair take the western path, then moved his second body uphill to check the route he would use tomorrow. There was enough daylight left to examine the difficult descent before turning toward quieter ground.
At the spring, his original body reached for a clean sheet of paper.
This time, he had more to offer Loriel than a drawing.

"No," she said.

Nerin shifted closer.

Edda nodded.

chapters.title: Chapter 719: What Loriel Didn’t Know
paragraphs: Loriel wanted to leave before Leon finished explaining the agreement.
She had already folded the drawing and reached for her bag when he mentioned that they were meeting Edda tomorrow afternoon.
"Tomorrow?" she said.
"The collectors need different containers. And I’d like to tell Bai Heng where we’re taking half his camp."
Loriel glanced toward the darkening tent flap. "I know. I wasn’t suggesting we drag everyone out tonight."
Her bag remained in her lap.
Leon tried not to smile too obviously. "She has dried reedlace for you to examine."
"That drawing isn’t enough to identify anything," Loriel said. "And you’ve made all the leaf veins the same thickness."
"I was rather busy finding out that people live here."
She looked up, her eagerness settling into something more thoughtful. "Her grandmother grew those plants?"
"According to her. We need to learn more, but I don’t think we watched an entire world being born."
Seraphine stood beside the closed flap. "The entrance."
"That’s what I think," Leon said. "We were measuring a connection from the wrong side of it."
He left the larger questions there. There would be time to investigate them, and no way to ask his master tonight.

The immediate business took the rest of the evening. Bai Heng listened to the description of the bloom, then asked what part of each plant held the useful material. Leon could answer only one of his questions.
"Bring the instructions back with the plants," the old man said. "Please."

Vyra entered the grower’s tenth as a cost of the outing, ahead of the normal division. The four collectors checked shallow cases and found clean cloth suitable for separating delicate specimens. Nothing from the mineral harvest needed to be dragged along merely because it had proved useful once.

They left after dawn with the same eighteen people who had gone to the storm field. Bai Heng stayed with the twelve at the spring. Tian acknowledged the new journey from the entrance base, where all eighteen under her command remained accounted for.

Leon gave both camps the expected route. They would reach the garden that afternoon, gather the following day, and return to the spring by dusk the day after that. A delay would have to be reported from working range. If the bloom ran late, they would return with less rather than disappear beyond their own deadline.

Wen Shu tested the plaques as they traveled. Before midday, the ridges began breaking the connection. She marked the last place where Bai Heng could hear an entire message and took a reply before putting her plaque away.
Beyond that point, the party followed the route Leon had checked through his second body.
He kept that body well away from the path now, exploring an empty ridge to the east. He had no wish to discover how quickly Nerin would notice meeting him twice.

The descent Edda had warned about slowed the carriers. Its stones shifted underfoot, and Leon shortened one bad crossing while Seraphine helped guide the cases across. They reached the garden with several hours of daylight remaining.
Nerin was waiting above the channel.
He counted them openly, then hurried down to help a carrier who had stopped at the wrong turn. Edda emerged from the beds with a bundle of drying screens beneath one arm.
"You brought the containers," she said to Leon.
"And the person who wanted to see your plants."
Loriel stepped forward. "May I?"
Edda looked at the excitement on her face and moved aside.

Leon watched Loriel crouch beside the reedlace without touching it. She studied the stems first, then the soil and the small outlets at the ends of the rows. When Edda offered her the lifting stick, she used it to turn a leaf just enough to examine the underside.
"The roots stay wet?" Loriel asked.
"Only briefly. The water passes through."
Loriel leaned closer to the outlet. "I would have given it a cooler bed. The coating looks like something that grows in shade."
"It thickens in shade," Edda said. "So does the stem. Then the useful part dries badly."
"May I see a cut one?"

Edda called Nerin for the packet. Within minutes, the two women had moved to a flat stone with dried pieces between them. Loriel compared the pale inner layers while Edda showed her where a poorly grown stem became woody.
Nerin brought a second packet from the drying rack. Loriel reached for it, then stopped when Edda shook her head.
"Different bed. Compare this one first."

Loriel put the pieces beside each other and bent over them again. Leon watched her expression change as she found the difference. She asked whether Edda dried both at the same temperature, and the answer led to another question about when the stems were cut.
For once, nobody was asking Loriel to heal an injury or identify something already broken. She could simply be curious.
Leon had expected a pleasant introduction. Instead, he had apparently delivered Loriel to the start of a very long conversation.
He left them to it.

Vyra recorded the agreement and read it aloud. Edda could not read the Palace script, so Nerin made his own record while she listened. Both versions described the same tenth, the same outing, and the same responsibilities. Once they were satisfied, the collectors brought their cases over for inspection.

One lining was too rough. Nerin showed Lu Pei how to fold spare cloth over it so the stems would not catch. The carrier responsible for that case helped make the change rather than leaving it for someone else.

Leon checked the dry ground above the channel. It was large enough for the party without spreading into the beds, and the scouts found a clear approach and a sheltered place for a watch. The household settled near him while everyone else arranged their own sleeping spaces.
By the time he returned to the flat stone, Loriel had a little brown fragment balanced on her fingertip.
"This one grew too wet," she told him. "The leaves can still look healthy when the inside starts going wrong."
"Is that useful to know?"
"For these, yes. For anything similar, perhaps." She looked pleased with the distinction. "I would want to check."
Edda took the fragment back. "She asked before offering to change my watering."
Leon glanced at Loriel. She was doing a poor job of hiding a smile.
"I’m learning," she said.
He felt an unexpected urge to kiss her forehead. With half the collecting party nearby, he settled for handing her the notebook she had left with him.
"I thought you might want this."
"Thank you, Young Master." Loriel accepted it, and her fingers rested against his for a moment longer than necessary.
As the evening cooled, Nerin went down to check the water gate. He called Edda before he reached it.
The bud Leon had examined yesterday was standing away from its support. Several others had tilted in the same direction. Loriel joined Edda at the row, her notebook still open.
A faint warmth rose through the ground beneath Leon’s boots. He watched a yellow line widen between the bud’s petals, then stop.
Edda examined the neighboring stems before looking toward the northern hills.
"We leave before sunrise," she said. "The hollow is waking up."

chapters.title: Chapter 720: Before the First Petal
paragraphs: Edda crushed a flower between her fingers and handed the remains to Lu Pei.
He accepted them with the uneasy care of a man wondering whether he had just been given something expensive.
"Road cup," she said. "Worth nothing to a refiner. Smell it."
The collector did. Leon caught the sharp green scent from beside him.
"That smell in your basket means you’ve damaged something," Edda continued. "Stop packing and find it. Don’t keep pushing flowers on top."
She wiped her fingers on a cloth. The demonstration had taken less than a minute, but all four collectors checked the spacing of their empty trays afterward.

They had left the garden before dawn. Nerin carried food and a stack of light screens; Edda wore her tool roll across one shoulder. With the two guides, twenty people now followed the narrow path toward the hollow.

Morning light reached the hills as they passed the first outlying gardens. A man stood on a low wall clearing leaves from a water trough. Farther down the slope, washing hung beside a roof mostly hidden by trees.
Nerin raised a hand to the man. The greeting was returned, followed by a long look at the unfamiliar party behind him.
Leon found himself looking back.

He had been inside the realm long enough to become used to abandoned camps and contested deposits. There was something strangely pleasing about laundry. Whoever had hung it expected to return, complain if it rained, and wear those clothes again tomorrow.
Then he noticed the cultivated trees below the house, each bearing fruit wrapped in fine mesh.
And probably knows exactly what those are worth.

He wanted to visit Asterbank when they had time. Not as eighteen armed strangers appearing without warning, but with something useful to trade and enough patience to learn what people here considered ordinary.
For now, Edda kept them moving.

The path climbed between stands of red-barked trees and emerged above a shallow valley. Leon felt the changing energy before he saw its effects. A patch of grass beside the path had put out fresh shoots, while the growth a few paces farther uphill remained unchanged.
He crouched and held his palm above it.
The difference was small but distinct. Energy rose through the lower soil in a slow, sustained current. The neighboring ground had not yet received it.
"It doesn’t come evenly," he said.
"No," Edda replied. "The hollow has deeper channels. The surge follows those first, then spreads."
Loriel knelt beside him. She examined the new shoots and looked toward the valley floor.
"So the plant on the warmer slope isn’t always first."
"Usually," Edda said. "Unless the ground beneath it is slow. Watch the plants, not just where they’re growing."

Leon let them compare what they sensed. Unequal supply had occupied enough of his recent research that he was tempted to sit down and study the difference properly. The plants ahead would not wait for him to finish taking notes.
He marked the place on his route sketch instead.

At their next stop, Edda showed the collectors an immature sun cup growing beside a stone. Its yellow petals remained folded around the center. Lu Pei had to lean close to see the clear point she indicated.
"The bead gathers here," Edda said. "Cut below the collar when it’s ready. Keep the cup upright."
She demonstrated the angle beside the stem without cutting it. Loriel asked whether the surrounding leaves continued feeding the flower during the window.
"Leave those on until we sort it," Edda said. "People who strip them in the field lose more than they save in space."
The second collector adjusted the sketch in his notes.

Leon watched them pass the plant one at a time. Four competent people could still ruin a valuable patch if they hurried past the part they did not understand. He had promised Edda they would listen. So far, they were keeping that promise for him.
Once the demonstration ended, he drew the household aside to set their priorities.

Sun cups came first if the field was ready. Frost-thread would be gathered separately when its stems developed the pale growth Edda had described. Emberseed could wait until they knew whether its later window fitted their return schedule.
Ira looked mildly disappointed at that last part, then glanced at the sun cup sketch.
"Bring back something worth waiting for," she told the collectors.
"We intend to," Lu Pei said.

Vyra assigned a carrier to each collector and kept the two recorders moving between the pairs. Edda’s share would be separated after sorting, so nobody needed to interrupt each cut with arithmetic. Seraphine checked the approaches with Wen Shu while Ira stayed near the rear of the column.

Loriel asked to work beside Edda during the first collection. Leon agreed. She would recognize changes the collectors might miss, and he wanted her to enjoy the chance to learn without being pulled away to answer every ordinary question.
The next ridge gave them their first clear view of the hollow.

Yellow flecks covered the lower slopes, with pale bands winding through the shaded ground beneath the trees. From this distance, the colors looked almost painted onto the land. Then a gust moved through them, and Leon saw thousands of closed flowers shift on their stems.
He smiled before he could help it.
There was enough here to make the cases at their backs seem very small.
Nerin saw his expression. "Wait until they open."

The young man shifted the screens on his back and began pointing out the strips that were easiest to reach. He knew where a basket could be set level and where the grass hid loose stones. Then he mentioned a drying frame he wanted to buy with his part of the earnings.
"Your own?" Leon asked.
Nerin nodded. "A small one. I use my father’s now, but his orders come first."
He sounded embarrassed by how modest it was. Leon looked at the screens he had carried all morning and hoped the harvest would cover it. Another capable supplier would suit him very well.
They descended toward a fork in the path and met a woman coming the other way with two empty baskets. A younger girl walked beside her, holding a bundle of cutting cloths against her chest.
Edda stopped. "You’re early, Tessa."
"Apparently we’re late." The woman lowered a basket. "Strangers are sitting across the lower path. They want half."
"Half of what?" Edda asked.
"Anything we take out." Tessa looked at Leon’s party. "Your people?"
"No," Leon said.
The girl beside her stared at the swords and cases with an expression he could not quite read. Tessa touched her shoulder and moved her farther up the path.
"I’ll try the western side," she told Edda. "My brother’s already over there."
Edda watched them leave, her mouth tightening.
Leon sent Wen Shu ahead before asking another question. While they waited, he checked the slope beside the path. The energy beneath it had strengthened since their last stop.
Wen Shu returned quickly.
"An armed group at the lower approach, Senior Brother. Their collectors are working behind them. They’ve put stakes across both paths."
Leon looked past her toward the yellow-covered ground.
The petals nearest the bottom had begun to lift.

sentences.text: Edda crushed a flower between her fingers and handed the remains to Lu Pei.
He accepted them with the uneasy care of a man wondering whether he had just been given something expensive.
"Road cup," she said.
"Worth nothing to a refiner.
Smell it."
The collector did.
Leon caught the sharp green scent from beside him.
"That smell in your basket means you’ve damaged something," Edda continued.
"Stop packing and find it.
Don’t keep pushing flowers on top."
She wiped her fingers on a cloth.
The demonstration had taken less than a minute, but all four collectors checked the spacing of their empty trays afterward.
They had left the garden before dawn.
Nerin carried food and a stack of light screens; Edda wore her tool roll across one shoulder.
With the two guides, twenty people now followed the narrow path toward the hollow.
Morning light reached the hills as they passed the first outlying gardens.
A man stood on a low wall clearing leaves from a water trough.
Farther down the slope, washing hung beside a roof mostly hidden by trees.
Nerin raised a hand to the man.
The greeting was returned, followed by a long look at the unfamiliar party behind him.
Leon found himself looking back.
He had been inside the realm long enough to become used to abandoned camps and contested deposits.
There was something strangely pleasing about laundry.
Whoever had hung it expected to return, complain if it rained, and wear those clothes again tomorrow.
Then he noticed the cultivated trees below the house, each bearing fruit wrapped in fine mesh.
And probably knows exactly what those are worth.
He wanted to visit Asterbank when they had time.
Not as eighteen armed strangers appearing without warning, but with something useful to trade and enough patience to learn what people here considered ordinary.
For now, Edda kept them moving.
The path climbed between stands of red-barked trees and emerged above a shallow valley.
Leon felt the changing energy before he saw its effects.
A patch of grass beside the path had put out fresh shoots, while the growth a few paces farther uphill remained unchanged.
He crouched and held his palm above it.
The difference was small but distinct.
Energy rose through the lower soil in a slow, sustained current.
The neighboring ground had not yet received it.
"It doesn’t come evenly," he said.
"No," Edda replied.
"The hollow has deeper channels.
The surge follows those first, then spreads."
Loriel knelt beside him.
She examined the new shoots and looked toward the valley floor.
"So the plant on the warmer slope isn’t always first."
"Usually," Edda said.
"Unless the ground beneath it is slow.
Watch the plants, not just where they’re growing."
Leon let them compare what they sensed.
Unequal supply had occupied enough of his recent research that he was tempted to sit down and study the difference properly.
The plants ahead would not wait for him to finish taking notes.
He marked the place on his route sketch instead.
At their next stop, Edda showed the collectors an immature sun cup growing beside a stone.
Its yellow petals remained folded around the center.
Lu Pei had to lean close to see the clear point she indicated.
"The bead gathers here," Edda said.
"Cut below the collar when it’s ready.
Keep the cup upright."
She demonstrated the angle beside the stem without cutting it.
Loriel asked whether the surrounding leaves continued feeding the flower during the window.
"Leave those on until we sort it," Edda said.
"People who strip them in the field lose more than they save in space."
The second collector adjusted the sketch in his notes.
Leon watched them pass the plant one at a time.
Four competent people could still ruin a valuable patch if they hurried past the part they did not understand.
He had promised Edda they would listen.
So far, they were keeping that promise for him.
Once the demonstration ended, he drew the household aside to set their priorities.
Sun cups came first if the field was ready.
Frost-thread would be gathered separately when its stems developed the pale growth Edda had described.
Emberseed could wait until they knew whether its later window fitted their return schedule.
Ira looked mildly disappointed at that last part, then glanced at the sun cup sketch.
"Bring back something worth waiting for," she told the collectors.
"We intend to," Lu Pei said.
Vyra assigned a carrier to each collector and kept the two recorders moving between the pairs.
Edda’s share would be separated after sorting, so nobody needed to interrupt each cut with arithmetic.
Seraphine checked the approaches with Wen Shu while Ira stayed near the rear of the column.
Loriel asked to work beside Edda during the first collection.
Leon agreed.
She would recognize changes the collectors might miss, and he wanted her to enjoy the chance to learn without being pulled away to answer every ordinary question.
The next ridge gave them their first clear view of the hollow.
Yellow flecks covered the lower slopes, with pale bands winding through the shaded ground beneath the trees.
From this distance, the colors looked almost painted onto the land.
Then a gust moved through them, and Leon saw thousands of closed flowers shift on their stems.
He smiled before he could help it.
There was enough here to make the cases at their backs seem very small.
Nerin saw his expression.
"Wait until they open."
The young man shifted the screens on his back and began pointing out the strips that were easiest to reach.
He knew where a basket could be set level and where the grass hid loose stones.
Then he mentioned a drying frame he wanted to buy with his part of the earnings.
"Your own?" Leon asked.
Nerin nodded.
"A small one.
I use my father’s now, but his orders come first."
He sounded embarrassed by how modest it was.
Leon looked at the screens he had carried all morning and hoped the harvest would cover it.
Another capable supplier would suit him very well.
They descended toward a fork in the path and met a woman coming the other way with two empty baskets.
A younger girl walked beside her, holding a bundle of cutting cloths against her chest.
Edda stopped.
"You’re early, Tessa."
"Apparently we’re late." The woman lowered a basket.
"Strangers are sitting across the lower path.
They want half."
"Half of what?" Edda asked.
"Anything we take out." Tessa looked at Leon’s party.
"Your people?"
"No," Leon said.
The girl beside her stared at the swords and cases with an expression he could not quite read.
Tessa touched her shoulder and moved her farther up the path.
"I’ll try the western side," she told Edda.
"My brother’s already over there."
Edda watched them leave, her mouth tightening.
Leon sent Wen Shu ahead before asking another question.
While they waited, he checked the slope beside the path.
The energy beneath it had strengthened since their last stop.
Wen Shu returned quickly.
"An armed group at the lower approach, Senior Brother.
Their collectors are working behind them.
They’ve put stakes across both paths."
Leon looked past her toward the yellow-covered ground.
The petals nearest the bottom had begun to lift.

chapters.title: Chapter 721: Their Price, His Answer
paragraphs: The strangers had brought more stakes than baskets.

Leon counted the nearest line as his party approached the hollow. It crossed the lower path, continued over a strip of bare ground, and ended beside a stand of closed sun cups that nobody was collecting.

Farther left, six people knelt among the flowers. Guards stood behind them while another pair watched the approach from a flat rock. Rust-colored sashes marked them as one expedition, though their armor varied. Several had narrow copper ornaments fitted along the ridges of their ears.
They watched the Palace party with considerably more interest than they had shown the two local growers leaving by the western path.
Wen Shu stopped beside Leon.
"Twenty-four that I could see. Most of the guards are Golden Core."
"Any movement above us?"
"None. The upper path is clear as far as the fork."
He nodded and let her return to the column.

The ground on their right formed a shallow crescent below the eastern slope. Sun cups grew there in dense clusters, separated from the occupied patch by a dry runnel and a few yards of exposed stone. Nobody had left tools among them. The strangers’ stakes simply reached far enough to claim that ground too.
Edda came to stand beside him.
"That patch will open shortly after theirs," she said. "The lower edge first."
"Does someone tend it?" Leon asked.
"No. These grounds are gathered when the bloom comes. People keep the paths clear, but the plants grow where they grow."
"Would taking that patch damage the next season?"
"Not if your people make the cuts I showed them."
That settled the question he cared about.

A man stepped down from the flat rock. He was thick through the shoulders, with a rust sash tucked beneath a dark breastplate. One copper ornament ran from the upper edge of his left ear to a stud near his jaw.
He stopped a few paces beyond the stakes.
"Which party?" he asked.
"Jade Moon Palace," Leon said.
The name produced no recognition. The man’s attention moved over Seraphine, then the carriers’ cases, before returning to Leon.
"Vard Kesh. We’re holding this hollow."
"I can see where you’re working." Leon indicated the empty crescent. "We’ll gather there."
"Same terms there." Kesh pointed to a row of open crates beneath the rock. "Half the harvest when you leave. Sorted before division."
Behind Leon, Nerin drew a sharp breath. Edda put a hand on his arm without looking away from Kesh.
"Half for what?" Leon asked.
"We reached it first. We’ve secured the approaches."
"From the people who gather here?"
Kesh’s expression cooled. "From anyone who might interrupt us. You can use the ground under the same protection."
Leon looked at the six collectors behind him. One was already carrying a shallow tray toward the crates. A guard took it and bent close to examine the contents.
So they understood that the harvest needed care. They simply preferred to have other people perform part of the work and surrender the result.
He could hardly object to the desire for a larger share. It was the assumption that he would give them his that irritated him.
Half, before we even start.

He had fought for the last harvest, paid for expertise that preserved it, and brought it back to be refined. Edda’s tenth bought knowledge he needed. Kesh’s demand bought permission from a man who had driven stakes into wild ground that morning.
"No," Leon said.
Kesh watched him for a moment, perhaps waiting for an offer.
Leon turned toward Vyra. "Use the eastern patch. Two pairs along the lower edge. The others above them once Edda confirms it’s ready."
"Yes, Young Master."
The collectors did not surge forward. Vyra brought them up in order, each with the carrier assigned to him. Their cases remained closed until they reached the dry strip beside the crescent.
Kesh moved into Leon’s line of sight again.
"You haven’t understood."
"I understood the price," Leon said. "I’m not paying it."
The nearest guard left the rock. Others began turning from the occupied patch, watching their leader for instructions.

Leon checked their positions and the spaces between his own people. The carriers needed somewhere clear to set down their cases. Any fight close to the flowers would make the outing more troublesome than it needed to be.
"Seraphine, the path," he said. "Ira, stay with the upper pair."
Both women moved without discussion. Seraphine stopped between the approaching guard and the collectors. Ira took the side nearest the unworked slope, her lance resting comfortably in one hand.
Kesh noticed. His gaze lingered on Ira’s apparent cultivation, then returned to Leon with renewed impatience.
"An attendant won’t keep this ground for you."
Leon had heard enough variations of that assumption lately. He stepped clear of the collectors so that anyone coming toward him would have to cross the bare runnel.
"Stay on your side," he said. "You have flowers opening."
For the first time, Kesh glanced back.
The nearest patch had brightened. Several cups now stood open, each holding a clear bead at its center. His collectors were working faster, trying to keep their sleeves from brushing the stems.
Leon felt a brief, unreasonable pleasure at the sight. The garden, the early walk, the unfamiliar instructions—all of it had led to something he could finally see for himself.
Then Loriel called softly from the eastern crescent.
"Young Master. Here."

Edda was kneeling beside the lower edge. A yellow cup had opened in front of her. As Leon watched, moisture gathered at its center, thickening into a bright, clear bead. Spiritual energy collected within it strongly enough that he could distinguish its warmth from the current in the soil.
Loriel looked up at him, excited despite the men assembling behind Kesh.
"It’s ready."
The grower had her knife out. Nerin stood beside the empty trays, pale but staying where she had placed him.
Leon glanced at Kesh one last time. The man raised his hand, and four guards started across the bare strip toward Seraphine. Two more turned uphill, trying to reach the carriers from the side.
There was still time for them to stop. Leon doubted they would use it.
He faced his collectors.
"Begin."
Lu Pei lowered his cutting tool beneath the first flower. Across the runnel, Kesh’s guards broke into a run.

chapters.title: Chapter 722: Keep Cutting
paragraphs: Lu Pei’s knife passed beneath the flower just as the first sword cleared its sheath.

Leon stepped into the runnel. The guard coming toward him thrust past his shoulder, aiming for Seraphine and the collectors behind her. His blade entered a fold in the air and emerged pointing at the stones beneath his own feet.

Before the man could withdraw it, Leon caught his wrist and drove him into the second guard. Both struck the bare ground hard enough to crack it. Leon took the sword from the first man’s hand and turned.

Seraphine had already reached the remaining two. Her sheathed sword caught one beneath the elbow; a brief flash carried her past his companion. The second man’s knees gave way before his raised blade completed its swing.

Above the crescent, Ira met the flankers with her lance held crosswise. She knocked one backward into the slope and caught the other’s weapon against the haft. He tried to pull free. Ira twisted, took the weapon, and struck him across the ribs with its own handle.
Nerin flinched at the sound. The tray in his hands tipped.
"Level," Edda said sharply.
He steadied it. Lu Pei laid the first sun cup inside, its clear bead trembling between the petals.
Kesh drew his sword.

Leon crossed the remaining distance before the man could finish gathering energy along it. He caught the flat of the blade between two fingers. Kesh’s shoulder jerked as he tried to wrench it loose, then a hard yellow light spread across his breastplate.
Leon put his other hand against it.
The protection broke. He pushed Kesh down onto one knee, pressed a little farther, and felt the man stop resisting.
Behind Kesh, several guards had started forward. Vyra lifted her hand. A thin line of flame appeared across the bare approach, close enough to their boots that they halted together.
Leon looked down at the man beneath his palm.
"Drop it."
Kesh’s fingers loosened. His sword fell between them.
The hollow was suddenly quiet enough for Leon to hear a collector asking Edda whether the next flower was ready.
"Yes," she answered. "Same cut."
Kesh stared at his own weapon. Leon watched the change in his face as he looked from the cracked breastplate to the six men on the ground. Anger remained, but it was no longer choosing his actions.

He released a cautious thread of perception toward Leon, as if another examination might explain what had happened. Leon let him find the same apparent cultivation he had dismissed a moment earlier. Kesh swallowed. His hand moved away from a second pouch beneath his sash and settled flat against his thigh.
"We yield," Kesh said.
"Tell your people."
Kesh raised his voice. "Weapons down. All of you."
Nobody argued. One guard took a moment to lower a half-drawn bow, watching the flame at his feet. Vyra waited until he had unstrung it before letting the line die.
Leon released Kesh and stepped back.

His own gatherers were still working. The upper pair had paused during Ira’s interception; now she waved them back toward their cases. Seraphine checked the fallen guards, moved their weapons out of reach, and returned to the path.
Not a single attack had reached the flowers.
Leon felt rather pleased about that. He had imagined spending the next hour listening to Edda explain exactly how much spiritual value a boot could destroy.
"Young Master." Vyra approached with one of the recorders. "Their belongings?"

"Treasure, valuable equipment, and everything they’ve gathered. Leave food, water, ordinary clothing, and enough basic tools to travel." Leon looked at Kesh. "Storage items opened by their owners. Nothing hidden."
The man’s mouth tightened. His gaze went briefly toward the crates beneath the flat rock.
"That’s several days’ work."
"Then you should have kept working."
Leon waited. Kesh looked away first and began removing the pouch at his belt.
Half of ours wasn’t enough. Now look at you.
He kept the thought to himself. There were twenty-four people to disarm, delicate stock to move, and a harvest progressing whether any of them felt properly humiliated or not.

Vyra directed the surrender on the bare ground beside the rock. Each owner opened their storage item and laid out its contents under supervision. Wen Shu watched the upper path while two Palace guards gathered weapons. The recorders divided their attention between the seized stock and the fresh trays arriving from the crescent.
Kesh’s six collectors stood apart from the fighters, cutting cloths still tied around their wrists. One kept glancing at a shallow wooden case among the surrendered goods.
"What’s in that?" Leon asked.
"Yesterday’s roots," the collector said. "They need the lid loosened. We close it for carrying, but they’ve been sitting in the sun."
Leon motioned him forward, with a guard beside him.
The man opened the vents along the case’s edge. A damp, earthy smell rose from within. He adjusted a folded cloth, then withdrew his hands and waited.
Leon had Edda inspect it when she could leave the first cutting pair. She crouched beside the box and lifted one corner of the lining.
"Keep these shaded," she said. "The packing’s sound."
"Can we carry them with ours?"
"Separately. I’ll show your carriers." Edda glanced at the defeated collectors. "They knew what they were doing."
"Their leader didn’t."
She gave Leon a brief look, then went to find spare screens.

The surrender produced several useful blades, two compact defensive instruments, storage pouches, mineral pieces wrapped in oilcloth, and the carefully packed roots. The fresh sun cups were easier to judge. Kesh’s collectors had begun before Leon arrived, and their first tray was already full.
Vyra kept that tray with the confiscated stock. When a recorder reached to add it to the party’s own harvest, she stopped him and pointed to the separate page.
"Taken from Kesh. These were already cut."
He corrected the entry.
Leon left her to the division and walked uphill. Ira stood over the two flankers while they helped each other rise. One held his side; the other had a swelling along his jaw. Both could walk.
"Anything broken?" Leon asked.
"Possibly his pride," Ira said, indicating the larger man. "He tried to take the lance back."

The guard kept his eyes on the ground. Leon checked the gathering pair a few paces beyond him. Their carrier had shifted a case away from the scuffle and was now carefully brushing dirt from its closed lid.
"All right?" Leon asked.
"Yes, Senior Brother." The carrier showed him the unmarked lining. "Nothing reached the inside."
"Good. Stay with your collector."
Down in the crescent, Nerin had recovered enough to bring another tray to Edda. His first attempt at setting it down rattled the cups. He stopped, took a breath, and lowered it properly.
Leon caught him staring a moment later.
"What?"
"I thought there would be more fighting." Nerin glanced toward Kesh. "There were so many of them."
"There are still flowers opening." Leon pointed toward the waiting collector. "He needs your tray."
Nerin hurried off. Leon watched him go with a small smile. The boy would probably have questions once his hands stopped shaking. Edda would make certain he finished his work before asking them.

By the time Vyra called Leon back, the surrendered expedition had gathered on the western path. Kesh’s breastplate lay among the seized equipment. Without it, he looked smaller, though the anger had returned to his face now that he was no longer beneath Leon’s hand.
Leon indicated the path out.
"Keep going until you’re clear of the hollow."
Kesh looked at the laden cases, then at Seraphine beside them. Whatever he considered saying remained unsaid.

His people collected their basic packs. Two supported the guard Leon had driven into the ground. The last of the six collectors lingered long enough to point out a loose fastening on a root case before following the others.
Leon watched until the rust sashes disappeared beyond the fork. He would have preferred to begin gathering without the interruption, but the return on it was difficult to dislike.
Loriel called from beneath the trees.
"Young Master, come look."
The shaded ground had changed. Pale growth was spreading along slender stems between the exposed roots, turning a patch of dull grass silver from within.
Edda was already pulling a different knife from her roll.
"Leave one pair with the cups," she told Vyra. "The frost-thread’s starting."

We close it for carrying, but they’ve been sitting in the sun."
Leon motioned him forward, with a guard beside him.
The man opened the vents along the case’s edge.
A damp, earthy smell rose from within.
He adjusted a folded cloth, then withdrew his hands and waited.
Leon had Edda inspect it when she could leave the first cutting pair.
She crouched beside the box and lifted one corner of the lining.
"Keep these shaded," she said.
"The packing’s sound."
"Can we carry them with ours?"
"Separately.
I’ll show your carriers." Edda glanced at the defeated collectors.
"They knew what they were doing."
"Their leader didn’t."
She gave Leon a brief look, then went to find spare screens.
The surrender produced several useful blades, two compact defensive instruments, storage pouches, mineral pieces wrapped in oilcloth, and the carefully packed roots.
The fresh sun cups were easier to judge.
Kesh’s collectors had begun before Leon arrived, and their first tray was already full.
Vyra kept that tray with the confiscated stock.
When a recorder reached to add it to the party’s own harvest, she stopped him and pointed to the separate page.
"Taken from Kesh.
These were already cut."
He corrected the entry.
Leon left her to the division and walked uphill.
Ira stood over the two flankers while they helped each other rise.
One held his side; the other had a swelling along his jaw.
Both could walk.
"Anything broken?" Leon asked.
"Possibly his pride," Ira said, indicating the larger man.
"He tried to take the lance back."
The guard kept his eyes on the ground.
Leon checked the gathering pair a few paces beyond him.
Their carrier had shifted a case away from the scuffle and was now carefully brushing dirt from its closed lid.
"All right?" Leon asked.
"Yes, Senior Brother." The carrier showed him the unmarked lining.
"Nothing reached the inside."
"Good.
Stay with your collector."
Down in the crescent, Nerin had recovered enough to bring another tray to Edda.
His first attempt at setting it down rattled the cups.
He stopped, took a breath, and lowered it properly.
Leon caught him staring a moment later.
"What?"
"I thought there would be more fighting." Nerin glanced toward Kesh.
"There were so many of them."
"There are still flowers opening." Leon pointed toward the waiting collector.
"He needs your tray."
Nerin hurried off.
Leon watched him go with a small smile.
The boy would probably have questions once his hands stopped shaking.
Edda would make certain he finished his work before asking them.
By the time Vyra called Leon back, the surrendered expedition had gathered on the western path.
Kesh’s breastplate lay among the seized equipment.
Without it, he looked smaller, though the anger had returned to his face now that he was no longer beneath Leon’s hand.
Leon indicated the path out.
"Keep going until you’re clear of the hollow."
Kesh looked at the laden cases, then at Seraphine beside them.
Whatever he considered saying remained unsaid.
His people collected their basic packs.
Two supported the guard Leon had driven into the ground.
The last of the six collectors lingered long enough to point out a loose fastening on a root case before following the others.
Leon watched until the rust sashes disappeared beyond the fork.
He would have preferred to begin gathering without the interruption, but the return on it was difficult to dislike.
Loriel called from beneath the trees.
"Young Master, come look."
The shaded ground had changed.
Pale growth was spreading along slender stems between the exposed roots, turning a patch of dull grass silver from within.
Edda was already pulling a different knife from her roll.
"Leave one pair with the cups," she told Vyra.
"The frost-thread’s starting."

chapters.title: Chapter 723: A Place for Life
paragraphs: The first frost-thread snapped in Lu Pei’s fingers.
He stared at the broken stem. A bead of cloudy moisture formed at the break and slid down onto his glove.
Edda took it from him before he could put it with the good stock.
"Too high. Hold below the pale growth."
"I barely touched it," he said.
"That’s why I’m showing you." She laid the damaged stem on a separate cloth. "It won’t mend because you’re offended."
Leon turned away before Lu Pei caught him smiling. The collector had faced armed men with considerably less distress than one ruined plant.

Under Edda’s guidance, the next stem came free intact. Lu Pei laid it across a narrow support in the tray while Nerin slipped a soft loop over its base. Nothing pressed against the pale growth. Once secured, the delicate thing could be carried without rattling against its neighbors.
The work was slower than cutting sun cups, but the energy held in each stem made Leon willing to wait.

He crouched beside the first completed tray. Coolness reached his fingers before he touched the wood. It had the clean, persistent quality of the blue-white mineral samples Bai Heng had prepared, though Leon could also sense something living beneath it.
If he can preserve that through refinement, this was worth the walk.
He left the stems alone. Admiring a resource did not qualify him to handle it.

The surge moved through the hollow unevenly. Sun cups above the eastern crescent remained closed while those near the runnel had already begun clouding. Beneath the trees, one strip of frost-thread brightened ahead of the rest, following a shallow depression that Edda had marked with her heel.

Loriel moved with her, comparing roots and soil before calling the collectors forward. They disagreed once over a patch near a fallen branch. Loriel thought the energy beneath it was strong enough to harvest; Edda pointed to the stiff tips and asked her to check lower down.
After examining a stem, Loriel nodded and marked it to leave.
Leon liked watching her learn. She did not pretend to know a plant because she understood ten thousand others. When something surprised her, she leaned closer.

The party settled into the work. One pair finished the usable cups while the others gathered frost-thread. Ira carried filled cases between the two patches, lifting them easily but walking with an exaggerated care that made Nerin watch her feet.
"I can carry one," he offered.
"You’re carrying the screens," Ira said. "I’d have to come back for those."
He considered that, then hurried ahead to clear a branch from her path.

Leon checked the approaches with Seraphine. There was no sign of Kesh returning. On the western side of the hollow, two local gathering parties had begun working beyond the trees. He recognized Tessa’s baskets among them. She raised a hand when she noticed him looking, then returned to her patch.

He had no objection to them using the ground his people could not reach. The open flowers already exceeded their cases, and Edda had warned that the later plants required different preparation. Claiming everything would only give him more to watch while it spoiled.
By late morning, the sun cups were finished. The collectors had begun bringing in trays from the shaded slope when Loriel called him over.
She knelt beside a cluster of low, rounded leaves. Between them stood a green stalk no longer than his hand, bent near the top as though somebody had folded it and changed their mind.
"Wellheart," Edda said. "Don’t stand on the roots."
Leon moved his foot.

Loriel had cleared a little soil from one side of the plant. Beneath the leaves, a pale root swelled into a tightly folded mass. Fine strands ran through its exposed surface, curving back on themselves without ending where he expected.
"What does it do?" he asked.
"Locals use prepared slices in restorative mixtures," Loriel said. "Edda says the root keeps growing denser after the leaves reach this size."
"Only during a good surge," Edda added. "Cut it too early and you’ve mostly bought water. Too late, and the inner folds turn hard."

Loriel guided his attention toward the living root. He sensed the vitality gathered within it, unusually concentrated for something so small. More curious was the way it continued moving. The outer tissue shifted gently as fresh energy passed inward.
"It hasn’t stopped circulating," Loriel said. "Even here." She indicated the tightest fold. "I want to see how it manages that."
Leon looked at her face. "For your Core?"
"Possibly." She sounded excited but careful. "Condensing vitality is one thing. Keeping it responsive afterward is another. I don’t want a Core that stores plenty and releases it poorly."

He remembered Seraphine sitting with her sword across her knees, refusing to accept a more stable arrangement that made her transitions sluggish. The women were approaching different problems, but none intended to settle for merely surviving a breakthrough.
"Can you take it?" Leon asked Edda.
"With the surrounding soil. If she wants to study it living, don’t peel it here."
Loriel had already reached for her tools.

They lifted the plant with its fine roots intact and placed it in a spare lined container. A second, smaller wellheart nearby had a damaged leaf and a thin root extending beneath a stone. Edda examined it, then showed Loriel where a small sample could be taken without ruining the main plant.
Leon stayed while they worked. He could have claimed another stretch of frost-thread during that time, but Loriel’s expression when the root came free made him glad he had not wandered off.

Edda showed her how to tuck damp soil around the fine roots without pressing against the swollen center. Loriel repeated the movement herself, then asked how much water it would need overnight. The questions had become very particular. She was already thinking past the return journey to where she would keep it beside her worktable.
She held the sample up to the light. "Look at the folds."
He looked. She turned it a little farther.
"I see them," Leon said.
"You don’t see why I’m pleased yet."
"Then show me."
She smiled at that, and he felt an entirely unreasonable satisfaction at having given the right answer.

They waited until the last frost-thread case was closed before testing it. Loriel chose a flat stone well clear of the packed harvest. She washed her hands, laid the sample in a shallow dish, and used two smooth pieces of her kit to steady it.
Edda watched from beside her. Nerin brought water and remained close enough to see, although Ira caught the back of his collar when he leaned over Loriel’s elbow.
"Give her room," Ira said.

Loriel introduced a thread of vitality into the cut surface. Leon followed its movement through the living tissue. The first portion passed easily. Where the folds grew tighter, it gathered more densely, then continued along a narrower path.
Loriel withdrew her hand and let the sample settle before trying again with gentle pressure from the smooth supports.
This time, the tissue compressed enough for Leon to see the change. The thread slowed, but when Loriel altered its flow, the vitality inside answered. It did not remain trapped in the densest part.
She stopped almost at once.
"Again?" Leon asked.
"Later. I want this piece alive for comparison." Loriel loosened the supports and examined the surface. "That was enough."
Edda peered into the dish. "Enough for what?"

"To know it’s worth studying." Loriel glanced up at Leon. "The tissue may be doing something I can’t preserve in an extract. Or it may react differently at the pressure a Core needs. I haven’t proved either."
Her caution did nothing to hide her pleasure. She packed the sample herself, then checked the larger plant as though it might have escaped while she was occupied.
Across the hollow, the late emberseed stalks had begun darkening. Edda studied them, looked at the sun, and shook her head. They would have to be left for another gathering party.
Leon found he did not mind very much.
Loriel picked up the wellheart’s container and held it close while he fastened the strap for her. Through the open top, he could still sense the dense vitality moving within its folds.
She looked down at it with a smile he wanted to see again.
"If I can learn how it keeps that passage open," she said quietly, "I may know what to change in mine."

chapters.title: Chapter 724: Worth the Walk
paragraphs: Edda moved a tray back across the cloth.
"Those are the cloudy ones."
The recorder checked his page. "They’re the same size."
"They won’t fetch the same price."
Vyra crouched beside them and examined the cups. Then she took a clear one from the neighboring tray and set it among Edda’s share.
"Separate quality before counting," she told the recorder. "We’ll do this row again."

Leon sat on a stone with his lunch cooling in his hand. He had expected the division to take time. Watching Edda catch the first mistake reassured him more than a quick acceptance would have done. A woman who knew the value of her tenth would also know whether the rest was worth bringing home.

They had left the hollow while there was still daylight for the return to the garden. Now the cases lay beneath Edda’s awning, sorted by species and condition. Nerin’s screens held the frost-thread clear of the damp ground.

The roots seized from Kesh remained on a separate cloth with his equipment and mineral stock. Edda’s payment came from what the party had gathered during the bloom. Vyra had made that distinction before opening the first case, and the grower had agreed without argument.

The wellheart needed more discussion. Loriel wanted to retain both living plants and her test sample. Edda valued them against a portion of good frost-thread; Vyra checked the comparison with the rest of the harvest, then adjusted the grower’s share accordingly.
When they finished, Edda examined her portion one last time.
"That will do."
Leon took another bite of bread. "Would you guide us again?"
"If there’s something worth gathering." She looked at the packed trays. "And if you still have people who listen."

Lu Pei, seated nearby, lifted his bandaged finger in acknowledgment. He had cut himself on an ordinary fastening after handling spiritual plants all morning. Ira had found this much funnier than he did.
Nerin brought Leon water and lingered beside the stone.
"We did well," he said, almost asking.
"Ask her." Leon nodded toward Edda.
"I did. She said we’d know when we sold it."
That sounded like Edda. Leon looked at the young man’s screen frames, repaired neatly despite their age.
"Which one are you hoping to buy?" he asked.

Nerin’s face brightened. He described a small frame with adjustable shelves, then admitted that he had only seen it once and the maker might have sold it. By the time he finished, Leon understood more about drying screens than he had intended to learn over lunch.
Edda overheard the last part.
"Trading day is in two days," she said. "You can look then. Finish covering these first."
Nerin went back to work without losing his smile.

Before the party left the following morning, Edda dictated the important handling instructions to a recorder. Loriel added sketches and asked her to repeat one warning about heat. Bai Heng would receive intact plants and useful directions this time.
They said goodbye above the repaired channel. Edda returned to her beds; Nerin walked with them as far as the red-barked trees before turning back.

The cases made the descent slower. Leon helped at the bad crossing, and the carriers took turns with the heavier loads. His other body continued along the empty eastern ridge, far from the route. He let it rest while he gave most of his attention to getting the harvest home.

Wen Shu regained a clear reply from the spring during the afternoon. She reported their number, their condition, and the packed harvest. Bai Heng asked about preservation before asking what they had brought.
Leon could hear the relief in his voice when Wen Shu mentioned written instructions.

They reached the spring before dusk, as promised. All eighteen came in together. The twelve who had stayed behind helped with the cases, and Tian’s reply from the entrance base confirmed that her own eighteen remained safe. The gateway site was unchanged.
Bai Heng had cleared a worktable before the first lid came off.

He read Edda’s instructions, asked Loriel two questions, and set the unfamiliar roots aside. The sun cups interested him immediately. By the time Leon finished the return report, the old man had selected a few for a small preparation test.
"Tomorrow," Bai Heng said, before Leon could ask. "I want to see what remains after the first separation."
Leon accepted that and went to find dinner.
The sample was ready after breakfast. Bai Heng presented a shallow sealed vial alongside a portion of the red mineral fuel they had already tested.
"The flower preparation releases more slowly," he said. "Less total energy in this amount, but it doesn’t fall away as sharply near the end. I kept the first batch small."
"Can they be used together?" Leon asked.
"The preparations remain sound beside each other. What happens in your circulation is for you to tell me."
Leon liked that answer. He took both portions to his tent, closed the wards, and entered his dimensional world where nobody outside could see the opening.

Xyra met him near his usual practice ground. She listened to his request, adjusted the local time without any visible effort, and left him with a few hours to compare the samples while little time passed at the spring.

He began with the mineral portion alone. Its familiar uneven release made the baseline easy to recognize: a stronger early supply, a dip, then another small rise as the remaining material yielded its energy. His circulation handled it, though he still had to adjust the intake.
With a modest amount of the flower extract added, the dip became shallower.
Leon repeated the cycle. The plant preparation continued releasing while the mineral portion weakened. There was still variation, but he no longer needed the same abrupt correction at that point.
He almost increased both amounts immediately.
Finish this one properly first.

He made himself record the result, then changed only the proportion of extract. More was worse. The slower release began lingering beyond the point where he wanted it, forcing an adjustment later in the cycle.

Leon returned to the earlier mixture. After several clean repetitions, he stood and continued circulating while walking across the practice ground. A familiar movement technique disturbed the flow briefly; he corrected the intake and tried again at a gentler pace.
Nothing in his foundation had changed. What had improved was the supply he was asking it to manage.
He grinned and sat down to write the quantities while they were fresh in his mind.
Back at the spring, Bai Heng read the practical part of his notes twice.
"This batch," the old man said. "The next flowers may vary."
"Then keep the preparations separate until we check them," Leon replied. "But make more of this one."
Bai Heng smiled and reached for a clean jar.

Outside, Vyra was sorting a small selection of trade goods. Trading day in Asterbank had begun that morning; there was still time for the five of them to reach it later in the day by the direct settlement path Edda had described.
Leon looked at the vial in his hand. One morning in a hollow had given him better fuel and Loriel a possibility she could hardly stop examining.
"Bring something a book seller might accept," he told Vyra. "I want to know what else we’ve been walking past."

The slower release began lingering beyond the point where he wanted it, forcing an adjustment later in the cycle.
Leon returned to the earlier mixture.
After several clean repetitions, he stood and continued circulating while walking across the practice ground.
A familiar movement technique disturbed the flow briefly; he corrected the intake and tried again at a gentler pace.
Nothing in his foundation had changed.
What had improved was the supply he was asking it to manage.
He grinned and sat down to write the quantities while they were fresh in his mind.
Back at the spring, Bai Heng read the practical part of his notes twice.
"This batch," the old man said.
"The next flowers may vary."
"Then keep the preparations separate until we check them," Leon replied.
"But make more of this one."
Bai Heng smiled and reached for a clean jar.
Outside, Vyra was sorting a small selection of trade goods.
Trading day in Asterbank had begun that morning; there was still time for the five of them to reach it later in the day by the direct settlement path Edda had described.
Leon looked at the vial in his hand.
One morning in a hollow had given him better fuel and Loriel a possibility she could hardly stop examining.
"Bring something a book seller might accept," he told Vyra.
"I want to know what else we’ve been walking past."

chapters.title: Chapter 725: The Little Blue One
paragraphs: The woman at the first stall poured hot sand over a bundle of leaves.
Loriel stopped so suddenly that Leon nearly walked into her.
"Won’t that damage them?" she asked.
The seller lifted a corner of the bundle with wooden tongs. Beneath the outer leaves, the pale inner layer had begun separating from its veins.
"Cold sand takes too long. Fire spoils the lining." She shook the bundle once. "First time seeing it done?"
Loriel admitted it was. The woman moved her bowl far enough for her to watch, then continued serving the customer waiting on the other side.

Leon stepped out of the lane and let a boy with a tray of cups squeeze past. Asterbank’s trading day filled the street from the well to the drying sheds. People argued over lengths of cloth, held roots up to the light, and called across stalls to neighbors who clearly owed them something.
The place smelled of hot grain, damp plants, and the faint sharpness of fresh-cut wood.
He had been expecting interesting resources. He had not expected to be hungry again so soon.

They had left twenty-five Palace members at the spring and eighteen at the entrance base. Bai Heng knew their route and when to expect them back; Wen Shu had the arrangements for a missed return. Here, with only the four women beside him, Leon could stop without making a whole column stop too.

He bought a packet of warm flatbread after Vyra negotiated a small exchange of ordinary preserved provisions for local coin. The seller examined the unfamiliar food before accepting it, then insisted Leon taste her bread while it was still hot.
Ira took a piece from the packet he offered and burned her fingers on the filling.
"You could have warned me," she said.
"She did." Leon pointed with his own half-eaten piece.
Ira looked at him, then laughed and ate more carefully.

Seraphine lingered at a stall selling straps and fitted weapon covers. She tested a buckle, asked about its metal, and put it back when the answer did not justify the price. Vyra bought spare fastenings after finding the same workmanship on an unadorned set farther down the table.
Loriel caught up with them carrying a little parcel of the processed leaf lining. The seller had let her keep an imperfect piece for comparison.
"Useful?" Leon asked.
"Possibly. It keeps moisture around certain cuttings without touching their surface." She glanced back at the stall. "I would have tried cloth first."
He offered her the last bread. She accepted it absently, then stopped to appreciate the filling.

They found the books beneath a patched awning near the drying sheds. Most were thin stitched volumes with stained covers. The seller had weighted the open pages with smooth stones, and one illustrated sheet showed a cut stem that Leon recognized.
"Reedlace," he said.

Loriel leaned beside him. The drawing included the inner layers Edda had shown her, with small marks beside each stage of preparation. She followed the sequence with her finger, careful not to touch the page.
"This one describes drying?" she asked the seller.
"Growing, cutting, drying, storage. Different sections." He opened the book farther back. "Common stock from the western settlements. Some upland plants too."
The writing meant nothing to Leon. He could hear every word the man said, yet the labels might as well have been decorative scratches.
Vyra tested the problem directly. She pointed to a line and asked him to read it, then compared the sound with the marks. Understanding the spoken sentence did not make its written form any clearer.
"We’ll need somebody to read parts of it aloud," she told Leon.
The seller named a price for the volume and another for an hour of his time. Vyra asked which entries the hour would cover. That began a negotiation Leon was happy to leave to her.

While they talked, he found a frost-thread illustration near the middle. A small drawing showed the growth supported at its base, exactly as Nerin had packed it. Another showed it hanging upside down over a shallow pan.
That could mean dry it. Or never do this.
He stopped trying to guess.

They bought the book. The seller agreed to read the sun cup and frost-thread entries first, including the warnings and measures, while Vyra wrote them in Palace script. Loriel remained to ask questions. Seraphine took a seat where she could watch the lane, and Leon went with Ira to inspect the living stock across from the awning.

Most plants were labeled with the same unreadable script. Ira pointed to a thorny shrub whose leaves gave off a little heat, asked its purpose, and lost interest when the owner explained that it kept a drying cupboard warm but spoiled if regularly scorched.
Leon was looking at a row of hanging baskets when Loriel joined them during a pause in the reading.
She went straight to a pot at the end of the table.

It held a low green plant with three small blue flowers. Their petals curled inward at the tips, leaving pale centers open to the light. When Loriel brushed a leaf, the nearest bloom turned slightly toward her fingers.
She smiled.
"What is it?" Leon asked.
"Bellshade," the owner said. "Likes a cool window. Don’t drown it."
"Does it need much room?" Loriel asked.
"A pot that size for another year."
She examined the soil and the underside of a leaf. Then she asked the price.
Leon waited for a question about its medicinal use. None came. Loriel chose a second pot with a better drainage hole and asked the owner to repack it for carrying.
"For your garden?" he asked.
"For wherever I sit." Loriel glanced at him. "I like the blue."
He looked at the flowers again. They were a good blue, clear and bright without glowing or emitting any remarkable pressure. He found himself smiling too.
When she reached for the wrapped pot, Leon took it first.
"You’ve got the sample parcel."
"I can carry both, Young Master."
"I know." He settled the pot against his arm. "Finish your questions about the book."
Loriel touched his sleeve before returning to the awning.

He carried the plant while they listened to the remaining instructions. From the corner of his eye, he saw her glance toward it twice, pleased in a way that had nothing to do with condensation or the value of a harvest.

By the end of the paid hour, Vyra had several pages of usable notes and a much longer list of passages still needing translation. The seller marked those with strips of cloth so they could find them again.
As he closed the volume, three workers passed carrying nested preparation pans. They set them outside the shop next door, where similar stacks already filled half the entrance.
Ira looked at the order. "Somebody’s planning to stay busy."
"Hollow Steps," the book seller said. "They’ll all want everything at once, then complain about the price."
Leon turned toward him. "What’s Hollow Steps?"
The man pointed next door.
"Ask Sella. She’s been supplying the teams for years. Old cultivation ground. The currents change while you’re sitting in them."
Leon looked down at the preparation manual, then at the stacked pans.
This time, he had several questions of his own.
