chapters.title: Chapter 726: The Ground That Changes
paragraphs: "No," the woman behind the counter said. "You ordered six shallow pans. Those are six shallow pans."
The customer pointed at the stack by the door. "They look deeper than the last ones."
"The last ones were your brother’s. He ordered deep pans and spent three days complaining that he couldn’t carry them full."
Leon waited outside while the argument ended. The customer measured a pan with his fingers, muttered something about his brother, and paid.
Only then did the woman turn toward the five visitors.
"Buying or asking?"
"Both, perhaps," Leon said. "The book seller sent us. He said you could tell us about Hollow Steps."
"He could have told you himself." She looked at the volume under Vyra’s arm. "But then he’d have had to stop selling you that."

She introduced herself as Sella Venn and moved a bundle of packing cloth off a bench. Her shop ran deeper than it appeared from the street. Shelves held jars, screens, sealed containers, and instruments whose purposes Leon could only guess at. A ledger lay open beside a bowl of cold food.
He set Loriel’s plant safely at the end of the bench before sitting.
"The currents change there?" he asked.
"Across the courts, yes. Sometimes within the same court. What are you looking to gather?"
"Materials of several affinities. And somewhere worth cultivating."
Sella studied him, then the women.
"You’ll find both. Whether you get much use from either depends on where you settle."

She took a rolled sketch from a shelf and spread it across the counter. Several stepped enclosures followed the slope of a hill, connected by narrow approaches. The lines were faded where people had touched the paper.
The labels remained unreadable, but Leon could follow the shape of the place as Sella explained it.

Hollow Steps had once been laid out for cultivation. Enough of its courts and channels remained usable that local teams returned when the surrounding spiritual currents entered their accessible phase. At other times, the approaches were too unstable for ordinary gathering, and much of what could be taken was still immature.
"About ten days," Sella said, tapping the lower approach. "That’s what the teams expect. They’ve had people checking the outlying channels since before trading day."
"A regular date?" Vyra asked.
"Regular signs. The date shifts." Sella indicated three stacks of containers. "Those buyers have put down deposits. They don’t do that because somebody heard a story over supper."
Leon leaned closer to the sketch.
"When you say the currents change, do you mean they grow stronger and weaker, or that the affinities change?"

"Both. One court may have a steady warm current in the morning and something much sharper later. Another stays mostly the same but receives it in waves. The people who go there to cultivate pay attention before sitting down."
That was more interesting than a simple increase in ambient energy.

His recent experiments had used prepared portions whose behavior he could measure and repeat. He could vary those portions, but he still chose when to make the change. A place that varied without waiting for him would test something different.
Assuming I can find a court that doesn’t throw half a mountain through my circulation.
He asked about the gentler areas first.

Sella pointed out the lower courts. People used them to learn the changes before moving uphill. The richest patches were less predictable, and the containers stacked by her door were intended for mineral accretions and plant growth collected there.
"I’ve bought material from three openings," she said. "I’ve supplied teams for more. If you want somebody who has sat in every court, that isn’t me."
"Have you been inside?" Leon asked.
"The lower ground, once. I went to settle an order dispute. I prefer buying what comes out."
He appreciated the distinction. So far, she had not promised him an inheritance, a miraculous breakthrough, or a treasure waiting politely for the first handsome stranger to arrive.
Loriel asked which plants grew near the changing channels. Sella named several and pointed to the preparation manual.
"Two should be in there. Ask the seller to read you the storage warnings before you pay for a case."

Vyra marked the names phonetically beside the pages Sella indicated. More translation, more useful work for the days before they left. Leon was already considering which samples Bai Heng should prepare first.
Seraphine examined the narrow approaches on the sketch.
"Who controls entry?" she asked.
"Nobody who can make the other settlements agree." Sella smiled briefly. "The paths are open. Once you’re inside, the larger parties try to keep the productive courts for their own people."
"And outsiders?" Leon asked.
"Can walk the same paths. Don’t expect anyone to save you a good place."
He had not expected that anywhere in this realm.
Ira leaned forward. "Do they fight over them?"

"Sometimes. Sometimes two leaders agree on a division. Sometimes the smaller group sees who arrived first and keeps walking." Sella glanced at Ira’s expression. "The ground is valuable even if you avoid a fight."
"I understood," Ira said, though Leon doubted she found the warning necessary.

He asked about travel next. At a gathering party’s walking pace, the main route took roughly two days from Asterbank. There was a shorter ascent, but Sella would not recommend it to anyone carrying delicate stock. She described the junctions aloud while Vyra drew a copy in their own notes.

Leon bought a modest set of the recommended containers through a trade of suitable mineral pieces from his available share. Sella inspected them with a small instrument, rejected one, and named what she would accept for the rest. Vyra checked the exchange before agreeing.

They left the bulky portion with her for collection after making arrangements at the spring. There was no need to carry a future expedition’s equipment through the market just because Leon had become impatient to begin it.
Outside, Loriel retrieved her plant from him and adjusted its wrapping. The blue flowers had turned toward the light at the shop entrance.
"You want to go," she said.
"Yes." Leon looked at the copied route. "I want to see what changes before I decide what to draw into my body. But if even the lower courts behave as she says, I can learn something there."
"And gather enough to make the trip worthwhile," Vyra added.
"That too." He smiled. "Preferably more than enough."

They still had preparations to make. Bai Heng needed the translated passages and the results of his first mixture test. Loriel wanted the wellheart kept somewhere she could study it without repeatedly disturbing its roots. The spring and entrance teams needed a workable arrangement before another party traveled farther away.
Ten days gave them room to do those things properly. Leon felt no urge to spend all ten staring at the road.

A line of porters came down the street while they were speaking. Behind them walked several cultivators in pale green coats, each wearing a small badge shaped like three willow leaves. They stopped outside Sella’s shop, and a young man near the front handed her a folded order.
"Three Willows Hall," she called to a worker. "The long cases and the covered frames."
The young man glanced at Leon’s new containers, then at the route sketch in Vyra’s hands. His attention sharpened for a moment before he turned back to his order.

Leon watched the porters begin loading. These people knew where they were going, what they wanted, and how to bring it back. He would need more than a strong arm to recognize the best of what lay inside.
He turned to the book seller’s awning.
"Let’s get those two entries translated before we leave."
Beyond him, the first of the Hall’s long cases went onto a waiting cart. Ten days before the opening, somebody was already packing for the ground Leon wanted.

chapters.title: Chapter 727: Something for Ourselves
paragraphs: Ira put her finger on the illustration before the scribe finished reading its heading.
"That one. What does it say?"

Pell Orrow looked over the manual at her. Sella had recommended him when the bookseller closed his awning for supper, and he had already made it clear that pointing at a different page did not finish the passage he was reading.
"The warning about drying racks first," he said. "Unless you intend to ruin whatever you bring back."
Ira withdrew her finger. Leon hid a smile and moved the lamp closer.

They had taken a room behind Pell’s shop for the evening. Loriel’s little blue plant occupied the windowsill, while Vyra had spread their notes across a table that barely accommodated them. Outside, the last market stalls were being packed away.
Pell finished the warning, waited for Vyra to write it down, and finally turned to Ira’s stone.
The drawing showed a dark red mineral inside a bed of paler rock. One specimen had been cut open to expose dense bands within it.

"Hearthseal," Pell read. "Found in the warm courts of Hollow Steps, where the channels run hot and slow. Heavy for its size. An intact skin retains the fire within. Once cracked, it can lose much of its stored energy within a day."
"How do you lift it?" Ira asked.
"By leaving enough of the surrounding bed to support it." He tapped the illustration. "This part stays attached. Trim it later, when you know what you’re doing."
Ira leaned closer. "And how do you tell whether the skin’s cracked?"
Pell read that passage too.

Leon watched her following the drawing with unusual patience. She had looked at plenty of fire materials since arriving in this world. Most had interested her for about as long as it took to learn what they did.
This one had kept her quiet through an entire warning about drying racks.
"It may not occur in the courts that become accessible this time," Vyra said, finishing a line.
"I know." Ira pointed at the intact specimen. "But this is one I actually want to examine."
Leon asked Pell to continue. They had come for information, and he was quite happy to pay for another passage if it kept that expression on her face.
The next illustration showed loose stones suspended above a channel.
"When the current reverses, leave the beds," Pell explained. "Get onto the bare steps. Put down anything you haven’t freed properly. People hurt themselves trying to save half-cut deposits."
Seraphine studied the drawing. "Does it lift everything?"

"Loose material near the channel. Not the whole hillside." Pell rubbed an ink stain on his thumb. "The collectors call it a court taking a breath. Watch the steam. If it starts running backward, don’t stand there wondering whether the warning applies to you."
Vyra marked that passage separately. They paid the agreed fee when she finished, then stayed the night in Asterbank.
By the following afternoon, the five were back at the spring.
Bai Heng took the translated pages before Leon had finished explaining them. His preparation bench held several covered trays, each marked with the date and the batch it belonged to.
"The frost-thread notes add a step after drying," he said. "That may help with the discoloration."
"Try a small portion first," Loriel told him. "Pell could read the instructions, but he doesn’t prepare it himself."
Bai nodded and put that page beside an unfinished tray.
Thirty Palace members were together at the spring again. Eighteen remained at the entrance site, and Tian’s reply confirmed that nothing had changed there. The missing gateway had not returned.
Leon discussed Hollow Steps with Wen Shu and Bai Heng that evening. Twenty-five would stay here when his household left; their collection and guard arrangements could continue without him.
"We’ll allow twelve days from departure," Leon said. "If we can reach plaque range sooner, we’ll report. Otherwise, expect us back by then."
"And if you’re late?" Wen Shu asked.
"Allow two more days, then send a pair to ask at Sella Venn’s shop. She’ll know our destination. Don’t send anyone into Hollow Steps after us."
Wen Shu repeated the arrangements before passing them to Tian through the camp’s tested link. Leon was glad she asked practical questions without turning his departure into an argument.

He wanted this trip for himself and the women. The spring was secure, the people staying behind had worthwhile work, and he did not need to apologize for wanting something more interesting than another evening beside the preparation bench.
Over the next five days, the household made ready.

Loriel settled her two living wellheart plants in shallow trays of their original soil. The small test sample remained separate. She checked the plants morning and evening, recording changes before attempting anything further with them.
Her bellshade sat beside the trays. Leon found her turning its pot toward the light one morning, smiling when a blue flower brushed her knuckle.
"Does that one need a record too?" he asked.
"No. It needs you to stop shading it."
He moved, and she caught his sleeve before he could go far enough to be offended.

Ira borrowed the hearthseal notes so often that Vyra made her a copy. She asked Bai Heng what preparations might preserve the mineral’s internal structure; he suggested possibilities, then admitted he would need an actual specimen.
Seraphine checked their route to Asterbank and chose the clearer ridge path. Vyra reviewed the containers awaiting them at Sella’s shop and added wrapping material for intact mineral beds.
Leon prepared one small jar of the mineral-and-plant mixture that had worked in his recent tests. He wanted a familiar comparison when he reached the changing courts.

His Scripture could already circulate uneven supplies. Adjusting the mixture before a session was manageable. Following a change while the whole arrangement kept running was less comfortable. He tended to ease the intake, alter the branches, and bring them back up together.
At Hollow Steps, the surroundings would not pause while he did that.
I’d like to get through one change without having to restart half the damn thing.

He kept the jar with his notes. The rest of the waiting passed in ordinary work, meals with the women, and the occasional check on what his other body was seeing farther afield. Nothing there required him to abandon this opportunity.

A week after Sella’s original assessment, they left the spring before dawn. They reached Asterbank that afternoon, collected the order, and planned to start the two-day northern walk the next morning.
"Two cases of lined boxes, drying screens, four sealed jars," Sella said, checking her slate. "Already paid."
Vyra inspected the contents. Leon stored the entire order in his ring as soon as she finished.
Sella watched the cases disappear. "Useful piece of work."
"Very," Leon agreed.
"The Hall collected yesterday. They’ll be on the northern road by now." She pointed past him. "And you should look from the end of the street before supper."
Leon followed her gesture.
Beyond the roofs, a thin white plume stood above the northern ridge. It had not been there when they first visited the market.
Ira joined him, her folded notes tucked inside her coat.
"That’s the Steps?" she asked.
Sella came to the doorway. "They started steaming this morning."
Leon watched the plume bend east. They had left enough time to arrive before the expected opening, and now he was glad of every day they had saved.

chapters.title: Chapter 728: The Waiting Steps
paragraphs: By noon on the second day, Leon could smell damp stone on the wind, though they had not crossed a stream since breakfast.

The northern road had climbed out of farmland that morning. Water channels and low green fields gave way to scrub, then bare slopes. Ahead, the white plume they had seen from Asterbank spread across the ridge.

Several other parties were taking the same road. Families pushed handcarts with wrapped tools tied beneath them. A larger company carried long poles and collapsible frames. Seraphine watched that group until it took another branch of the path, showing no interest in them.
Leon’s household had no cart to slow them. Their supplies were in his ring, along with enough empty containers to make the trip thoroughly worthwhile.
Ira was trying to work out how long hearthseal took to form.
"Longer than this opening," Loriel said. "The manual describes an old deposit becoming accessible. It doesn’t say the stone grows in a morning."
"I wasn’t asking whether I could sit down and watch one grow."
"You asked how long you’d have to wait for another."
Leon glanced back at Ira. She considered defending the question, then shrugged.
"If it was a week, I’d wait."

Vyra laughed. The conversation moved on, and for a while they walked without discussing cultivation at all. Leon liked that nearly as much as the prospect of the harvest. Nobody was asking him to lead thirty people around the next bend.
They reached the ridge late in the afternoon.

Hollow Steps occupied most of the opposite slope. Broad courts had been cut into the hillside in uneven rows, linked by stairs and narrow approaches. Low walls divided them, and channels followed the rear edges beneath the higher ground.
Steam rose from those channels. Some courts were pale and almost bare. Others carried dark growth around their margins or patches that glittered in the lowering sun.

At the foot of the slope, roughly two hundred people waited among tents and handcarts. Several camps had permanent stone fire pits. Children carried water under close supervision, and an older man was sharpening a set of long-handled hooks while arguing with someone inside a tent.
Leon stopped to take it in. After so many empty reaches of the realm, the noise of people preparing supper still surprised him.
A girl was trying to repair a basket handle with cord. Her father showed her the knot once, then waited while she undid her first attempt and tried again.
The nearest approach was a ramp of broken stone. Pebbles slid down it despite the absence of anyone climbing, and a larger piece turned slowly against the slope before dropping back.
"Not yet," Seraphine said beside him.
"No." Leon followed the current moving through the rubble. "But it’s easing."
They chose a place at the edge of the gathering. Before their small shelter was ready, the young man from Sella’s shop came over.
"You collected your boxes, then."
Leon recognized the pale green coat and three-leaf badge. The man had a serious face, looked around Leon’s age, and still had ink on two fingers.
"We did," Leon said.
"Tobin Arle, Three Willows Hall." He gave a polite bow. "I saw you on the lower road. First visit?"
"Yes. Leon." He returned the greeting. "You’ve been here before?"
"For six openings. The Hall’s records go back much farther." Tobin glanced at the containers Vyra was arranging. "What are you hoping to collect?"
Leon considered how much to tell him. Their interest would be obvious soon enough.
"Hearthseal, if we find suitable pieces. Cultivation fuel as well."
"The warm courts," Tobin said. "Which ones will stay warm is what everyone wants to know."
"Where was it last time?" Ira asked from beside the shelter.

"Fourth row from the top, east side. It doesn’t always return there." Tobin pointed up the hill. "Slow steam along a channel usually means a steady supply. Watch it speed up. That often comes before a change."
"And if it reverses, leave the beds," Leon said.
Tobin looked pleased. "Someone translated the warning for you."
"Pell Orrow."
"Then he probably made you listen twice." Tobin’s mouth twitched. "My first time, I thought I could pull out one more piece before the turn. I spent the rest of the day looking for my tools."
Leon could appreciate the admission. It was more useful than being told the ground was dangerous by someone determined to sound mysterious.

He asked about the upper courts. Tobin explained that they were rich at present, but that supply sometimes drained toward the eastern rows during the early changes. His Hall would watch before choosing where to settle.
"Are you always this helpful to people who might take your ground?" Leon asked.
"If you break a bed while we’re beside it, it becomes our problem." Tobin nodded toward the slope. "And I haven’t told you which court I want."
"That’s fair."
The young man returned to the pale green tents. Seraphine watched him go, then resumed fastening their shelter.
"He chose what he shared," she said quietly.
"So did I." Leon crouched to help her. "I’d be more worried if he offered us everything."

They ate before dark and watched the channels from their camp. The steam was visible long after the hillside lost its color. Leon could feel currents strengthening beneath some courts and weakening beneath others, but he resisted deciding too quickly what that meant.
The locals had returned here for years. His senses gave him an advantage; they did not tell him which pale root was worth a jar or which glittering deposit would spoil when cut.
He woke before dawn to the sound of cart wheels.
Outside, people were packing with the practiced haste of an expected departure. The steam had begun moving along the channels in smooth streams. At the lower ramp, the rubble lay still.
Leon examined the approach while the women finished packing. The troublesome current had withdrawn from between the stones, leaving a rough but stable path.
The first families began climbing. Three Willows moved with them, its porters carrying the folded frames.
Leon’s household entered Hollow Steps among the early parties.

As they climbed, he extended his perception across the slope. He possessed every elemental affinity, and the differences reached him separately: heavy Earth beneath the pale courts, Water along the planted margins, Fire gathering farther east, colder currents feeding the glittering upper ground.

The nine affinities developed within his Scripture were only the beginning of what he intended that method to carry. Here, the breadth of what he could sense mattered before he drew anything into himself.
He stopped at a junction.

The upper courts were rich, but their supply was beginning to decline. Through a lower connection he felt Fire strengthening while the surrounding Earth remained steady. The change was still slight. It was also continuing.
Ira looked toward the summit, where several parties were heading.
"Young Master?"
Leon followed the gathering Fire to a row of plain courts on the east side.
"There," he said. "Fourth row from the top."
Across the next approach, Tobin had stopped to consult an older Hall member. The man pointed at the steam, then east.
Leon smiled and started up the narrower stair.
"We should hurry."

chapters.title: Chapter 729: First to the Fire
paragraphs: Tobin’s party took the broad stair. Leon took the narrow one, and by the time the first Hall disciple reached the fourth row, Seraphine was already crossing its eastern court.
The ground still looked thoroughly uninteresting.
Leon stepped over a shallow drain and stopped beside the rear channel. Behind him, Ira rested a hand on the stone, feeling for what he had sensed from below.
"It’s warming," she said.
"And the supply’s increasing." Leon looked toward the neighboring court. "Leave that western approach clear."
Tobin came up with two disciples, then halted when he saw where Leon stood. His remaining people followed at a more measured pace with their equipment.
For a moment the young man examined the channel without speaking. Steam ran slowly along it, scarcely visible against the pale wall.
"You turned before the upper vents changed," Tobin said.
"I felt it gathering here."
"So did our fire specialist. Once we were halfway up." He looked back toward the summit. "I hoped we’d reach this row first."
Leon could have pretended the outcome had been accidental. He saw no reason to.
"The east section is taken."
"I can see that." Tobin crouched beside the drain, then called one of his people forward. The older disciple touched a small instrument to the stone and showed him the result.
They spoke quietly. Leon let them finish while he watched the supply build beneath his feet.

The cold current above was thinning. Fire was gathering along this channel, and the surrounding Earth remained stable enough to hold it. Feeling those changes together had let him choose earlier than someone watching only the steam or waiting for the ground to warm.
He still did not know how much hearthseal lay underneath.
Enough to justify running up all those bloody stairs, I hope.
Tobin straightened.
"The west section will receive the same turn, though less of it. We’ll work there. Our rear ledge reaches the channel without crossing your bed."
Leon followed his gesture. A narrow strip of solid stone ran behind the channel, accessible from the Hall’s side.
"That drain is the boundary," Leon said. "Your ledge stops where it meets the line. Don’t undercut our side."
"Then don’t cut past it from yours," Tobin replied. "The rock’s joined below."
"Agreed."
Tobin hesitated over the best channel mouth, which lay east of the drain. Leon waited, quite prepared to refuse if he asked for it.
Instead, the young man turned to his people.
"Frames on the west. Keep the ledge clear."
Vyra passed Leon on her way to lay out their boxes.
"A reasonable neighbor," she said quietly.
"So far."
He had the better section and a workable boundary. That suited him far more than throwing twenty people down a staircase and spending the harvest window dealing with the consequences.
Within half an hour, a red flush appeared beneath the grey surface near the rear wall.
Ira knelt to examine it. A thin covering of pale grit loosened as the bed warmed, revealing darker seams below.
"There’s an old deposit under this," she said. "The current’s opening the surface."
Seraphine tested one seam with the tip of her blade. It parted along an existing weakness, exposing a rounded mineral enclosed in red rock.
Ira leaned close enough that Leon caught her by the back of her belt when he stepped around her.
"You’re in my way."
"Go around the other side, Young Master." She did not look up.
He did, smiling despite himself.
The first hearthseal was small, but its weight settled heavily in Ira’s palm once she lifted it with a supporting piece of rock. She adjusted her grip and passed her other hand over its dark skin.
"Barely warm."
Leon examined it with his perception. Fire filled the interior in close, dense bands, with very little escaping through the outer layer.
Ira saw his expression and grinned.
"Yes. That."
They began collecting in earnest.

Seraphine opened seams with fine cuts, leaving generous margins around the hearthseal. Ira checked each specimen before it went into a lined compartment. Vyra marked damaged pieces separately and packed the intact ones so their supporting beds could not knock together.

Leon stored each completed box in his ring and moved along the rear wall to find the next promising seam. There was ample room for what they could collect. He was more interested in taking the best pieces than in proving he could empty an entire court.

Loriel examined an adjoining pale shelf below their section, within easy calling distance. It held ordinary Earth- and Water-bearing accretions exposed by the same shift. When she asked whether he wanted them, Leon went down to inspect a sample.
Bai Heng would still need to prepare it, but the quantity and character of the stored energy looked useful.
"Take the cleanest sections," Leon told her. "I’ll bring another case."

On the neighboring bed, Three Willows worked with the advantage of practice. Their covered frames supported cut pieces while the collectors freed the underside. Tobin corrected a young worker’s angle, then returned to the channel instead of watching Leon continuously.
Leon was glad of that. He had no wish to spend a good morning performing for an audience.
Ira called him back near the second hour.
She had found an egg-sized hearthseal in a shallow cup of red stone. Its skin was darker than the others, even in color, and so intact that she could detect almost no escaping heat.
"Look at this one."
Leon crouched beside her. The Fire within was densely contained, with none of the obvious breaks he had found in several lesser specimens.
"It’s a good piece."
"It’s an excellent piece," Ira corrected. She turned its bed carefully between her hands. "Whether it likes my fire is another question."
"You haven’t tried?"
"Not while I’m still deciding which part I can touch without ruining it."
He liked hearing that from her. Ira could be impatient, but she knew the difference between a fight she could win and material she could spoil with a careless experiment.
Vyra found a separate padded container for the specimen. Ira watched it being secured, then asked Leon to keep it apart from the general harvest.
"That one’s mine to test."
"I had noticed."
By the third hour, the supply had stopped increasing. The court held a steady warmth, and most of the easy seams on their side were open.

Near the deepest part of the rear channel, Leon found a darker patch beneath a thick slab. Ira joined him and felt along its edge. Through the surrounding rock lay a larger hearthseal, its inner Fire even denser than that of her first choice.
"I want that one too," she said.
Leon examined the seam holding it. "You’ll need to take the whole bed."
"I can. Give me room along this side."
They had barely begun exposing its edge when the steam stopped above the channel.
Across the drain, Tobin raised his head.
"Off the beds!" he called. "It’s turning!"
The steam reversed. Beneath Ira’s hand, the slab shifted, and loose stones began lifting from the rear of the court.
She looked at Leon rather than retreating.
"Hold the pieces around it. I can take the specimen clean."

sentences.text: Tobin’s party took the broad stair.
Leon took the narrow one, and by the time the first Hall disciple reached the fourth row, Seraphine was already crossing its eastern court.
The ground still looked thoroughly uninteresting.
Leon stepped over a shallow drain and stopped beside the rear channel.
Behind him, Ira rested a hand on the stone, feeling for what he had sensed from below.
"It’s warming," she said.
"And the supply’s increasing." Leon looked toward the neighboring court.
"Leave that western approach clear."
Tobin came up with two disciples, then halted when he saw where Leon stood.
His remaining people followed at a more measured pace with their equipment.
For a moment the young man examined the channel without speaking.
Steam ran slowly along it, scarcely visible against the pale wall.
"You turned before the upper vents changed," Tobin said.
"I felt it gathering here."
"So did our fire specialist.
Once we were halfway up." He looked back toward the summit.
"I hoped we’d reach this row first."
Leon could have pretended the outcome had been accidental.
He saw no reason to.
"The east section is taken."
"I can see that." Tobin crouched beside the drain, then called one of his people forward.
The older disciple touched a small instrument to the stone and showed him the result.
They spoke quietly.
Leon let them finish while he watched the supply build beneath his feet.
The cold current above was thinning.
Fire was gathering along this channel, and the surrounding Earth remained stable enough to hold it.
Feeling those changes together had let him choose earlier than someone watching only the steam or waiting for the ground to warm.
He still did not know how much hearthseal lay underneath.
Enough to justify running up all those bloody stairs, I hope.
Tobin straightened.
"The west section will receive the same turn, though less of it.
We’ll work there.
Our rear ledge reaches the channel without crossing your bed."
Leon followed his gesture.
A narrow strip of solid stone ran behind the channel, accessible from the Hall’s side.
"That drain is the boundary," Leon said.
"Your ledge stops where it meets the line.
Don’t undercut our side."
"Then don’t cut past it from yours," Tobin replied.
"The rock’s joined below."
"Agreed."
Tobin hesitated over the best channel mouth, which lay east of the drain.
Leon waited, quite prepared to refuse if he asked for it.
Instead, the young man turned to his people.
"Frames on the west.
Keep the ledge clear."
Vyra passed Leon on her way to lay out their boxes.
"A reasonable neighbor," she said quietly.
"So far."
He had the better section and a workable boundary.
That suited him far more than throwing twenty people down a staircase and spending the harvest window dealing with the consequences.
Within half an hour, a red flush appeared beneath the grey surface near the rear wall.
Ira knelt to examine it.
A thin covering of pale grit loosened as the bed warmed, revealing darker seams below.
"There’s an old deposit under this," she said.
"The current’s opening the surface."
Seraphine tested one seam with the tip of her blade.
It parted along an existing weakness, exposing a rounded mineral enclosed in red rock.
Ira leaned close enough that Leon caught her by the back of her belt when he stepped around her.
"You’re in my way."
"Go around the other side, Young Master." She did not look up.
He did, smiling despite himself.
The first hearthseal was small, but its weight settled heavily in Ira’s palm once she lifted it with a supporting piece of rock.
She adjusted her grip and passed her other hand over its dark skin.
"Barely warm."
Leon examined it with his perception.
Fire filled the interior in close, dense bands, with very little escaping through the outer layer.
Ira saw his expression and grinned.
"Yes.
That."
They began collecting in earnest.
Seraphine opened seams with fine cuts, leaving generous margins around the hearthseal.
Ira checked each specimen before it went into a lined compartment.
Vyra marked damaged pieces separately and packed the intact ones so their supporting beds could not knock together.
Leon stored each completed box in his ring and moved along the rear wall to find the next promising seam.
There was ample room for what they could collect.
He was more interested in taking the best pieces than in proving he could empty an entire court.
Loriel examined an adjoining pale shelf below their section, within easy calling distance.
It held ordinary Earth- and Water-bearing accretions exposed by the same shift.
When she asked whether he wanted them, Leon went down to inspect a sample.
Bai Heng would still need to prepare it, but the quantity and character of the stored energy looked useful.
"Take the cleanest sections," Leon told her.
"I’ll bring another case."
On the neighboring bed, Three Willows worked with the advantage of practice.
Their covered frames supported cut pieces while the collectors freed the underside.
Tobin corrected a young worker’s angle, then returned to the channel instead of watching Leon continuously.
Leon was glad of that.
He had no wish to spend a good morning performing for an audience.
Ira called him back near the second hour.
She had found an egg-sized hearthseal in a shallow cup of red stone.
Its skin was darker than the others, even in color, and so intact that she could detect almost no escaping heat.
"Look at this one."
Leon crouched beside her.
The Fire within was densely contained, with none of the obvious breaks he had found in several lesser specimens.
"It’s a good piece."
"It’s an excellent piece," Ira corrected.
She turned its bed carefully between her hands.
"Whether it likes my fire is another question."
"You haven’t tried?"
"Not while I’m still deciding which part I can touch without ruining it."
He liked hearing that from her.
Ira could be impatient, but she knew the difference between a fight she could win and material she could spoil with a careless experiment.
Vyra found a separate padded container for the specimen.
Ira watched it being secured, then asked Leon to keep it apart from the general harvest.
"That one’s mine to test."
"I had noticed."
By the third hour, the supply had stopped increasing.
The court held a steady warmth, and most of the easy seams on their side were open.
Near the deepest part of the rear channel, Leon found a darker patch beneath a thick slab.
Ira joined him and felt along its edge.
Through the surrounding rock lay a larger hearthseal, its inner Fire even denser than that of her first choice.
"I want that one too," she said.
Leon examined the seam holding it.
"You’ll need to take the whole bed."
"I can.
Give me room along this side."
They had barely begun exposing its edge when the steam stopped above the channel.
Across the drain, Tobin raised his head.
"Off the beds!" he called.
"It’s turning!"
The steam reversed.
Beneath Ira’s hand, the slab shifted, and loose stones began lifting from the rear of the court.
She looked at Leon rather than retreating.
"Hold the pieces around it.
I can take the specimen clean."

chapters.title: Chapter 730: Heat Worth Keeping
paragraphs: Leon caught the first rising slab before it struck the hearthseal’s bed.
The stone stopped a handspan above Ira’s fingers. Around it, smaller fragments lifted from the channel, turning as the reversed current pulled them upward.
Ira moved her hand out from beneath the slab and tested the seam again.
"That side," she said, indicating a narrow connection to the court. "If it twists there, the skin will split."
"I see it."

Leon steadied the rock supporting the specimen, then extended his control across the space above them. A section roughly ten paces wide stopped shedding debris. Broken stones hung where he held them while loose pieces outside his reach continued rising.
He had no intention of interfering with the current feeding the whole court. That was keeping the deposit accessible. He only needed the surrounding rock to stop battering what Ira wanted.

On the western half, Tobin’s people withdrew onto the bare ledge behind their work. Two disciples dragged a covered frame clear before the last collectors stepped away. Their response was quick and orderly.
A long slab rose beyond Leon’s held section, caught another current, and swung toward the ledge.
Seraphine crossed its path. Her sword flashed twice, breaking it along empty seams. She turned the pieces down toward an unoccupied stretch of stone before they could reach the Hall workers.
"Keep behind the wall," she told them.
Tobin moved his nearest collector back without arguing.

Vyra had two open boxes still on the bed. She closed one, passed it to Leon for storage, and drew a narrow curtain of flame above the other. It diverted the smaller fragments long enough for her to secure the lid.
Loriel came up from the lower shelf with her final container tucked beneath an arm. She set it on bare stone and looked toward Ira.
"Is the specimen sound?" she asked.
"So far." Ira crouched beside the hearthseal. "I’m separating the last seam."
There was room to step out whenever she wanted. She remained because the larger piece was worth keeping intact, and because Leon had given her the steady working space she needed.
He watched her place two fingers against the surrounding red rock.

A fine thread of her flame entered the seam. It heated only the narrow connection to the channel bed, softening an edge that had already begun to part. Ira kept the hearthseal itself well clear of the contact.
The detached rock shifted.
Leon adjusted his hold to support it from beneath, and Ira slid her hands under the freed block. She lifted the whole bed without twisting it and walked onto the bare step beside him.
"Clear," she said.

He guided the suspended debris away from the opened seam. A few fragments tried to rise again, but the reversed current was already weakening. When the steam returned to its earlier direction, he lowered the remaining stones into the cleared patch.
The last slab landed with a heavy scrape.
Ira stood with a block the size of a loaf in her arms. In its center, the dark hearthseal remained unmarked.
She looked up at him, pleased enough that he almost forgot to check the rest of the court.
"That," she said, "was worth staying for."
Leon brushed dust from its supporting bed. "Let me see the underside."
She turned it so he could inspect the place she had heated. The seam was clean, and her flame had stopped well short of the specimen.
He nodded. Ira’s smile widened.

Across the boundary, Tobin was checking his people. None had been struck. One man was complaining about a broken hook, but he stopped when the older disciple pointed at the replacement tied to his pack.
Only after the Hall had accounted for everyone did Tobin approach Leon.
"You held that section still," he said.
"Yes."
"Through the reversal." Tobin glanced at the broken slabs, then at Ira’s intact block. "I’ve never seen anyone harvest during one."
"We didn’t want it cracked," Leon said.
"I gathered that." The young man studied him for another moment before bowing. "And your guard kept a slab off our ledge. Thank you."
Seraphine inclined her head from beside the boxes.
Tobin did not ask for a demonstration or an explanation of Leon’s technique. He returned to his own people and had them examine the ledge before resuming work.
Leon approved of him a little more.

The warmth in their section gradually declined. They finished the remaining accessible seams without chasing the supply as it moved elsewhere. There was already enough in his ring to make him reluctant to risk the quality by taking everything indiscriminately.

Vyra completed the tally on a clean corner of her slate. Twenty-three lined boxes held hearthseal specimens in their supporting beds. Loriel’s work had added eleven boxes of Earth- and Water-bearing deposits. They had also collected plainer fire ore suitable for refinement.
The two pieces Ira had selected for herself were listed separately. The smaller one stayed in its padded case; the larger required a deeper container from Sella’s order.
"Several useful batches," Vyra said, passing Leon the slate. "Depending on what survives preparation."
He looked over the quantities. There were damaged pieces among the lesser material, but those were marked, and the best specimens had been packed before the current turned.
Bai Heng is going to want to open every box before he lets me eat.
He found himself looking forward to that argument.
Tobin came over once more while they were packing the tools. This time, he stopped at the boundary and pointed toward the upper vents.
"How early did you feel the supply moving?"
"Before we reached the junction below."
"Our instrument didn’t register this bed until we were above it." He considered that. "Were you following the Fire alone?"
"More than one current," Leon said.
Tobin accepted the limit of the answer. "I’ll have our people record the signs from this opening. The old notes put the eastern turn later."
"Was the previous one weaker?" Leon asked.
"I’d need to compare the records. My teacher measured it." Tobin glanced at the opened seam. "If you’re still here when he finishes below, perhaps we can compare observations."
"Perhaps."
It was a useful acquaintance to have. Leon would decide what to share when he knew what the Hall could offer in return.

They left the worked terrace in the early afternoon and descended to a quieter row. The pale court they chose had mild currents, room to sit, and a wall high enough to give some privacy from the busier approaches.
Seraphine checked the stair while Loriel unpacked water. Vyra put away the tally and accepted a portion of food without trying to count anything else.
Ira asked Leon for the deeper case before she sat down.
He took it from his ring and set it between them. She opened the lid, looked at the dark stone, and rested her hand on its red bed with a care he had rarely seen her give an object.
"What?" she asked when she caught him watching.
"Nothing." Leon sat beside her. "I was wondering what you’re going to try first."
Ira looked back into the case.
For once, she did not answer immediately.

chapters.title: Chapter 731: What Comes Back
paragraphs: "I want to know how much it can hold before it starts losing anything," Ira said.
Leon looked from her to the hearthseal. "Wouldn’t you have to damage it to find out?"
"Not this one." She drew the smaller specimen’s case toward her. "We kept pieces with cracked skins. I can compare those first. Find out where the heat gets through."
That was a better answer than pouring her flame into the best stone and seeing what survived. Leon opened his food packet and offered her half.
She took it without looking, still studying the specimen.
"The manual tells us how to preserve it," she said. "It doesn’t tell me how to make use of what it does."
"We can get more passages translated."
"Yes. But I’ll still have to test it with my own flame."

Across the court, Vyra and Loriel were discussing where to place the mineral cases when they returned. Seraphine had settled by the stair with her food. Their voices were low enough that Ira no longer needed to maintain the polite distance she used around outsiders.
She shifted closer, her shoulder resting against Leon’s.
"What do you want it to change?" he asked.
Ira considered the question while chewing. He waited instead of offering an answer for her.

"I can keep my flame contained now," she said. "You know that. But when I push it to the highest intensity, some of it escapes before I’m ready. Less than it used to. Still enough that I can feel the waste."
"Heat around the strike?"

"That, and what I lose carrying it." She held one hand out, fingers half closed. "I want more of it here. Packed close. If I form a Core that can support that density, I want the force to stay available until I choose where it goes."
Leon remembered fighting beside her. Ira liked committing to an attack, closing the distance and making the impact count. She had never needed someone to encourage her to hit harder.
It pleased him that she was thinking about what happened before the strike.
"Would you use the stone as a material for condensation," he asked, "or study it to change your circulation?"
"Possibly both." Ira looked down at the case. "I don’t know yet. I’m not going to put it into anything until I know how my fire behaves against it."
"That sounds sensible."
"You don’t have to look so surprised."
"I’m trying to remember the expression for later."
She bumped his shoulder, then leaned back against it. Leon put his arm around her and finished eating with one hand.

For a while, they watched people moving on the opposite courts. Someone had set up a cloth screen around a cultivation place. Farther up, two collectors were arguing over a broken basket while a third quietly gathered the spilled material.
Ira followed his gaze.
"We did well," she said.
"Yes."
"I like going out with just us."
"So do I." Leon glanced at the closed cases. "Especially when we come back with this much."
She laughed, warm against his side. He had spent enough time worrying about what everyone needed. Being pleased with what they had gained required no more explanation than that.
When they finished resting, Ira helped him secure the specimens in his ring. She made certain he knew which damaged pieces she wanted first when they next had space to experiment.
Leon then walked along the pale court, studying its currents before selecting a place to sit.

The strongest flow lay near the rear wall. He chose a gentler patch farther forward, where Earth predominated and Water passed through in a smaller, fluctuating supply. He could follow the changes without drawing them into himself at full intensity.

The women spread out around the approaches. To anyone watching from the next row, he would look like another cultivator making use of the opening. His public presence still carried the familiar weight of Peak Golden Core.
The native foundation he was developing beneath that remained at the middle stage.

He took out the small jar from the spring and examined the prepared mixture once more. Its known behavior would give him a comparison later. For now, he closed it and put it away. Adding fuel would only make it harder to identify which changes came from the court.
Leon settled his breathing and began the Scripture’s current circulation.

It held comfortably. He knew this arrangement well enough to recognize the ordinary variations without hunting for each one. The long work inside his dimensional world had earned him that familiarity, even if it had felt painfully repetitive at the time.
Then he admitted a measured amount of the surrounding energy.

He left the other branches supplied by the energy already in circulation. Drawing from the court was an addition, and he kept it small enough to trace. If he changed every source at once, he would have no useful comparison when something went wrong.

That restraint took more patience than accepting the energy required. The court offered far more than he was using, and he could sense richer patches only a few paces away. He understood why people settled here to cultivate. Later, with a method he trusted, he would enjoy doing the same. Today he wanted to know what happened to one change before adding another.
Earth entered steadily. Water followed in a thinner stream. He kept their intake well below what the court could supply and let the cycle settle before attempting anything new.
Several minutes passed. A cool draft crossed his face, and the Water supply diminished as Earth strengthened.
Leon responded in the familiar way. He eased the intake, adjusted the Earth branch, allowed the returns to settle, and brought the cycle back to its previous pace.
It worked. It also interrupted the smooth circulation he had established.
By the time he finished, the court had changed again.
That’s why I came here. Stop fixing yesterday’s problem.
He opened his eyes long enough to check the channels. The steam was moving steadily. Nobody nearby had begun packing or withdrawing, and Seraphine gave him a small nod from the stair.
He closed his eyes and began again.

This time he allowed a small increase through without immediately throttling the intake. His existing arrangement could bear that much. He followed the energy through Earth, watching how the increased demand affected the shared center and the neighboring branch.
The disturbance did not begin where he expected.

Earth accepted the fuller flow. The trouble appeared when it returned. Under this load, the branch took slightly longer to complete its passage, while Water reached the center at its earlier timing. Leon felt the uneven meeting before it developed into anything harmful and steadied the cycle.
He stayed still, tracing what had happened.

His first response had been to slow the incoming Earth until the old timing worked again. That made the arrangement comfortable by forcing it back toward a condition the surroundings had already left behind.
He had another option.
The Earth return was later. He could try adjusting Water to meet it, provided he did not disrupt everything else in the process.
Leon let the ordinary cycle settle and waited for the next change.
This time, his attention remained on what came back.

He understood why people settled here to cultivate.
Later, with a method he trusted, he would enjoy doing the same.
Today he wanted to know what happened to one change before adding another.
Earth entered steadily.
Water followed in a thinner stream.
He kept their intake well below what the court could supply and let the cycle settle before attempting anything new.
Several minutes passed.
A cool draft crossed his face, and the Water supply diminished as Earth strengthened.
Leon responded in the familiar way.
He eased the intake, adjusted the Earth branch, allowed the returns to settle, and brought the cycle back to its previous pace.
It worked.
It also interrupted the smooth circulation he had established.
By the time he finished, the court had changed again.
That’s why I came here.
Stop fixing yesterday’s problem.
He opened his eyes long enough to check the channels.
The steam was moving steadily.
Nobody nearby had begun packing or withdrawing, and Seraphine gave him a small nod from the stair.
He closed his eyes and began again.
This time he allowed a small increase through without immediately throttling the intake.
His existing arrangement could bear that much.
He followed the energy through Earth, watching how the increased demand affected the shared center and the neighboring branch.
The disturbance did not begin where he expected.
Earth accepted the fuller flow.
The trouble appeared when it returned.
Under this load, the branch took slightly longer to complete its passage, while Water reached the center at its earlier timing.
Leon felt the uneven meeting before it developed into anything harmful and steadied the cycle.
He stayed still, tracing what had happened.
His first response had been to slow the incoming Earth until the old timing worked again.
That made the arrangement comfortable by forcing it back toward a condition the surroundings had already left behind.
He had another option.
The Earth return was later.
He could try adjusting Water to meet it, provided he did not disrupt everything else in the process.
Leon let the ordinary cycle settle and waited for the next change.
This time, his attention remained on what came back.

chapters.title: Chapter 732: Where the Steps Continue
paragraphs: Leon delayed Water’s return by too much.
He felt the mistake before the two flows met. Earth reached the center ahead of the correction he had intended to make, and Water followed late enough to produce a second uneven pulse.
He eased the intake and restored the familiar cycle.
The interruption was small, but irritating. He had known what he wanted to do and still managed to make the original problem worse in the opposite direction.
Less. You’re nudging it, not moving the whole branch.

He waited while the court settled into a steady supply, then reviewed the timing without changing it. His mistake had been treating the visible increase in Earth as a measure of how much Water needed to move. They were different things. The delay in the return was slight, and his correction only needed to match that delay.
The Lord of Illusion and Mystery’s observation came back to him: balance need not mean equal flow.
He had spent months learning to give that idea a workable form. It was easy to agree with a sentence. Keeping several branches in harmony while one of them changed was considerably less convenient.
On the next rise, he allowed Earth to take the measured increase and eased Water’s return by a smaller amount.
They met without the earlier uneven pulse. Leon kept the intake open at its controlled level and followed the next complete circuit, ready to correct it.
The cycle continued.
He felt a quick surge of satisfaction and almost opened his eyes to tell someone. Instead, he made himself wait.
Do it twice before you start grinning.

The next change favored Water. He watched its actual passage rather than assuming the reverse correction would be identical. Its fuller return also arrived slightly later under the new load, so he delayed Earth enough to meet it while maintaining the other branches.
That adjustment worked too.

Over the following hour, he tried several more changes. Twice he needed additional corrections at the center. Once he reduced the intake because he had followed a variation too late. None of it justified letting the Scripture run without his attention.
But he no longer had to interrupt the whole cycle for every mild change. He could adjust intake and individual returns while the wider circulation continued.

He tested the same approach through another gradual rise, then let the new supply taper off. His foundation remained settled when he finished. No sudden advance followed, and he had not expected one. What he had gained was a more useful way to work with the strength and structure he already possessed.
Leon opened his eyes.
Loriel was sitting near the wall with her notebook. She looked up at once.
"Better?" she asked.
"I kept it running through the changes." He stretched his legs. "Most of them. I still had to make every adjustment myself."
"Did anything hurt?"
"No."
"Then you may keep looking pleased."

He laughed and reached for the water she offered. Only after drinking did he write the successful sequence in his own notes. He marked the conditions beside it: mild currents, controlled intake, Earth and Water changing most noticeably. A good result here did not tell him what would happen under a sudden surge of Fire or several changes at once.
That was work for later. For now, he was pleased enough that even the cramped line at the bottom of the page annoyed him less than usual.
Ira came over while he was closing the notebook.
"Can you do it while moving?" she asked.
"I haven’t tried this adjustment that way yet."
"You should. Unless you’re planning to sit through every fight."

Leon rose and walked slowly along the bare front edge, maintaining a reduced circulation. Movement itself presented no new difficulty. When the Water supply shifted, however, he stopped beside the wall to follow its return properly.
Ira waited without saying anything.
"More practice," he admitted.

She accepted that with a nod. He added a short note before putting the book away: the adjustment worked while seated and attentive; doing it during ordinary movement still needed testing. That was useful to know before confidence became an expensive mistake.
He was putting the notes away when the steam changed direction across the slope.

This time, the movement extended far beyond their court. Several upper channels turned north and west, carrying their supply toward the hillside’s shoulder. People stopped working to look. A collector on the next row called for someone to bring a viewing lens.
Leon stood and followed the change with his perception.
Above the highest occupied courts, the thick bank of steam lying against the western slope began drawing aside. Dark stone appeared beneath it, then a landing and the first stretch of a narrow stair.
Seraphine came to his side.
"That wasn’t visible this morning."
"No." He watched another section emerge. "The steam covered the whole approach."

The stair climbed over the shoulder and disappeared beyond it. Deep channels ran between its worn blocks, their arrangement unlike the shallower cuts around the occupied courts. Several strong currents followed those channels, crossing and separating around the landings.
Leon could feel distinct energies moving through the same small area without merging into a single muddled flow.
He wanted to get closer immediately.
Below them, Tobin had left the Hall’s resting place and was staring toward the same stair. Leon went down, the women following once their belongings were stored.
"I’ve seen a drawing of that," Tobin said before Leon could ask.
"In your records?"

"The older ones. A stair above the western shoulder, with a broken gateway halfway along it." He pointed. As the steam thinned, two leaning pillars appeared on a landing. "There. That’s what I remember."
"What did the record call it?" Leon asked.

"The old court. There wasn’t a proper account of entering it. Just the drawing and a note saying the Steps concealed the approach." Tobin rubbed the ink-stained fingers of one hand together. "My teacher thought the route might have collapsed."
"Have any of your people been there?"
"Not that I know of. Certainly nobody on this expedition."
Leon studied the broken pillars. Beyond them, another stretch of stairs was emerging. Mineral growth caught the light along the deeper channel edges, though he could not judge its quality from here.
The route looked promising. It also looked old enough to have more wrong with it than a little loose stone.
Tobin glanced toward his people, then back at Leon.
"Are you going up?"
"Yes," Leon said. "I’ll examine the approach first."

He had no intention of sitting below it until someone else found out what was there. The harvest was secure, his household was ready, and the circulation he could sense along those channels was more interesting than anything he had tested that afternoon.

Ira adjusted the fastening of her coat beside him. Seraphine was already studying the exposed landings. Vyra tucked away the route notes, while Loriel followed a line of growth beside the newly visible stone.
Leon waited long enough to see that the first stretch remained clear as the steam withdrew.
Then he started toward the western shoulder.
Behind the broken gateway, another landing emerged, and the channels continued beyond it.

chapters.title: Chapter 733: Beyond the Broken Gate
paragraphs: Five elemental currents ran up the stair without disturbing one another. Leon stopped with one foot over the broken lintel.

The gateway’s posts still stood, each wider than his outstretched arms. Its fallen lintel lay in three mossy pieces across the approach. Above it, the steam was withdrawing from five narrow channels carved into the steps.

On the lower terraces, changes in supply had repeatedly displaced the productive ground. Here, heat, wind, frost, earth, and lightning traveled side by side. The gap between channels was barely a finger’s width.
He had sensed several flows from below. This close, their separation was even cleaner than he had expected.
How are they keeping that stable?
He went down on one knee and held his hand over the gap between fire and wind. He felt both currents press against his palm, and the narrow strip of stone between them stayed perfectly quiet.
"Young Master." Seraphine’s voice came from just behind him, low. "We have company."
Tobin Arle was climbing toward them with three green-coated Hall disciples. He held a sheet of old paper against his open satchel to keep the wind from taking it.
"You didn’t wait," Tobin said, a little out of breath.
"You didn’t ask me to," Leon said.

"Fair." Tobin showed him the drawing: this stair, its gateway, and a level court beside a long wall. "My teacher’s teacher copied a description. Nobody from our expedition has stood here." His gaze returned to the channels. "The drawing doesn’t show these running."
"Where does that wall go?" Leon asked.
Tobin traced the drawing upward with one ink-stained finger. "The court. Then a second door. After that the drawing just says below."

The court at the top was smaller than Leon had expected, perhaps forty paces across, and the five channels ended in five shallow basins along the foot of the long wall. The wall itself was covered in writing.

Rows of script ran across it, cut deep, with diagrams between them: a figure seated with lines running through its body, a basin drawn in cross-section, a stair winding down into a wide, round space. Some panels had crumbled. Most were whole.

Vyra had her paper out before anyone told her to. Loriel walked along the basins and crouched beside the one that smelled of clay, watching how the water in it turned slowly without overflowing. Ira went straight to the basin with the heat and held her hand above it and grinned.
Leon looked at the pillars.

Ten pillars stood along the wall. Seven bore emblems, though only four remained clear: a tree with hand-shaped roots, three nested rings, a wave over a tower, and an open eye. The other three pillars were blank.
"Tobin," he said. "What are these?"
Tobin came over and stood in front of the tree pillar for a long moment.

"Route marks," he said finally. "The Hall has a few of them on old pottery. We always thought they were workshop signs." He touched the line of script under the tree. "The road from Aelmar. And this one — the road from the Ringed Kingdom. They’re doors. Each of these was a door to somewhere else."
"Other worlds," said Vyra, without looking up from her copying.
"Other worlds," Tobin repeated. "We knew outsiders had come before. I didn’t realize this place had been built to receive them."
Leon studied the blank pillars. Perhaps they had been left for roads that never opened. Their own entrance was new, yet the place receiving it was old enough to have forgotten its visitors.
"Read the long panel," he said. "The one with the stair."
Tobin read slowly, and he admitted it when he wasn’t sure.

The court had been an instruction annex. Visitors arriving through the outer doors learned to cultivate in its currents before descending to the sanctuary, the Hall of Many Streams, where the source rose and divided.

"And this part." Tobin’s finger stopped at a smaller block of text set inside a carved frame. "This is a calendar. Steps’ reckoning. We still use it. Days are counted from first steam." He read it twice under his breath before he said it aloud. "On the thirteenth day from first steam, the outer doors wake. They stand open until the twenty-fifth. Those who came by them should be ready."
Leon did the count in his head. The Steps had first steamed the morning they arrived at Asterbank.
"Today’s the fourth day from first steam," he said.
"Yes," Tobin said.
"Then the doors should reopen in nine days," Leon said. "And remain open for twelve."
Tobin hesitated. "If this is right. It’s a forecast. It was right for people a thousand years ago."
"We’ll check the signs as we go," Leon said. For the first time since Tian reported the missing gateway, he had something better than hoping it would return.

First steam had appeared on the morning they left the spring. This was their fourth day away. With twelve days allowed for the outing, they had time to investigate here and return with the calendar before the predicted reopening.
He couldn’t tell Bai Heng from here. The plaque wouldn’t reach. He could only copy the wall, carry it back, and say it in person.
"Vyra, make a second copy," Leon said.
"Already doing it, Young Master." She shifted the first sheet out of the damp. "I’ll copy the diagrams around it too."
The last panel was set apart from the others, on the face of the stone beside the second door, and the script was newer and rougher. Someone had cut it with a poorer tool.
"This one’s from after," said Tobin. "After the doors stopped." He frowned at it. "I know this. Everyone in the south knows some version of it. I didn’t know it was written down here."
"What does it say?" Leon asked.
"When the many streams answer one hand," Tobin said, "a new dawn may reach the land beneath the veiled sky."
Ira’s head turned, very slightly, toward Leon. Seraphine didn’t move at all.

"The streams are supposed to be the elements," Tobin went on, more comfortable now that he was explaining something. "That part everyone agrees on. Some say it means the doors will open again. Some say it means a cultivator will come who can hold every path. My teacher says dawn just meant better harvests to the people who wrote it." He shrugged. "Nobody knows who cut it. Nobody knows who it’s for. Every few years some boy in Asterbank decides it’s him."
Leon looked at the rough letters and didn’t like them.
One hand. Every stream. That’s uncomfortably close.

He had come looking for useful materials and a better understanding of his circulation. He had four women beside him and forty-three Palace members waiting elsewhere. A stranger’s prophecy could find somebody else to owe this land a sunrise.
"It’s a nice saying," he said.
"An old saying," Tobin replied, and moved toward the second door. Beyond his shoulder, pale light climbed from a stair descending into the hill.

Leon felt the supply before he saw the first pool. Fire and ice were rising from the same depth without either weakening. He glanced at the diagrams he had spent the afternoon copying, then put his paper away.
Someone had already built what he was still trying to understand. Whatever he thought of their prophecy, he was going down there.

chapters.title: Chapter 734: Every Color, One Source
paragraphs: Beyond the second door, the channels descended toward more energy than Leon had felt anywhere else inside the realm.
The stair was wide enough for six people abreast. Pale light moved far below, illuminating the outer wall and its five parallel channels.

He extended his senses carefully. Fire, water, earth, wind, and lightning rose from a common depth, alongside light, cold, and living green energy. He paused to distinguish the overlapping supplies. Their separation persisted well beyond the court above.

He had rationed expensive fuel and postponed experiments for lack of the right supply. Down there, he might finally have enough to work without counting every failed attempt against the next month’s cultivation.
"Young Master," said Seraphine quietly. "Now?"
"Now," Leon said, starting down.
The stair ended in a hollow so large Leon couldn’t see the far wall.

The ceiling was lost in a pale mist that glowed from inside, which explained the light. Below it, the floor of the hollow fell away in broad terraces, and every terrace held a pool. Some of the pools were water. Some were sand that rippled like water. One was a slow red glow. One was nothing but moving air, held inside a ring of stone, and the grass around its edge leaned outward as if blown.
At the bottom of the hollow, in the very center, a column of light rose out of the ground and divided as it climbed into dozens of thinner streams, and each stream curved away to a different pool.
"The Hall of Many Streams," Tobin murmured.

Leon walked to the edge of the first terrace and looked down at two pools side by side, one of fire and one of ice. They sat less than ten paces apart. Fire breathed heat across the gap, and ice breathed cold, and between them was a band of ordinary stone where a person could sit comfortably.

He watched for a while. The fire pool refilled fast, in quick pulses through a narrow channel. The ice pool refilled slowly through a wide, shallow one, and held much more. They took different amounts, at different speeds, by different shapes of route, and neither one starved or flooded.
Balance need not mean equal flow.
The Lord’s advice came back immediately. These neighboring pools were sustaining different demands without forcing either current to imitate the other.

A blue-coated expedition came out of a side passage on the eastern terraces, twenty or so of them, and Leon recognized the woman at the front before she had finished counting her people out of the tunnel. Orrin Vessian had the same short cropped hair and the same habit of looking at a place’s exits before she looked at anything else.
She saw him and raised a hand, and walked over along the terrace.
"I’d hoped we were first," she said.
"You’re second," Leon said.

"I can see that." She glanced at Tobin’s green coat and nodded to him as well. "We had a man at Asterbank market when the Steps started steaming. One of the old women there sells charms with that prophecy on them, and she told him the deep court opens when the steam leans east. We came round by the gorge. There’s an old door on that side too." She looked at the column of light and was quiet for a moment. "Well. This is a lot better than the mineral field."
"We’d like to keep it peaceful," said Leon.

"So would I." She said it without any fuss. At the mineral field, she had watched him deal with the Ashvard crew and then take exactly the share he’d agreed to and no more. She seemed to remember that. "Tell me what you’ve learned, and I’ll tell you what we’ve seen on the way in."
They traded at the edge of the terrace. Tobin read out the calendar, and Orrin wrote the thirteenth day on the back of her glove with charcoal.
The treasure wasn’t hard to find. Everyone in the hollow was looking at it within the hour.

It sat in a cradle of white stone at the foot of the central column, a crystal the size of Leon’s palm. Colors moved through it slowly, red into blue into green into gold, always moving, always circling a small clear point at its center that never changed at all.

The cradle had writing around its rim, and a diagram cut into the floor in front of it: a hand holding a small flame over the crystal, then the crystal held over a heap of stones, then a flame rising from the stones.
Tobin read the rim. "Give it a taste of what you want," he said. "Then feed it what you have."
"That’s all?" Leon asked.
Tobin ran a finger over the damaged lettering. "That’s all that’s left. The rest of the rim’s worn."

Leon studied the crystal with his senses before he touched it. The clear point at its center was neutral. Everything that came near it lost its character for a moment, like water losing its color in a still glass. Around that center, a ring of structure waited to be told what shape to make.
He looked at Tobin and then at Orrin. "I’m going to try it. Small."
"Be careful with it," said Orrin.
"I intend to be."
He lifted it out of the cradle. It was cool and heavier than it looked, and it did nothing at all. It just sat in his hand and waited.
He touched one fingertip to it and gave it a thread of fire, plain and controlled, the way he’d give a sample to an alchemist.
The colors stopped circling. Red spread through the outer ring and settled there, steady.
He took a lump of earth-heavy ore from his ring. He had plenty of earth fuel; fire was what he wanted for this trial. He set the ore beneath the crystal.

The ore grayed. Then it crumbled at the edges, slowly, and from the top of the crystal came a small, clean warmth that ran into his palm and up his wrist, and it was fire, plain fire, exactly the kind he had shown it.
Leon felt his breath go out of him.

He stopped halfway through the lump. By his estimate, roughly two-thirds of its available energy had emerged as fire. The rest had been lost during conversion. He would need other tests to learn how much the loss varied.
I can afford that.

He tried the second thing without putting the crystal down. He walked to the edge of the wind pool, lifted the crystal into its current, and waited. It took longer. The air around it thinned, a faint draft gathered toward his hand, and fire trickled out the top of the crystal, slower than before and weaker, but steady.
"It drinks from what’s around it," said Orrin.
Leon nodded. He couldn’t stop smiling.

Useful fuel no longer had to arrive in precisely the proportions his Scripture required. He could reshape a surplus instead of buying another rare material. The crystal worked gradually and lost energy in the process, but it could make resources he already owned serve a different branch.
I want this.
He lowered the crystal, still smiling. Tobin and Orrin were watching it with the same attention. Leon closed his fingers around the cool stone before either could reach for it.

The stair was wide enough for six people abreast.
Pale light moved far below, illuminating the outer wall and its five parallel channels.
He extended his senses carefully.
Fire, water, earth, wind, and lightning rose from a common depth, alongside light, cold, and living green energy.
He paused to distinguish the overlapping supplies.
Their separation persisted well beyond the court above.

"Now?"
