chapters.title: Chapter 735: A Year Before Morning
paragraphs: "I’m claiming the crystal," Leon said. "Tell me what you want in exchange."

Tobin considered him before answering. "Your observations from the terraces, and your support while the Hall copies the annex. Three days without another party driving us away." He glanced at the crystal. "I know what we’re conceding."
"You can have what I observed," Leon said. "Not the method I used to perceive it."
Tobin looked toward his companions, then nodded. "The observations, then."

Orrin claimed priority over the eastern sand and metal pools. Leon agreed to defend that arrangement against later arrivals while he remained here. She would handle her own harvest and guards during his seclusion. Their bargain gave both expeditions something worth keeping; neither mistook the crystal for a curiosity useful only to him.
"The other parties coming down will want their own share," Orrin said. "You understand that I mean those pools, not whatever is left after they’ve helped themselves?"
"I understand," Leon replied.

She studied his face, then offered her hand. He took it with the crystal still in his other palm. The exchange was uneven, and all three of them knew it. Tobin wanted time and access his Hall could use for years. Orrin had people to supply and a harvest she could carry home. Neither wanted to fight Leon for a stone he had already decided to keep.
He wasn’t inclined to persuade them otherwise.

Before leaving the cradle, Leon checked its connections. The source fed around the empty socket without faltering; removing the crystal had not interrupted a single pool. They filled sealed jars and stored saturated mineral beds from the western terraces. Then he chose an old cultivation cell with a heavy stone door.
He told Tobin and Orrin the household would be studying and cultivating inside for a while, and asked not to be disturbed until the next morning.
When the door had shut, he put his hand flat on its inner face.

Leon laid a small illusion over the door’s cracks and threshold, obscuring the seams through which someone might peer. Months of private practice had brought his Illusion to Rank 1 Aura. He settled the effect against the existing stone rather than presenting an elaborate false room, then checked it from both sides.
Loriel looked at the inside of the door, then at him. "That’s new."
"That’s private," said Leon, and she smiled.
The crystal went into his ring with the gathered supplies. A knock interrupted him before he opened the aperture.

It was Tobin’s voice, low through the door. "Leon. Sorry. One more thing." A pause. "One of my people came down from the old court. A runner from Asterbank reached our camp an hour ago. Mardoc Hollin was seen on the north road yesterday morning. He’s coming here."
"Who’s Mardoc Hollin?" asked Leon.

"Mardoc’s from the Graywater hills," Tobin said. "Half-step Earth Immortal. A runner saw him on the north road yesterday. He’d reach us tomorrow night on foot, but he can travel much faster. I wouldn’t count on the road giving you that long."
Leon looked toward the women. There was no need to explain why the crystal might interest such a man.
Nine outside hours. If we get them, that’s a year.
"Thank you," Leon told Tobin. "Send word if he arrives."
"We’ll check outside as we work," Leon told the women. "I want the whole Foundation section finished, but I won’t sit blind to what’s happening here."
Once the door was secured and the passage clear, he opened the aperture. Xyra met them on the grass inside his dimensional world.
"You’ve brought rather a lot," Xyra said, studying the jars and mineral beds coming out of his ring. Her attention lingered on the crystal. "Do you want the accelerated zone?"
"A thousand to one," Leon said. "Enough time for a year of work."
"Easily." Xyra walked across the grass and marked the edge of a localized zone. "You can use this area. The rest of the world will carry on at its usual pace."
"And I’ll check the outside room between sessions," Leon said.
Xyra nodded and stepped aside for them.

It was evening in the sanctuary. Nine outside hours would take them into the following morning, the fifth day since leaving the spring. Mardoc might arrive sooner; their pauses to check the cell and messages would count against that margin.
He crossed the line, and the four women came after him.

Leon set out twelve sanctuary jars and saturated stones beside their earlier harvest. Ira put her two selected Hearthseal specimens aside before the ordinary material was sorted for fuel. They had twenty-three boxes of Hearthseal, the comparison mixture Bai Heng had prepared, fresh supplies from several currents, and a way to convert them.
The crystal could draw from this world or the resources in front of him. It could not reach back through a closed aperture to the sanctuary. He divided the supply accordingly.
The first subjective month went into the common structure beneath his branches.

At the sanctuary, the pools had received different quantities at different rates. Their shared source did not have to absorb every fluctuation immediately. In his own Foundation, changes still reached the common center too abruptly.

His adjustments on the terraces had kept mild variations from interrupting circulation. Larger changes needed room to settle before the returns met. He began reshaping the areas around those junctions, testing each alteration at low volume.

For the first few days, having enough fuel made him careless. He increased two supplies together, pleased that neither ran short, and spent the rest of the session chasing disturbances through the Water return. By evening his notes described four possible causes. He could not tell which had started it.
He set the page aside without tearing it up. Ji would have asked why he had changed both at once, and he disliked how easily he could imagine her expression.
The next morning he measured one change at a time.
He let the crystal turn a lump of mixed ore into fire and run it into his fire branch, steadily, and watched what happened to the rest.
The fire came in hot and quick, the way fire liked to come. Water, beside it, slowed in sympathy. Earth, further away, barely noticed.
Let it settle before it reaches the others.

He spent six days forming a small holding space between one return and the shared center. Earth needed more room than fire. Lightning passed through quickly. He measured what happened instead of assuming matching shapes would produce matching behavior.

The first arrangement still wobbled. He widened the Earth holding space and tried again. Three days of clean circulation followed, including deliberate changes in supply. Water no longer slowed each time fire surged.

He checked it again while eating, with one hand around a bowl and his attention on Ira’s account of her latest trial. The return stayed steady when he stopped watching it. That small success pleased him almost as much as the previous three days.

Before beginning the next arrangement, he left the accelerated zone and opened a narrow aperture inside the locked cell. The sanctuary was quiet. He listened at the stone door, checked the passage, and returned to the others. Barely half an outside hour had passed; his first pile of discarded diagrams was already thick enough to slide off the table.
Leon set a fresh sheet beside the successful diagram. Keeping the first nine branches steady was only the beginning. The next drawing needed room for a route he had never built into that arrangement.
He left the center running and began.

chapters.title: Chapter 736: What They Made Their Own
paragraphs: Ira pushed the smaller Hearthseal specimen away. After a month of trials, she knew which one she wanted beside her when she condensed.

The egg-sized stone and the larger specimen still resting in its red mineral bed had spent weeks on a flat rock beside her practice area. Leon found her turning the larger one toward the evening light.
"The little one takes quickly and releases too sharply," Ira told him. "This one stores more evenly. It doesn’t waste nearly as much when I draw on it."
"Then you’ve chosen?" Leon asked.
"Yes. I’m keeping it beside me while I condense." She tapped the red bed. "I want to learn how it holds the heat. I don’t want my Core answering as slowly as the stone."
"You’ve been thinking about that since the Steps," Leon said.
"You asked what kind of fighter I wanted to become." Ira grinned at him. "I did listen."
She prepared the mineral as the manual instructed, trimming its surrounding bed without damaging the skin. Eleven days of precise work left the Hearthseal inside a thin protective shell.

When Ira began condensation, her Qi Sea resisted the pressure. She could have forced it smaller; that had never been the difficulty. Keeping its circulation responsive while the foundation platform drew inward required more patience.
She rested the Hearthseal against her lower abdomen, drawing measured warmth from it while its dense structure gave her a pattern to study.
Keep the heat. Keep the movement.

She compressed the sea and platform together in stages, allowing the developing Core Embryo to settle between them. The material beside her helped replenish what the long work consumed, but every adjustment inside the embryo remained hers.

Once, the warmth reached her faster than she expected. Her first impulse was to take it all. She had chosen the larger specimen for a reason, and letting good energy escape offended her almost as much as missing a clean strike.
She stopped her intake instead.

The embryo was already carrying as much as its unfinished route could move. More would only crowd it. She waited through the urge to push, feeling the circulation settle before accepting another measured thread.
I’ll hit harder when it’s ready.
That was easier to tell herself than to do. She did it anyway.
During the third week, she found the limit she had been looking for.

The dark-red embryo could take more compression. She tested a little and felt its response slow. There was greater density within reach, but a delay between intention and flame would cost her more than it gave.
She remembered the Hearthseal bed lifting free on the Steps and the speed she had needed to carry it out.
She eased off one degree.
The Embryo held. It turned. It stayed hot and quick under her hand, and when she touched it with her will it answered at once, without the delay she had felt before.
She circulated through the embryo once, then twice. On the third uninterrupted circuit, its structure crystallized around the path she had maintained.
Leon felt the change across the grass and looked up. Ira sat with both hands against her stomach, staring at something only she could sense.
Then she laughed, once, and put her face in her hands.
He went over and sat beside her and didn’t say anything. After a while she leaned sideways into his shoulder.
"It’s mine," she said into his coat. "Leon. It’s mine."
"I know," Leon said, resting his cheek against her hair.

"I didn’t let it get slow." She lifted her head. Her eyes were wet and she didn’t seem to mind. "I wanted to be the kind of fighter who holds it all in and lets it go exactly when she says. And I am. I can feel I am."
He touched her cheek with his thumb. She turned and kissed his palm, quickly, and then stood up, still holding his hand, and pulled him with her.
"Watch," she said.

She raised her other hand and opened it. A flame the size of a coin appeared above her palm, white at the heart. It didn’t flicker. It hung there, dense and quiet, and the grass a pace away began to curl brown from the heat.
She closed her hand, and it was gone at once, and the grass stopped curling.
"There," said Ira. "That’s the one I wanted."

By the fourth month, their practice area had acquired a table, a fire ring, and a little garden. Leon came back from checking the outside cell to find Loriel studying the wellheart leaves beside her notes.
"Still looking for the difference?" Leon asked, taking the opposite bench.
"I found it." Loriel turned a leaf to show him the fine veins beneath it.

"My vitality slows when I compress it this way," Loriel said, indicating her notes. "The wellheart holds it densely, but these small circuits keep feeding into larger ones. There’s movement throughout the structure."
"Can you use that?" Leon asked.
"I think so. I need to find the arrangement that suits me."
It took her six weeks.

She used a prepared cutting to study the effect while compressing her Qi Sea and foundation platform into their embryo. The smaller loops fed larger ones without abandoning the circulation between them. Leon checked on her and left her room to work.
Twice she stopped to correct a failure. One imbalance made the cutting root abruptly and then wilt. Another left her dizzy enough to require two days of rest. She recorded both before trying again.
Leon brought her food during those two days and found her staring at the failed cutting.
"Have you learned anything from glaring at it?" he asked.
Loriel looked up. "I fed the new growth before the older veins could sustain it. I thought it was responding well because the roots grew so quickly."
"And now?"
"Now I know what I missed." She moved the cutting beside her notes rather than throwing it away. "I wish it hadn’t needed to die for me to notice."
He put the bowl within reach. She ate while he stayed, then returned to the little drawing of veins that had kept her occupied all morning.
On the forty-third day of this work, a ring of grass and small white flowers spread around her feet.
It stopped a pace away. Loriel completed another circulation through the newly crystallized Core before opening her eyes.
"Early Golden Core," Loriel said, hoarse from the long silence. Then she smiled. "It kept moving. All the way through."

Later, after resting, she demonstrated on three seedlings. Each received a different measured flow: one barely stirred, one unfurled a leaf, and the third began to bud. She altered the last without disturbing either of the others.
"Now you’re showing off," Vyra said.
"Yes," Loriel admitted, pleased enough not to deny it.

She spent the following months consolidating, as Ira was doing with her own Core. Neither mistook first success for completed preparation. By the ninth month, both could sustain their new circulations through sleep and ordinary activity.
Leon later found Loriel watering the ordinary bellshade before either of the wellheart specimens.
"It still doesn’t do anything useful," she told him. "I still like it best." She moved aside to show him a new blue flower, and he stayed until she had finished watering it.

He would have liked another quiet afternoon there. Instead, he checked the time and went to inspect the room outside. Mardoc had already been on the road when they entered, and their private year was nearly over.

"The little one takes quickly and releases too sharply," Ira told him.
"This one stores more evenly.
It doesn’t waste nearly as much when I draw on it."
"Then you’ve chosen?" Leon asked.
"Yes.
I’m keeping it beside me while I condense." She tapped the red bed.
"I want to learn how it holds the heat.
I don’t want my Core answering as slowly as the stone."
"You’ve been thinking about that since the Steps," Leon said.
"You asked what kind of fighter I wanted to become." Ira grinned at him.
"I did listen."
She prepared the mineral as the manual instructed, trimming its surrounding bed without damaging the skin.
Eleven days of precise work left the Hearthseal inside a thin protective shell.
When Ira began condensation, her Qi Sea resisted the pressure.
She could have forced it smaller; that had never been the difficulty.
Keeping its circulation responsive while the foundation platform drew inward required more patience.
She rested the Hearthseal against her lower abdomen, drawing measured warmth from it while its dense structure gave her a pattern to study.
Keep the heat.
Keep the movement.
She compressed the sea and platform together in stages, allowing the developing Core Embryo to settle between them.
The material beside her helped replenish what the long work consumed, but every adjustment inside the embryo remained hers.
Once, the warmth reached her faster than she expected.
Her first impulse was to take it all.
She had chosen the larger specimen for a reason, and letting good energy escape offended her almost as much as missing a clean strike.
She stopped her intake instead.
The embryo was already carrying as much as its unfinished route could move.
More would only crowd it.
She waited through the urge to push, feeling the circulation settle before accepting another measured thread.
I’ll hit harder when it’s ready.
That was easier to tell herself than to do.
She did it anyway.
During the third week, she found the limit she had been looking for.
The dark-red embryo could take more compression.
She tested a little and felt its response slow.
There was greater density within reach, but a delay between intention and flame would cost her more than it gave.
She remembered the Hearthseal bed lifting free on the Steps and the speed she had needed to carry it out.
She eased off one degree.
The Embryo held.
It turned.
It stayed hot and quick under her hand, and when she touched it with her will it answered at once, without the delay she had felt before.
She circulated through the embryo once, then twice.
On the third uninterrupted circuit, its structure crystallized around the path she had maintained.
Leon felt the change across the grass and looked up.
Ira sat with both hands against her stomach, staring at something only she could sense.
Then she laughed, once, and put her face in her hands.
He went over and sat beside her and didn’t say anything.
After a while she leaned sideways into his shoulder.
"It’s mine," she said into his coat.
"Leon.
It’s mine."
"I know," Leon said, resting his cheek against her hair.
"I didn’t let it get slow." She lifted her head.
Her eyes were wet and she didn’t seem to mind.
"I wanted to be the kind of fighter who holds it all in and lets it go exactly when she says.
And I am.
I can feel I am."
He touched her cheek with his thumb.
She turned and kissed his palm, quickly, and then stood up, still holding his hand, and pulled him with her.
"Watch," she said.
She raised her other hand and opened it.
A flame the size of a coin appeared above her palm, white at the heart.
It didn’t flicker.
It hung there, dense and quiet, and the grass a pace away began to curl brown from the heat.
She closed her hand, and it was gone at once, and the grass stopped curling.
"There," said Ira.
"That’s the one I wanted."
By the fourth month, their practice area had acquired a table, a fire ring, and a little garden.
Leon came back from checking the outside cell to find Loriel studying the wellheart leaves beside her notes.
"Still looking for the difference?" Leon asked, taking the opposite bench.
"I found it." Loriel turned a leaf to show him the fine veins beneath it.
"My vitality slows when I compress it this way," Loriel said, indicating her notes.
"The wellheart holds it densely, but these small circuits keep feeding into larger ones.
There’s movement throughout the structure."
"Can you use that?" Leon asked.
"I think so.
I need to find the arrangement that suits me."
It took her six weeks.
She used a prepared cutting to study the effect while compressing her Qi Sea and foundation platform into their embryo.
The smaller loops fed larger ones without abandoning the circulation between them.
Leon checked on her and left her room to work.
Twice she stopped to correct a failure.
One imbalance made the cutting root abruptly and then wilt.
Another left her dizzy enough to require two days of rest.
She recorded both before trying again.
Leon brought her food during those two days and found her staring at the failed cutting.
"Have you learned anything from glaring at it?" he asked.
Loriel looked up.
"I fed the new growth before the older veins could sustain it.
I thought it was responding well because the roots grew so quickly."
"And now?"
"Now I know what I missed." She moved the cutting beside her notes rather than throwing it away.
"I wish it hadn’t needed to die for me to notice."
He put the bowl within reach.
She ate while he stayed, then returned to the little drawing of veins that had kept her occupied all morning.
On the forty-third day of this work, a ring of grass and small white flowers spread around her feet.
It stopped a pace away.
Loriel completed another circulation through the newly crystallized Core before opening her eyes.
"Early Golden Core," Loriel said, hoarse from the long silence.
Then she smiled.
"It kept moving.
All the way through."
Later, after resting, she demonstrated on three seedlings.
Each received a different measured flow: one barely stirred, one unfurled a leaf, and the third began to bud.
She altered the last without disturbing either of the others.
"Now you’re showing off," Vyra said.
"Yes," Loriel admitted, pleased enough not to deny it.
She spent the following months consolidating, as Ira was doing with her own Core.
Neither mistook first success for completed preparation.
By the ninth month, both could sustain their new circulations through sleep and ordinary activity.
Leon later found Loriel watering the ordinary bellshade before either of the wellheart specimens.
"It still doesn’t do anything useful," she told him.
"I still like it best." She moved aside to show him a new blue flower, and he stayed until she had finished watering it.
He would have liked another quiet afternoon there.
Instead, he checked the time and went to inspect the room outside.
Mardoc had already been on the road when they entered, and their private year was nearly over.

chapters.title: Chapter 737: A Foundation That Can Grow
paragraphs: Leon added another branch without dismantling the Foundation around it. This time, the rest of the circulation continued while the new return settled.

His work had continued alongside the women’s preparations. The first nine branches had given him a working basis, never a limit to his affinities. During the fifth month, he began testing small Metal and Wood routes alongside them, applying the same principles to different demands.

Metal favored a narrower passage in this arrangement; Wood required more room to distribute its flow. He worked through the adjustments and watched them for a fortnight. Then he changed their input while leaving the original branches active.

Adding them was easier than removing their supply. When he cut the Metal intake, the remaining flow drained toward the empty branch and unsettled the neighboring returns. He caught the imbalance before it hurt him, but had to stop that trial.

For several days he tried to support the branch with smaller quantities. That hid the problem without solving it. He would not always have the right material ready, even with the crystal working beside him.

He returned to the junction and changed how it accepted an inactive route. The passage could remain available without drawing the rest of the circulation toward it. When he tested the revised arrangement, he let Metal dwindle gradually, then cut its input outright. Both times the other branches continued.
He wrote the result down, smiled, and underlined it once.

The whole structure accommodated the addition. By the seventh month, he had finished the Foundation design and tested the revisions against the combinations available to him. Higher realms would impose different demands. He had finally completed the part he was cultivating now.
Then came cultivation, which was slower.

Ore and stored energy passed through the crystal and into his growing Foundation. His meridians strengthened around the new circulation. The Qi Sea deepened and the platform steadied beneath it. The native framework was becoming a better vessel for strength his body and Hearts already possessed.
At the start of the eighth month, he felt the shift. The platform settled into a new density, and the whole structure rose with it.
Late Foundation.
He didn’t stop. He kept the circulation running through the change, and that was the real test. It held.

Three more months of cultivation brought the sea, platform, meridians, and body into a stable harmony. He recognized the change during a morning session. The structure no longer felt as though its parts needed constant correction to support one another.
Peak Foundation Establishment.
He sat with the result long enough to enjoy it. Then he stood. He had several weeks left to test it before their planned year ended.
He began with the test he had failed on the Steps: walking through a change in supply without stopping to manage it.

He walked the edge of the accelerated area with the circulation running and changed what he fed it as he went. A handful of fire-converted ore, then nothing but what the air gave off, then a jar of sanctuary water. Each change rippled through the holding spaces and was absorbed. The center barely moved.
Then he drew his sword.

He practiced familiar sword movements while changing the native circulation beneath them. Wind gave way to lightning, then fire and space. His retained abilities had always been available; now the newly built Foundation supported those changes without the small interruptions that had annoyed him on the terraces.

Near the end, he ran fire and ice through the same cut using the revised native circulation. The center strained. He gave it his full attention and corrected the returns without stopping the movement.
It held.
Difficult is fine. I can practice difficult.
Seraphine waited at the edge of the practice area until he lowered his sword.
"You lifted your shoulder before the change," she said.
Leon glanced at it. "Did I?"
"Twice. You were concentrating on something inside."
She showed him the movement, small enough that he would have dismissed it from anyone else. In a fight, someone watching closely would have advance warning of when he meant to change his attack.
"Again?" he asked.
Seraphine drew her sword. "Until you stop telling me."

They kept the exchange controlled. She touched his shoulder with the flat three times before he learned to make the adjustment without preparing his whole body for it. When she finally missed the cue, he grinned at her and nearly lost the next exchange for being pleased with himself.

The Foundation section of the Formless Myriad Scripture was complete. It could take changing intake, unequal flows, and new combinations without being rebuilt each time. Golden Core would be another matter entirely, but this part was done.

Seraphine used the long interval to refine her existing Core. She practiced faster changes between lightning and light, then repeated them until they remained precise when she was tired. Near the end, she split a falling leaf into four pieces with successive cuts.
"Mid Golden Core is closer," she told Leon beside the fire. "I’m staying here until these transitions are as easy as the old ones."

Vyra gave the crystal a controlled fire sample from her cultivation and measured the output. It reproduced the elemental supply, not the will and technique that shaped her Crownfire. The loss was greater than in Leon’s first trial, but the result still gave her a useful way to prepare fuel. She set aside the four best Hearthseal stones Ira hadn’t used and studied the sanctuary observations for her own condensation.
"I know more clearly what I need now," Vyra told him. "I’m not going to rush the last part just because those two finished first."
On the last night, they ate together at the table under Vyra’s cloth.

The path between the table and Leon’s practice platform had worn into the grass. Loriel’s seedlings needed larger beds, and Ira had cut her hair twice. Eleven months and several weeks of shared work were visible wherever he looked.
Ira reached over and stole a piece of fruit from Leon’s plate, and he let her.

He had spent much of the year wanting to finish. Now he looked at the table, their mismatched cups, and the place Loriel had insisted they leave free for her flowers. They would carry everything away after breakfast. He found himself reaching for another piece of fruit simply to have a reason to sit there longer.
"A year," Seraphine said, looking around. "It felt like a year."
"It was a year," Loriel replied. "For us."
"Nine hours for everyone else," said Vyra. She stood. "And we should go back before someone opens that door."
They returned to the cell the following morning, roughly nine outside hours after entering. Leon checked the closed aperture before opening the stone door.
He stepped out onto the terrace and stopped.
The hollow had gone quiet. Tobin’s green coats were standing in a cluster near the stair, very still. Orrin’s blue coats were gathered at the eastern edge with their hands near their weapons.
Down on the central floor, at the foot of the column of light, an old man in gray was sitting on the empty white cradle, looking up at the terraces.
He was looking straight at Leon.

chapters.title: Chapter 738: The Man Who Would Take It
paragraphs: Tobin reached Leon before he had crossed the terrace, keeping his voice low.
"He came an hour ago," Tobin said. "Down the main stair. He walked to the cradle, saw it was empty, and sat down. He hasn’t said a word since." He swallowed. "That’s Mardoc Hollin."
"I knocked twice," Tobin added. "You didn’t answer. I wasn’t opening that door with him watching."
Leon looked down at the old man.

He was thin, with a short white beard and bare feet, and he wore a gray robe that had been mended so many times it was mostly patches. There was nothing remarkable about him at all, except that the column of light beside him bent, very slightly, away from where he sat.
The pressure was far beyond any of the foreign entrants. Tobin’s warning fit what Leon could feel: a cultivator at the edge of Earth Immortal advancement, with an enormous foundation beneath him.
Leon had spent a year testing his new circulation. Looking at the old man’s bare feet on the stone, he wished he had been given a less thorough first opponent.
"He’s strong," said Seraphine quietly, beside him.
"Yes," said Leon.
The old man stood up when they came down the last terrace. Leon came first, with the four women behind him in a loose line. The cultivators on the terraces above had gone silent.
"You have it," said Mardoc Hollin. His voice was dry and ordinary. "I can feel it on you."
"I have it," Leon said.

"I’ve waited sixty-one years for that door to open in my lifetime." He looked at the empty cradle. "I knew what was down here before your grandfather was born. I’ve gathered earth for half a century. Every vein in the Graywater hills. It’s not enough. It never will be. My path wants a stream my land doesn’t give." He looked back at Leon. "The stone turns what I have into what I need. With it, I can make the step."
"I know what it does," said Leon.

"Then you know why I want it." Mardoc held out his hand, palm up. "You’re a foreigner. You’ll be gone in two weeks. You’ll take it out of this realm, where it was made, and use it to grow a little faster at home." He said it without contempt, just as a fact. "I’m offering to let you go home."
Leon thought about the year of work, Ira’s Hearthseal, the jars Vyra had labeled, and every ration of ore he’d counted for months.
The crystal sat in his inner pocket, steady and warm.
"No," he said.
Mardoc didn’t seem surprised. "It’s not a request, boy."
"I didn’t think it was. It’s still no." Leon kept his voice level. "I found it. I learned to use it. It’s going to carry me a very long way. I’m keeping it."
Mardoc lowered his hand and pressed his bare heel into the floor. A crack opened beneath it.
The crack ran straight at Leon, and the stone on either side of it rose in two walls that slammed toward each other like jaws.
Leon stepped sideways out of it. The jaws met where he had been with a sound like a hill falling, and splinters of rock sprayed across the floor, toward the terraces, toward the people on them.

Ira’s flame met the first spray in the air. It was a narrow white thread, fast, and it took a piece of rock the size of a man’s head and burned it to grit before it reached the second terrace. A second piece. A third. She hadn’t moved from where she stood, and her hand barely moved either.
"Young Master!" Tobin, from somewhere above. "The east arcade! The visitors’ hall! The walls are three paces thick and there’s a stair to the annex!"
"Get everyone behind those walls," Leon called back.
"Blue coats, east!" That was Orrin, already moving. "Green coats follow me! Single file, stay off the open floor!"

They went. Leon heard them go, boots on stone, the scrape of someone being half-carried. A Hall disciple had been caught by a splinter in the thigh. Loriel was already beside him on the terrace, hands on the wound, and Leon saw the bleeding stop before she had finished kneeling.
"Young Master—" Seraphine began.
"I know," said Leon. "Go."
She went. Vyra went with her, a curtain of Crownfire unrolling along the base of the terraces behind them to catch whatever fell.

Leon spread his Illusion Aura along the inner court while the last witnesses withdrew. It followed the real walls, dust, and crossing currents, confusing the view through the remaining gaps. He left the enemy inside the concealment with him.

The deep elemental channels already muddled spiritual perception across the court. When Leon reached outward to check, Seraphine met his probe at the arcade and pressed it back. She and Vyra would keep the withdrawn cultivators from reaching their senses through that approach. The stone blocked direct sight; his illusion obscured what remained.
The witnesses would know a powerful fight was taking place. They would not see how he fought it.
Mardoc’s perception pushed through the edge of the illusion from inside. His eyes shifted toward the arcade, then back to Leon.
"A veil," said Mardoc. "For them, not me."
"For them," Leon said.

He could feel Seraphine waiting just beyond the last clear sightline. She had understood his order and obeyed it, but she wasn’t going to withdraw farther than she had to. He sent one brief pulse toward her, confirming that he was ready. Her answering pressure moved back toward the crowded stair.
He could not keep looking over his shoulder. That part was theirs.
"You’re hiding something," Mardoc observed.
"You didn’t come here to ask about my techniques."
The old man smiled for the first time. "True."
The floor came up under Leon.
He had expected the floor. He hadn’t expected all of it.

The entire inner ring of the hollow lifted under his feet like a wave. Leon stepped onto empty air and the wave followed him upward. He drew his sword and cut down into it with wind and lightning together, and the stone parted, and closed again around his blade.
The stone caught his blade for an instant. He tore it free before it could close around his wrist, and a brief memory of the forest struck him.

Qingyue had once stood between him and a threat he could not handle. He remembered his relief as clearly as his helpless anger. This time he had the strength to stay in the fight. He intended to use it.

He threw a fold of space between himself and the next wave. It struck the fold and slowed. It didn’t stop. The fold buckled. A second wave came behind it, and a third, all earth, all heavy, and all of it pressing on the same point.
The fold broke.
Leon was flung back across the hollow. He hit the base of the first terrace hard enough to crack it, felt the air go out of him, and came back up onto his feet with blood in his mouth.
Mardoc Hollin hadn’t moved from the cradle.
"You’re strong for a foreigner," the old man said. "You hide it well. It won’t be enough."
Leon spat red onto the stone and wiped his mouth with the back of his wrist.
His Foundation kept circulating despite the impact. He could still draw upon the strength of the Primordial Void Heart. The other Heart remained separate, its holy energy held back.
All right. Everything, then.

When Leon reached outward to check, Seraphine met his probe at the arcade and pressed it back.
She and Vyra would keep the withdrawn cultivators from reaching their senses through that approach.
The stone blocked direct sight; his illusion obscured what remained.
The witnesses would know a powerful fight was taking place.
They would not see how he fought it.
Mardoc’s perception pushed through the edge of the illusion from inside.
His eyes shifted toward the arcade, then back to Leon.
"A veil," said Mardoc.
"For them, not me."
"For them," Leon said.
He could feel Seraphine waiting just beyond the last clear sightline.
She had understood his order and obeyed it, but she wasn’t going to withdraw farther than she had to.
He sent one brief pulse toward her, confirming that he was ready.
Her answering pressure moved back toward the crowded stair.
He could not keep looking over his shoulder.
That part was theirs.
"You’re hiding something," Mardoc observed.
"You didn’t come here to ask about my techniques."
The old man smiled for the first time.
"True."
The floor came up under Leon.
He had expected the floor.
He hadn’t expected all of it.
The entire inner ring of the hollow lifted under his feet like a wave.
Leon stepped onto empty air and the wave followed him upward.
He drew his sword and cut down into it with wind and lightning together, and the stone parted, and closed again around his blade.
The stone caught his blade for an instant.
He tore it free before it could close around his wrist, and a brief memory of the forest struck him.
Qingyue had once stood between him and a threat he could not handle.
He remembered his relief as clearly as his helpless anger.
This time he had the strength to stay in the fight.
He intended to use it.
He threw a fold of space between himself and the next wave.
It struck the fold and slowed.
It didn’t stop.
The fold buckled.
A second wave came behind it, and a third, all earth, all heavy, and all of it pressing on the same point.
The fold broke.
Leon was flung back across the hollow.
He hit the base of the first terrace hard enough to crack it, felt the air go out of him, and came back up onto his feet with blood in his mouth.
Mardoc Hollin hadn’t moved from the cradle.
"You’re strong for a foreigner," the old man said.
"You hide it well.
It won’t be enough."
Leon spat red onto the stone and wiped his mouth with the back of his wrist.
His Foundation kept circulating despite the impact.
He could still draw upon the strength of the Primordial Void Heart.
The other Heart remained separate, its holy energy held back.
All right.
Everything, then.
